myth: 'Get the red out' eye drops are fine to use every day.
fact: Redness-relief drops work by narrowing blood vessels on the eye. Used often, the eye can become dependent on them, and redness can come back worse when they wear off (rebound redness).
explanation: They are meant only for occasional short-term use, and they do not treat the cause. Ongoing red eyes can be due to dry eye, allergies, infection or other problems that need different treatment. A red eye with pain, light sensitivity or blurred vision needs prompt medical attention.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Red eye drops

myth: 'Leaky gut syndrome' is behind most chronic illnesses and special supplements or diets can heal it.
fact: The gut lining does become more permeable in some diagnosed conditions, such as coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease. 'Leaky gut syndrome' as a cause of fatigue, autism, skin problems or most chronic illness is not a recognised diagnosis, and there is no reliable test or proven supplement to 'heal' it.
explanation: Researchers are studying gut permeability, but it is not yet clear whether it causes disease or is a result of it. Products marketed for leaky gut can be expensive and may delay proper diagnosis. Ongoing gut symptoms such as diarrhoea, weight loss or blood in your poo should be checked by a doctor.

sources.label: Harvard Health Publishing — Leaky gut: what is it, and what does it mean for you?

myth: "Light", "mild" or menthol cigarettes are safer than regular ones.
fact: "Light" and "mild" cigarettes are not safer. Smokers tend to inhale more deeply, take more puffs or block the filter vents, so they take in similar amounts of harmful chemicals. Menthol cigarettes are not safer either.
explanation: Many countries have banned the terms "light" and "mild" because they misled people. Stopping smoking completely is the best thing a smoker can do for their health, and support and stop-smoking medicines greatly increase the chance of success.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — "Light" cigarettes and cancer risk

myth: 5G mobile networks spread COVID-19 or cause its symptoms.
fact: Viruses cannot travel on radio waves or mobile networks. COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus and spreads between people, mainly through droplets and tiny particles in the air when an infected person breathes, talks, coughs or sneezes.
explanation: The rumour began in early 2020 because 5G was being rolled out at the same time as the pandemic, but COVID-19 also spread widely in countries with no 5G network at all. The radio waves used by mobile networks are low-energy and, at the levels allowed by international limits, have not been shown to harm health. Believing the myth can lead people to skip measures that really do reduce spread, such as vaccination, ventilation and staying home when ill.

sources.label: WHO — Radiation: 5G mobile networks and health

myth: A baby under 3 months old with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical advice.
fact: Health services advise getting urgent medical help for a baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher, even if they otherwise seem well. Very young babies can become seriously ill quickly and may not show other signs.
explanation: In older children, a fever on its own is usually a sign the body is fighting a common infection. Call an emergency number for any child who is floppy, hard to wake, has a rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass, or has difficulty breathing.

myth: A baby's heart rate above 140 beats a minute means it's a girl.
fact: Studies comparing heart rates of boys and girls in the womb have found no meaningful difference. A baby's heart rate changes with the stage of pregnancy and with the baby's activity, not with its sex.
explanation: A normal fetal heart rate is roughly 110 to 160 beats a minute and is faster in early pregnancy. Midwives listen to the heartbeat to check the baby's wellbeing, not to guess the sex. An ultrasound scan is the usual way to see the baby's sex.

myth: A cancer diagnosis is a death sentence.
fact: Survival rates for many cancers have improved greatly, and many cancers can be cured or controlled for years, especially when found early. Outcomes depend strongly on the type of cancer, its stage and the treatment available.
explanation: Fear of cancer can make people avoid seeing a doctor about symptoms or skip screening. Some cancers, such as many testicular, thyroid and early-stage breast cancers, have high survival rates. Getting checked early gives the best chance of successful treatment.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Common cancer myths and misconceptions

myth: A child with an ear infection always needs antibiotics.
fact: Most ear infections get better on their own within about 3 days, and antibiotics are often not needed. Many are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not treat.
explanation: Pain relief such as children's paracetamol or ibuprofen helps while the infection clears. Doctors may prescribe antibiotics if symptoms last longer, the child is very young or unwell, or there is fluid coming from the ear. Seek advice if symptoms do not improve after 3 days or the child seems very unwell.

myth: A contact lens can get lost behind your eye.
fact: A contact lens cannot slip behind the eye. A thin membrane (the conjunctiva) lines the inside of the eyelids and folds over onto the white of the eye, forming a closed pocket that stops anything from passing behind the eyeball.
explanation: A lens can move up under the upper eyelid and feel 'lost', especially after rubbing the eye. Rinsing with sterile saline or lens solution and gently massaging the closed lid usually brings it back into view. If you cannot find it and your eye is painful or red, see an optometrist or eye doctor.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Contact lens use
American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye myths

myth: A daily multivitamin prevents heart disease and cancer.
fact: Large studies have generally found that multivitamins do not prevent heart disease, cancer or early death in well-nourished people. Some groups do benefit from specific supplements, such as folic acid before and in early pregnancy.
explanation: Taking a multivitamin feels like an easy health insurance policy. A varied diet provides most nutrients for most people. People with specific needs, such as older adults, vegans, or those with absorption problems, may be advised to take particular supplements.

myth: A dark, quiet and cool bedroom helps you sleep better.
fact: A bedroom that is dark, quiet and comfortably cool is recommended as part of good sleep habits. The body's temperature naturally drops as you fall asleep, and light and noise can disturb sleep.
explanation: Blackout curtains, an eye mask, earplugs and keeping the room on the cool side can help. Other helpful habits include going to bed and waking at regular times and keeping the bedroom for sleep rather than work or screens.

sources.label: Sleep Foundation — Best temperature for sleep

myth: A drink before bed helps you sleep better.
fact: Alcohol may help you fall asleep faster, but it disrupts sleep later in the night, reduces sleep quality and can worsen snoring and sleep apnoea.
explanation: Because the first effect is drowsiness, many people believe it helps. As alcohol wears off, sleep becomes lighter and more broken. Using alcohol to sleep can also lead to dependence.

myth: A drink or two is a good way to calm anxiety.
fact: Alcohol may ease anxious feelings briefly, but as it wears off it can worsen anxiety and low mood and disrupt sleep. Relying on alcohol to cope can lead to a cycle where anxiety and drinking feed each other.
explanation: Health services suggest cutting down on alcohol as part of managing anxiety. Other approaches, such as exercise, breathing techniques, talking therapies and in some cases medicine, help in the longer term. If you find you need a drink to get through the day, talk to a GP.

sources.label: NHS — Generalised anxiety disorder in adults

myth: A fever fit (febrile seizure) causes brain damage or means the child has epilepsy.
fact: Febrile seizures are frightening to watch but are usually harmless. They do not cause brain damage, and most children who have them do not go on to develop epilepsy.
explanation: They are fairly common in children aged about 6 months to 5 years and are triggered by a rising temperature. During a seizure, place the child on their side on a soft surface and do not put anything in their mouth. Call an ambulance for a first seizure, one lasting more than 5 minutes, or if the child has trouble breathing or does not recover.

myth: A glass of fruit juice is just as healthy as eating whole fruit.
fact: Fruit juice contains some vitamins, but juicing removes most of the fibre and releases the sugars, which are easier to over-consume and can damage teeth. In the UK, juice and smoothies count as a maximum of one portion of your 5 A Day, limited to 150 ml a day.
explanation: Whole fruit is more filling and its fibre benefits digestion and heart health. If you drink juice, keep it to a small glass with a meal. Water and milk are better everyday drinks.

myth: A glass of red wine a day is good for your heart.
fact: Earlier observational studies suggested light drinkers had less heart disease, but more recent research suggests this was largely due to other differences between drinkers and non-drinkers. Health bodies do not recommend starting to drink for heart health.
explanation: Red wine contains compounds such as resveratrol, which are often credited with heart benefits, but the amounts are small. Alcohol raises blood pressure and the risk of irregular heart rhythms and several cancers. If you do drink, keeping within low-risk limits is advised.

myth: A gluten-free diet is healthier for everyone.
fact: A gluten-free diet is essential for people with coeliac disease, but there is no evidence that it benefits people who do not have coeliac disease or a gluten-related condition. Gluten-free processed products are often lower in fibre and can be higher in sugar or fat.
explanation: Some people feel better after cutting gluten, often because they also cut down on processed foods. If you suspect coeliac disease, get tested before going gluten-free, because the tests need you to be eating gluten to be accurate. Whole grains that contain gluten, such as wholewheat, barley and rye, provide fibre and nutrients.

myth: A heart attack always causes sudden, crushing chest pain.
fact: Chest pain or pressure is the most common symptom, but some people, more often women, older adults and people with diabetes, have milder or different symptoms such as shortness of breath, nausea, sweating, or pain in the arm, jaw, neck, back or stomach.
explanation: Films often show heart attacks as dramatic collapses, so people may wait if symptoms seem mild. Any suspected heart attack is an emergency: call your local emergency number straight away. Do not drive yourself to hospital.

sources.label: American Heart Association — Warning signs of a heart attack

myth: A heart attack and a cardiac arrest are the same thing.
fact: A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart muscle is blocked; the person is usually awake and may have chest pain. A cardiac arrest is when the heart suddenly stops pumping effectively; the person collapses, is unresponsive and is not breathing normally.
explanation: A heart attack can lead to a cardiac arrest. For a suspected heart attack, call an ambulance. For a cardiac arrest, call an ambulance, start CPR straight away and use a defibrillator (AED) if one is available.

myth: A home IgG blood test can tell you which foods you're intolerant to.
fact: IgG antibodies to foods are a normal response to eating them and do not show intolerance or allergy. There is no reliable test for most food intolerances; the usual approach is to keep a food and symptom diary and try cutting out a suspected food under guidance.
explanation: These tests often list many everyday foods, leading people to cut out large parts of their diet unnecessarily, which can cause nutritional problems, especially in children. Food allergies are diagnosed differently, with skin-prick or specific IgE blood tests interpreted by a doctor. Coeliac disease also has its own specific tests.

myth: A home-made mix of garlic, lemon, ginger, apple cider vinegar and honey unclogs blocked arteries.
fact: No food or drink mixture has been shown to clear blockages from arteries. Fatty plaques in artery walls build up over many years and are not dissolved by home remedies.
explanation: This recipe is often shared as an alternative to heart surgery or angioplasty. A heart-healthy diet, not smoking, exercise and medicines such as statins can slow or stabilise plaque and lower the risk of heart attacks. Never stop prescribed heart medicines in favour of a home remedy.

myth: A juice cleanse is a healthy way to detox and kick-start weight loss.
fact: There is no good evidence that juice cleanses or 'detox' programmes remove toxins or lead to lasting weight loss. Any quick drop on the scales is mostly water and food in the gut, and it usually comes back once normal eating resumes.
explanation: Your liver, kidneys and gut already clear waste products from the body. Juice-only plans are low in protein and fibre, can be high in sugar, and may cause problems for people with kidney disease or diabetes. A steady, balanced eating pattern does more for weight and health than a few days of juice.

sources.label: NCCIH — "Detoxes" and "cleanses": what you need to know

myth: A liver or gallbladder 'flush' with olive oil and lemon juice makes you pass your gallstones.
fact: There is no good evidence that 'flushes' remove gallstones. The green 'stones' people pass afterwards are thought to be lumps formed from the oil and digestive juices in the gut, not real gallstones.
explanation: Gallstones that cause no symptoms often need no treatment. Gallstones that cause repeated pain are usually treated with keyhole surgery to remove the gallbladder. Severe tummy pain with a high temperature or yellowing skin or eyes needs urgent medical help.

sources.label: NCCIH — "Detoxes" and "cleanses": what you need to know

myth: A lump that doesn't hurt can't be cancer.
fact: Many cancerous lumps are painless, especially early on. Any new lump or swelling that does not go away should be checked by a doctor, whether or not it hurts.
explanation: Most lumps turn out not to be cancer, but getting them checked is the only way to know. Cancers found early are usually easier to treat. Other signs worth checking include unexplained weight loss, unusual bleeding and changes to moles.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Symptoms of cancer

myth: A mole that changes in size, shape or colour should be checked by a doctor.
fact: A new mole, or a mole that changes in size, shape or colour, bleeds, itches or becomes crusty, can be a sign of melanoma skin cancer and should be checked by a GP. Most changes turn out not to be cancer, but melanoma is much more treatable when found early.
explanation: Melanoma can appear anywhere on the body, including areas that don't get much sun, such as the soles of the feet and under the nails. Checking your skin regularly and taking photos can help you notice changes. Avoiding sunburn and sunbeds lowers your risk.

myth: A mouth ulcer that won't heal is nothing to worry about.
fact: Most mouth ulcers clear up on their own within a week or two. But an ulcer that lasts longer than 3 weeks should be checked by a dentist or GP, because a persistent ulcer can occasionally be a sign of mouth cancer.
explanation: Common causes of ordinary ulcers include biting the cheek, sharp teeth, stress and some foods. A pharmacist can suggest mouthwashes or gels to ease pain. Also get checked if an ulcer is unusually large, keeps coming back, or you have a red or white patch or lump in the mouth.

myth: A puffy 'cortisol face' or belly fat means your cortisol is too high and you need a cortisol detox or supplements.
fact: A rounder face or fat around the middle is very common and is usually down to weight gain, genes, age, fluid, sleep or alcohol, not a hormone problem. Truly high cortisol (Cushing's syndrome) is uncommon, has other signs as well, and is diagnosed with medical tests, not by looking in a mirror.
explanation: Social media trends that label normal faces and bodies as 'cortisol face' often lead on to selling supplements or 'cortisol cocktails' that have not been shown to lower cortisol. Cushing's syndrome is most often caused by long-term steroid medicines; other signs can include purple stretch marks, thin skin that bruises easily, and muscle weakness. If you are worried, a GP can arrange proper tests. Day-to-day stress management, sleep and activity are good for health, but no product 'flushes out' cortisol.

myth: A red face from rosacea means the person drinks too much alcohol.
fact: The cause of rosacea is not known, and many people with it drink little or no alcohol. Alcohol is one of several things that can trigger flare-ups, along with spicy food, hot drinks, sunlight, temperature changes, exercise and stress.
explanation: This assumption can be hurtful. Rosacea is a common long-term skin condition that causes flushing, redness and sometimes spots, mainly on the face. Avoiding personal triggers, sun protection and prescription treatments can help, so it's worth seeing a GP.

myth: A shot of brandy or whisky will warm up someone who is very cold.
fact: Alcohol makes you feel warmer by widening blood vessels near the skin, but this actually increases heat loss from the body. Someone who may have hypothermia should not be given alcohol.
explanation: Move the person somewhere warm, remove wet clothing, wrap them in blankets and give warm, non-alcoholic drinks and sugary food if they are fully alert. Don't rub their arms and legs or put them in a hot bath. Hypothermia is a medical emergency, so call for help.

myth: A slipped disc means a disc has slipped out of place and must be pushed back in.
fact: A 'slipped' disc does not actually slip. The soft cushion of tissue between the bones of the spine bulges outwards, and it is painful if it presses on a nerve. It cannot be manipulated back into place.
explanation: Most slipped discs get better on their own within weeks to months. Keeping active, gentle exercise and pain relief help; physiotherapy may be offered, and surgery is only needed for a few people. Seek urgent help for numbness around the bottom or genitals or loss of bladder or bowel control.

myth: A small dog or cat bite doesn't need medical attention if it isn't bleeding much.
fact: Animal and human bites that break the skin can easily become infected, even when the wound looks small. Health services advise cleaning the bite straight away and getting medical advice, as antibiotics or a tetanus jab may be needed.
explanation: Cat bites are especially likely to become infected because their teeth make deep, narrow punctures. Bites from animals abroad may carry a risk of rabies and need urgent advice. Watch for signs of infection such as redness, swelling, warmth, pus or fever.

myth: A smear test checks for ovarian cancer, womb cancer and STIs.
fact: Cervical screening (a smear test) checks for high-risk HPV and for changes in the cells of the cervix that could turn into cervical cancer. It does not test for ovarian or womb cancer or for sexually transmitted infections.
explanation: This means a normal smear result does not rule out other conditions. Symptoms such as persistent bloating, bleeding after the menopause, bleeding between periods or after sex should be checked by a GP even if your screening is up to date. STI testing is available separately from sexual health services.

myth: A sore throat always needs antibiotics.
fact: Most sore throats are caused by viruses and get better on their own within about a week. Antibiotics do not help viral infections and are only needed for some bacterial throat infections.
explanation: Pain relief, warm or cold drinks and gargling with salty water (for adults) can ease symptoms. See a doctor urgently if you have difficulty swallowing or breathing, drooling, a muffled voice, or a very high temperature, or if the sore throat does not improve.

myth: A special detox or 30-day programme can cure type 2 diabetes for good.
fact: There is no detox, juice, tea or short programme that permanently cures type 2 diabetes. Some people can bring blood sugar back to a normal range through significant weight loss, which is called remission, but it needs to be maintained and checked.
explanation: Programmes promising a cure often sell supplements or expensive plans and may encourage people to stop their medicines, which can be dangerous. If you want to try for remission, do it with your doctor or diabetes team so your medicines can be adjusted safely.

myth: A twitching eyelid is a sign of a serious brain or nerve problem.
fact: Eyelid twitching (myokymia) is very common and almost always harmless. It is often linked to tiredness, stress, caffeine, alcohol or eye strain, and usually goes away on its own.
explanation: Rest, cutting down on caffeine and managing stress can help. See a doctor if twitching lasts for weeks, the eyelid closes completely, other parts of the face twitch, or there is drooping or weakness, as these can be signs of other conditions.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eyelid twitching

myth: A vasectomy will lower your sex drive or affect your erections.
fact: A vasectomy does not affect testosterone, sex drive, erections or the amount of fluid ejaculated in any noticeable way.
explanation: The procedure only blocks the tubes that carry sperm. It is meant to be permanent, so it is important to be sure before having it.

myth: A vasectomy works immediately.
fact: After a vasectomy, sperm can remain in the tubes for some time. Other contraception is needed until a semen test confirms there is no sperm.
explanation: This usually takes a couple of months. Skipping the follow-up test is a common reason for unexpected pregnancy after vasectomy.

myth: Acne is caused by dirty skin and not washing enough.
fact: Acne is not caused by poor hygiene. Washing too often or scrubbing hard can actually irritate the skin and make acne worse.
explanation: Blackheads look dark because of a chemical reaction with air, not dirt. Gentle washing twice a day and non-comedogenic products are usually recommended.

myth: Adding cereal to a baby's bottle helps them sleep through the night.
fact: Adding cereal to bottles does not reliably improve sleep and can increase the risk of choking and overfeeding.
explanation: Babies sleep longer as they grow, regardless of cereal. Solid foods are generally introduced around six months, by spoon, unless a health professional advises otherwise.

myth: ADHD isn't real; it's just bad behaviour or bad parenting.
fact: ADHD is a well-studied neurodevelopmental condition affecting attention, activity and impulse control. It is not caused by bad parenting, though a supportive environment helps.
explanation: ADHD is strongly influenced by genetics and often continues into adulthood. Diagnosis needs a careful assessment, and treatment can include behavioural support, education adjustments and medication.

myth: ADHD only affects children; adults grow out of it.
fact: ADHD often continues into adulthood, although hyperactivity may become less obvious and show more as restlessness, disorganisation or difficulty focusing. Many adults are diagnosed for the first time later in life.
explanation: Adults with ADHD may struggle with time management, work, relationships or impulsive decisions, and may have spent years being called lazy or careless. Treatment, which can include medicine, talking therapy and practical strategies, can help at any age.

myth: Adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening on two days.
fact: WHO and national health services recommend that adults do at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, a week, plus muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days. Some activity is better than none.
explanation: Moderate activity includes brisk walking, cycling or dancing; vigorous activity, such as running or swimming fast, makes it hard to say more than a few words. Activity can be spread across the week in whatever chunks suit you. Reducing long periods of sitting also helps.

sources.label: NHS — Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64

myth: After a head injury, you must keep the person awake all night.
fact: It is fine to let someone sleep after a minor head injury if they are alert, behaving normally and have no worrying symptoms, but a responsible adult should stay with them for the first 24 hours. Worrying signs, such as being hard to wake, repeated vomiting or confusion, need emergency care.
explanation: The old advice to keep people awake came from fear that drowsiness hides a brain bleed. The key is watching for warning signs rather than preventing sleep. Seek urgent help after any head injury with loss of consciousness, a seizure, clear fluid from the nose or ears, or worsening headache.

myth: After a heart attack you should avoid exercise for the rest of your life.
fact: Gradually returning to physical activity is an important part of recovering from a heart attack. Cardiac rehabilitation programmes offer supervised exercise, education and support, and they lower the risk of another heart attack.
explanation: How quickly you can increase activity depends on your heart and should be guided by your care team. Most people can return to normal activities, including work and sex, over a period of weeks. Stop and seek help if you have chest pain, severe breathlessness or dizziness during activity.

myth: After laser eye surgery you'll never need glasses again.
fact: Laser eye surgery can correct short-sightedness, long-sightedness and astigmatism for many people, but it does not stop age-related changes. Most people will still need reading glasses as they get older, usually from their 40s.
explanation: Some people also need a touch-up procedure or glasses for certain tasks such as night driving. Not everyone is suitable for laser surgery, and it carries risks such as dry eyes and glare. A careful assessment with a surgeon helps set realistic expectations.

sources.label: NHS — Laser eye surgery and lens surgery

myth: After using an adrenaline pen (EpiPen), you don't need to go to hospital if you feel better.
fact: Anyone who has used an adrenaline auto-injector for anaphylaxis should call emergency services and be checked in hospital, even if they feel better. Symptoms can return after the adrenaline wears off.
explanation: Feeling better quickly after adrenaline can make people think the danger has passed. A second reaction can happen hours later, and a second dose may be needed if symptoms do not improve after 5 minutes. Lie down with legs raised, or sit up if breathing is difficult.

myth: Air pollution increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes.
fact: Yes. Long-term and short-term exposure to air pollution, especially fine particles, increases the risk of heart disease, stroke and other illnesses, as well as lung disease.
explanation: Fine particles can reach the bloodstream and cause inflammation and damage to blood vessels. People with existing heart or lung disease are most at risk. On high-pollution days, reducing time spent exercising near busy roads may help, and cleaner household fuels reduce indoor pollution.

sources.label: WHO — Ambient (outdoor) air pollution and health

myth: Alkaline water balances your body's pH and makes you healthier.
fact: Your body tightly controls blood pH through the lungs and kidneys, and drinking alkaline water does not change it in a meaningful way. There is no good evidence that alkaline water offers health benefits over ordinary safe drinking water.
explanation: Alkaline water is marketed with claims about neutralising acidity, boosting energy and preventing disease. Stomach acid neutralises much of what you drink anyway. Staying hydrated with tap water, where it is safe, is just as good and cheaper.

myth: All vaccines contain pork, so they are forbidden for Muslims and Jews.
fact: Most vaccines contain no pork products. A few, such as the children's nasal flu spray and one brand of MMR vaccine, contain highly purified porcine gelatine as a stabiliser, and alternatives without gelatine are often available.
explanation: If this matters to you, ask the nurse or doctor which brand is being used and whether a gelatine-free option exists, for example a flu injection instead of the nasal spray. Many religious scholars have said that vaccines are acceptable because they protect life. Missing vaccines leaves children open to serious diseases such as measles.

sources.label: NHS — MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine

myth: Allergy immunotherapy (desensitisation) can reduce allergies in the long term.
fact: For some allergies, such as severe hay fever, insect venom allergy and some others, immunotherapy can lessen the body's reaction over time. It involves gradually giving small, increasing amounts of the allergen as injections or tablets under the tongue.
explanation: Treatment usually lasts several years and is given or started under specialist supervision because it can cause reactions. It is generally offered when other treatments have not worked well enough. It is not a quick cure, and not every allergy can be treated this way.

myth: Aluminium pans and cans cause Alzheimer's disease.
fact: Research has not shown that everyday exposure to aluminium from cookware, cans or antiperspirants causes Alzheimer's disease.
explanation: The idea came from studies in the 1960s and 1970s that later research did not support. Main risk factors for Alzheimer's are age, genetics and cardiovascular risk factors.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Alzheimer's and dementia are the same thing.
fact: Dementia is an umbrella term for a group of symptoms caused by different diseases that damage the brain. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia, but there are others, such as vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia.
explanation: The type matters because symptoms, progress and treatment can differ. For example, some medicines help Alzheimer's symptoms but are not suitable for every type. Many people have more than one type at once (mixed dementia).

myth: Alzheimer's can be cured or reversed with coconut oil, special diets or supplements.
fact: There is currently no cure for Alzheimer's disease, and no diet or supplement has been shown to reverse it. Medicines can help relieve some symptoms for a time, and newer treatments may slow progression in some people at an early stage.
explanation: Claims about coconut oil and other 'cures' are based on personal stories rather than good-quality trials. A healthy diet is good for overall health but is not a treatment. Support for people with dementia and their carers can make a real difference to quality of life.

myth: Amber teething necklaces ease teething pain by releasing a natural painkiller.
fact: There is no reliable evidence that amber necklaces or bracelets relieve teething pain. Regulators such as the US FDA warn against teething jewellery because babies can choke on the beads or be strangled by the cord.
explanation: The claim is that skin warmth releases succinic acid from the amber, but this has not been shown to happen in a way that affects pain. Safer ways to soothe teething include a clean, chilled (not frozen) teething ring, rubbing the gums with a clean finger and, if needed, an age-appropriate dose of infant paracetamol or ibuprofen.

sources.label: FDA — Safely soothing teething pain in infants and children
NHS — Tips for helping your teething baby

myth: An alkaline diet or alkaline water can cure cancer because cancer cannot survive in an alkaline body.
fact: Food and drink cannot meaningfully change the pH of your blood, which the body keeps in a narrow range. There is no evidence that alkaline diets or alkaline water prevent or treat cancer.
explanation: The claim distorts laboratory findings that the area immediately around tumours can be acidic. What you eat can change the acidity of your urine, but not of your blood or tumours. Alkaline diets often include lots of fruit and vegetables, which are healthy, but they are not a cancer treatment.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Common cancer myths and misconceptions

myth: An all-meat carnivore diet is the healthiest way to eat.
fact: There is no good evidence that an all-meat diet is healthy in the long term. Diets rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, pulses and nuts are consistently linked with lower risks of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers.
explanation: A carnivore diet lacks fibre and many vitamins and plant compounds, and it is often high in saturated fat, which can raise LDL cholesterol. Eating a lot of red and processed meat is linked to a higher risk of bowel cancer. Short-term weight loss on any very restrictive diet does not prove it is healthy.

myth: An antihistamine tablet is enough to treat a severe allergic reaction.
fact: Anaphylaxis is a medical emergency that needs adrenaline and emergency care. Antihistamines can ease mild symptoms like itching or hives but do not treat the life-threatening breathing and circulation problems of anaphylaxis.
explanation: People sometimes delay using an adrenaline pen while waiting to see whether an antihistamine works, which can be dangerous. Signs of anaphylaxis include swelling of the throat or tongue, difficulty breathing, wheezing, dizziness or collapse. If in doubt, use adrenaline and call emergency services.

myth: An ectopic pregnancy can be moved into the womb so it can continue.
fact: There is no medical procedure that can move an ectopic pregnancy into the womb. An ectopic pregnancy, usually in a fallopian tube, cannot survive, and it can cause life-threatening bleeding if left to grow, so it needs treatment.
explanation: Treatment may be careful monitoring, medicine (methotrexate) or keyhole surgery, depending on the situation. Symptoms can include one-sided tummy pain, vaginal bleeding and shoulder-tip pain; sudden severe pain or collapse is an emergency. Many people go on to have healthy pregnancies afterwards.

myth: An enlarged prostate is an early stage of prostate cancer.
fact: An enlarged prostate (benign prostatic enlargement) is not cancer and does not turn into cancer. It is very common in men over 50 and can cause symptoms such as a weak flow, needing to pee often and getting up at night.
explanation: Because prostate cancer can cause similar urinary symptoms, it is important to get them checked by a GP rather than assume the cause. Enlarged prostate symptoms can often be helped with lifestyle changes, medicines or, sometimes, surgery.

myth: An irregular or fluttering heartbeat is never anything serious.
fact: Many palpitations are harmless, but an irregular heartbeat can be a sign of atrial fibrillation, which greatly increases the risk of stroke and can be treated.
explanation: Get your heartbeat checked if it often feels irregular, fast or fluttery. Get urgent help if palpitations come with chest pain, breathlessness, fainting or dizziness. Atrial fibrillation is often treated with medicines to control the heart rate and blood thinners to prevent stroke.

myth: Anabolic steroids are safe if you 'cycle' them and use them sensibly.
fact: Using anabolic steroids without medical need can cause serious side effects, including heart and liver problems, high blood pressure, infertility, shrunken testicles, breast growth in men, severe acne, mood changes and dependence. 'Cycling', 'stacking' or extra drugs do not make them safe.
explanation: Many people who use steroids believe they can manage the risks, but there is no proven safe way to use them for muscle building. Products bought illegally may contain unknown substances, and injecting carries infection risks. Confidential support is available from GPs and drug services.

myth: Animal dewormers like fenbendazole or ivermectin cure cancer.
fact: Fenbendazole and ivermectin have not been shown in clinical trials to cure cancer in people. Results from cells in a lab dish or from personal stories are not evidence that a drug works or is safe in patients.
explanation: Taking livestock products or high doses of antiparasitic drugs can cause side effects, including liver damage, and they may interact with cancer treatment. Some drugs are being studied in research, but anyone considering them should talk to their cancer team rather than stopping proven treatment.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Complementary and alternative medicine
FDA — Products claiming to "cure" cancer are a cruel deception

myth: Antibacterial soap protects you better than ordinary soap.
fact: There is no evidence that antibacterial soaps sold for home use prevent illness better than plain soap and water. In the US, the FDA banned several antibacterial ingredients, including triclosan, from consumer hand washes in 2016 because manufacturers had not shown they were safe and more effective.
explanation: Labels saying 'kills 99.9% of germs' make antibacterial products seem stronger. Plain soap works mainly by washing germs away, which is effective. Some antibacterial chemicals raised concerns about contributing to resistance.

sources.label: FDA — Antibacterial soap? You can skip it

myth: Antibiotic resistance is a problem for the distant future, not today.
fact: Antimicrobial resistance is already causing deaths around the world today. Infections such as pneumonia, urinary tract infections, gonorrhoea and tuberculosis are becoming harder, and sometimes impossible, to treat with standard antibiotics.
explanation: Resistance makes surgery, cancer treatment and childbirth riskier, because they depend on antibiotics to prevent and treat infections. Everyone can help by using antibiotics only when prescribed, taking them as directed and never sharing them, and by preventing infections through vaccination and hygiene.

myth: Antibiotics can treat colds and the flu.
fact: Colds and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only work against bacteria. Taking antibiotics for viral infections is ineffective and fuels antibiotic resistance.
explanation: Most colds, flu and sore throats are caused by viruses and get better on their own. Using antibiotics when they are not needed can cause side effects and makes bacteria more resistant, so antibiotics may not work when they are really needed.

myth: Antibiotics only kill the bad bacteria.
fact: Antibiotics also affect the helpful bacteria in your gut, skin and elsewhere. This is why they can cause diarrhoea and thrush, and in some cases a serious gut infection called Clostridioides difficile.
explanation: Antibiotics target features common to many bacteria, not just harmful ones. Most side effects are mild and settle after the course ends. Severe or bloody diarrhoea during or after antibiotics should be checked by a doctor.

myth: Antidepressants are addictive like drugs.
fact: Antidepressants do not cause craving or the compulsive use seen with addictive drugs. However, stopping them suddenly can cause discontinuation (withdrawal) symptoms, so doses should be reduced gradually with a doctor.
explanation: The worry is understandable because discontinuation symptoms such as dizziness, irritability or flu-like feelings are real for some people and can occasionally be long-lasting. That is different from addiction. Never stop an antidepressant abruptly without medical advice.

myth: Antidepressants change who you are and turn you into a zombie.
fact: Antidepressants are meant to relieve symptoms of depression or anxiety, not alter personality. Some people do notice side effects such as emotional numbness, which can often be managed by adjusting the dose or medicine.
explanation: When treatment works, people often say they feel more like themselves again. If a medicine makes you feel flat or unlike yourself, tell your prescriber rather than stopping suddenly.

myth: Antioxidant supplements protect you from cancer.
fact: Clinical trials have not shown that antioxidant supplements prevent cancer. In some trials, beta-carotene supplements increased lung cancer risk in smokers, and vitamin E supplements were linked to a higher risk of prostate cancer.
explanation: Antioxidants in foods like fruit and vegetables are part of a healthy diet, which led to the assumption that concentrated pills would help even more. The effects of isolated, high-dose supplements can differ from those of whole foods. People having cancer treatment should check with their care team before taking antioxidants.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Antioxidants and cancer prevention

myth: Antiperspirants and deodorants cause breast cancer.
fact: Studies have not found a link between using antiperspirants or deodorants and breast cancer. Claims about aluminium or parabens from these products causing cancer are not supported by research.
explanation: This rumour spread by email for decades, partly because many breast cancers start near the armpit. The upper outer part of the breast simply contains more breast tissue. Being aware of how your breasts normally look and feel and attending screening when invited are proven steps.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Common cancer myths and misconceptions

myth: Any fever in a child is dangerous and must be brought down immediately.
fact: Fever is a normal response to infection and is usually not harmful in itself. Treating fever is mainly for comfort; how the child is behaving matters more than the number.
explanation: Babies under three months with a temperature of 38C or above, and children with signs such as a rash that does not fade, drowsiness, breathing difficulty or a fit, need urgent medical help. Febrile seizures can be frightening but rarely cause lasting harm.

myth: Any vaginal discharge means you have an infection.
fact: Vaginal discharge is normal and helps keep the vagina clean and healthy. The amount and texture change during the menstrual cycle, in pregnancy and with hormonal contraception.
explanation: Discharge may be a sign of infection if it changes colour, smell or consistency, or comes with itching, soreness or pain. Thrush, bacterial vaginosis and some sexually transmitted infections can all change discharge and are treatable. Washing inside the vagina or using scented products can make problems more likely.

myth: Apple cider vinegar cures diabetes.
fact: There is no evidence that apple cider vinegar cures diabetes. Some small studies suggest vinegar may slightly lower blood sugar after a meal, but the effect is modest and not a replacement for treatment.
explanation: Apple cider vinegar is promoted online for many conditions, often based on small or short studies. Drinking it undiluted can damage tooth enamel and irritate the throat, and it may affect potassium levels or interact with some medicines. Anyone with diabetes should keep taking prescribed treatment.

myth: Apricot kernels or 'vitamin B17' (laetrile) cure cancer.
fact: Laetrile, sold as 'vitamin B17', is not a vitamin and has not been shown to treat cancer in clinical studies. Apricot kernels and laetrile can release cyanide in the body and have caused serious poisoning.
explanation: Laetrile was promoted as a natural cancer cure from the 1950s onward and still circulates on social media. A clinical trial sponsored by the US National Cancer Institute found no benefit. Signs of cyanide poisoning include headache, dizziness, nausea and confusion, and need urgent medical care.

myth: Artificial trans fats are bad for your heart.
fact: Yes. Industrially produced trans fats, made by partially hydrogenating vegetable oils, raise LDL cholesterol and lower HDL cholesterol, increasing the risk of heart disease and death. The WHO has called for them to be eliminated from the food supply.
explanation: They have been used in some margarines, vanaspati and other hydrogenated cooking fats, fried foods, baked goods and snacks. Many countries now ban or limit them. Check labels for "partially hydrogenated" oils where they are still allowed.

myth: Ashwagandha is a natural herb, so it's safe for everyone to take.
fact: Ashwagandha may cause drowsiness and stomach upset, and rare cases of liver injury have been linked to it. It should be avoided in pregnancy and while breastfeeding, and it is not recommended for people with thyroid or autoimmune conditions or before surgery.
explanation: It may interact with medicines for diabetes, high blood pressure, thyroid problems, epilepsy and with sedatives and immunosuppressants. Some studies suggest possible benefits for stress or sleep, but the evidence is limited and long-term safety is not well known.

myth: Asking someone if they are thinking about suicide puts the idea in their head.
fact: Research shows that asking directly about suicide does not increase suicidal thoughts and may reduce distress. It can open the door to getting help.
explanation: Many people fear that raising the subject will make things worse, so they say nothing. A calm, caring question gives the person permission to talk. If someone is in immediate danger, call your local emergency number or a crisis line and stay with them.

myth: Aspartame and diet drinks give you cancer.
fact: In 2023 a WHO cancer agency classed aspartame as "possibly carcinogenic", based on limited evidence. At the same time, a WHO and FAO expert committee kept the acceptable daily intake unchanged, meaning normal consumption is considered safe.
explanation: The acceptable daily intake is 40 mg per kg of body weight a day, which for most adults is far more than they would get from a few cans of diet drink. "Possibly carcinogenic" reflects uncertainty in the evidence, not proof that aspartame causes cancer. Research is continuing.

sources.label: WHO — Aspartame hazard and risk assessment results released
National Cancer Institute — Artificial sweeteners and cancer
FDA — Aspartame and other sweeteners in food

myth: Asthma inhalers are addictive, and steroid inhalers are dangerous.
fact: Asthma inhalers are not addictive. Inhaled steroids (preventers) deliver low doses directly to the airways and are safe and effective for long-term use; they greatly reduce the risk of severe attacks.
explanation: People confuse inhaled corticosteroids with anabolic steroids or with long courses of steroid tablets, which have more side effects. Needing your reliever inhaler often is a sign asthma is poorly controlled, not addiction, and should prompt a review. Rinsing your mouth after using a steroid inhaler reduces the risk of oral thrush.

myth: Asthma is a minor condition and nobody dies from it.
fact: Asthma can usually be well controlled, but severe asthma attacks can be life-threatening. People still die from asthma each year, and many of these deaths are thought to be preventable with good routine care.
explanation: Taking preventer medicine as prescribed, checking inhaler technique, having a written asthma action plan and attending asthma reviews all lower the risk. Needing a reliever inhaler more often, or waking at night with symptoms, are signs asthma is not well controlled.

myth: Asthma is all in the mind and caused by nerves.
fact: Asthma is a long-term condition of the airways, which become inflamed and narrow in response to triggers. It is a physical illness that needs proper treatment, usually with inhalers.
explanation: Strong emotions and stress can trigger asthma symptoms in some people, which may be where the idea came from, but they are not the underlying cause. Common triggers include colds, pollen, dust mites, smoke, cold air and exercise. Treating asthma as 'just nerves' can lead to dangerous delays in getting help.

myth: Autism is caused by cold or bad parenting.
fact: Autism is not caused by parenting. Research shows that it is strongly influenced by genes and early brain development before birth.
explanation: The idea of 'refrigerator mothers' from the mid-20th century was disproved long ago, but it caused lasting harm and guilt. Autism is also not caused by vaccines, diet or screen time. Understanding and support help autistic children and adults thrive.

myth: Autism only affects boys, so girls and women can't be autistic.
fact: Autism affects people of all genders. It is diagnosed more often in boys, but girls and women are more likely to be missed or diagnosed later, partly because they may hide or 'mask' their differences.
explanation: Autistic women and girls may be first diagnosed with anxiety, depression or eating disorders. Recognising autism can help people understand themselves and get the right support. Health services describe signs in adults, and a GP can refer for assessment.

sources.label: NHS — Signs of autism in adults

myth: Babies need solid food from about 3 or 4 months because milk is no longer enough.
fact: The WHO and NHS recommend starting solid foods at around 6 months. Until then, breast milk or infant formula provides all the nutrition a baby needs.
explanation: By about 6 months most babies can sit up, hold their head steady and swallow food rather than pushing it out. Waking more at night or chewing fists are often taken as signs of hunger but are normal at this age. If you are thinking of starting earlier, for example for a premature baby, ask a health visitor or doctor.

sources.label: NHS — Your baby's first solid foods
WHO — Infant and young child feeding

myth: Babies should sleep on their tummy so they don't choke if they are sick.
fact: Babies should always be put to sleep on their back. Back sleeping greatly reduces the risk of sudden infant death syndrome and does not increase choking.
explanation: Healthy babies naturally swallow or cough up fluids. Since back-sleeping campaigns began, SIDS rates have fallen dramatically. Keep the cot clear of pillows, bumpers and loose bedding.

myth: Babies under 6 months need extra water when the weather is hot.
fact: Fully breastfed babies do not need any water until they start solid foods, even in hot weather; they may just want to feed more often. Formula-fed babies may be offered a little cooled boiled water in hot weather, as advised by health services.
explanation: Giving young babies a lot of water can fill them up so they take less milk, and in rare cases can upset the balance of salts in the blood. Signs a baby may be dehydrated include fewer wet nappies, a dry mouth and a sunken soft spot; seek advice if you notice these.

sources.label: NHS — Drinks and cups for babies and young children
WHO — Infant and young child feeding

myth: Baby teeth don't matter because they fall out anyway.
fact: Baby teeth are important for eating, speech and holding space for adult teeth. Decay in baby teeth can cause pain, infection and problems with the adult teeth.
explanation: Tooth decay is one of the most common chronic diseases of childhood. Brushing with fluoride toothpaste from the first tooth and regular dental visits are recommended.

myth: Baby walkers help babies learn to walk sooner.
fact: Baby walkers do not help babies learn to walk and may delay it. They also cause many injuries, especially falls down stairs.
explanation: The American Academy of Pediatrics advises against using mobile baby walkers. Plenty of floor time and stationary play centres are safer alternatives.

myth: Bad breath usually comes from your stomach.
fact: Most bad breath starts in the mouth, from bacteria on the tongue, gum disease, tooth decay or food between the teeth. Strong foods, smoking, dry mouth and some conditions such as tonsillitis or acid reflux can also cause it.
explanation: Brushing twice a day, cleaning between teeth, gently cleaning the tongue and regular dental check-ups usually help. Mouthwash may mask the smell for a short time but does not fix the cause. See a dentist if bad breath continues despite good cleaning.

myth: Bad heartburn in pregnancy means your baby will be born with lots of hair.
fact: Heartburn in pregnancy is very common and is caused by pregnancy hormones relaxing the valve at the top of the stomach and by the growing baby pressing on the stomach. It is not a reliable way to predict how much hair a baby will have.
explanation: Plenty of people with severe heartburn have babies with little hair, and the reverse. Heartburn usually eases after birth. Eating smaller meals, avoiding eating late at night and asking a midwife or pharmacist about pregnancy-safe remedies can help.

sources.label: NHS — Indigestion and heartburn in pregnancy

myth: Bald men have more testosterone.
fact: Male-pattern baldness is mainly due to inherited sensitivity of hair follicles to DHT, a hormone made from testosterone. Bald men do not generally have higher testosterone levels.
explanation: Because hormones are involved, the idea has a grain of truth, but it is the follicles' genetic sensitivity that matters, not the amount of testosterone.

myth: Baldness is only inherited from your mother's side.
fact: Pattern hair loss is influenced by many genes from both parents. One important gene is on the X chromosome, which comes from the mother, but it is not the whole story.
explanation: Men whose fathers are bald also have a higher chance of baldness. Looking at relatives on both sides gives a better clue than the maternal grandfather alone.

myth: Bed rest is the best treatment for back pain.
fact: For most back pain, staying as active as possible and continuing normal activities helps recovery more than bed rest.
explanation: Long bed rest can lead to stiffness and slower recovery. Pain relief, gentle movement and exercise are usually recommended. Back pain with numbness around the bottom or genitals, loss of bladder or bowel control, or leg weakness needs urgent medical help.

myth: Beef tallow is the best natural moisturiser and clears up acne and eczema.
fact: There is little scientific research on beef tallow for skin. It is a heavy fat that can help seal in moisture on dry skin, like other ointments, but there is no evidence that it treats acne or eczema, and it may clog pores in people prone to spots.
explanation: For dry skin, dermatologists recommend fragrance-free creams or ointments, such as petroleum jelly, applied to damp skin. Homemade animal-fat products are not standardised and can go rancid or become contaminated. Persistent eczema or acne usually responds better to proven treatments, which a pharmacist or GP can advise on.

sources.label: American Academy of Dermatology — Tips to relieve dry skin
American Academy of Dermatology — What causes acne

myth: Being cold gives you a cold.
fact: Colds are caused by viruses, not by low temperatures. Colds are more common in winter mainly because people spend more time indoors close together, and some cold viruses spread more easily in cool, dry air.
explanation: The name 'cold' reinforces the belief, and many people notice symptoms after being chilled. Some research suggests cooler airways may make it slightly easier for viruses to take hold, which is why the claim is not entirely baseless. But without exposure to a virus, being cold will not give you a cold.

myth: Being overweight increases your risk of some cancers.
fact: Yes. Excess body fat is linked to a higher risk of at least 13 types of cancer, including bowel, breast (after menopause), womb, kidney, liver and oesophageal cancers.
explanation: Body fat affects hormones such as oestrogen and insulin and causes long-term inflammation, which can encourage cancer growth. Not everyone with obesity gets cancer, but keeping to a healthy weight, being active and eating a healthy diet lower the risk.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Obesity and cancer

myth: Being overweight is simply a lack of willpower.
fact: Body weight is shaped by many things at once, including genes, hormones, medicines, sleep, stress, income, the food environment and how active daily life allows people to be. The World Health Organization describes obesity as a complex, chronic disease, not a personal failing.
explanation: Individual choices matter, but they are made in an environment full of cheap, high-calorie food and little need to move. Some medicines and medical conditions also cause weight gain. Blame and stigma tend to make things worse, for example by putting people off seeing a doctor, while practical support and treatment can help.

myth: Berberine is 'nature's Ozempic' and works just as well as weight-loss injections.
fact: Berberine is a plant compound sold as a supplement. Small studies suggest it may have modest effects on blood sugar and weight, but it has not been shown to work anything like prescription weight-loss medicines, and supplements are not tested the way medicines are.
explanation: Berberine can cause stomach upset and may interact with other medicines, including diabetes medicines. Supplement products can vary in what they actually contain. Anyone considering it, especially if pregnant, breastfeeding or taking other medicines, should check with a doctor or pharmacist.

sources.label: NIDDK — Prescription medications to treat overweight & obesity

myth: Bilberry supplements improve your night vision.
fact: There is no good evidence that bilberry improves night vision or treats eye conditions. The idea is often traced to Second World War stories about pilots, but controlled studies have not supported it.
explanation: Bilberry is a fruit related to blueberries and is fine as food. Supplements are not regulated like medicines and may interact with blood-thinning medicines. Difficulty seeing at night can be an early sign of cataracts or other eye problems, so an eye test is a better first step.

myth: Bipolar disorder is just having mood swings like everyone does.
fact: Bipolar disorder involves distinct episodes of mania or hypomania and depression that last days to weeks and affect energy, sleep and behaviour. This is very different from ordinary ups and downs.
explanation: Everyday mood changes are normal. Bipolar disorder is a long-term condition that usually needs medical treatment, and with the right support many people do well.

myth: Black coffee or a cold shower will sober up someone who has drunk too much.
fact: Only time lets the body clear alcohol. Coffee and cold showers do not lower blood alcohol, and a cold shower can make the person dangerously cold.
explanation: Someone very drunk should not be left to 'sleep it off' alone, because alcohol levels can keep rising and they could choke on vomit. Keep them sitting up or on their side in the recovery position and stay with them. Call emergency services if they are confused, can't be woken, have slow or irregular breathing, are having a seizure or are very pale or cold.

myth: Bladder leaks are just part of getting old, and nothing can be done.
fact: Urinary incontinence becomes more common with age but it is not an inevitable part of ageing, and it can often be treated or improved. Options include pelvic floor exercises, bladder training, lifestyle changes, medicines and surgery.
explanation: Causes vary, from weak pelvic floor muscles to an overactive bladder, an enlarged prostate in men or side effects of medicines. Many people do not seek help because of embarrassment, but a GP or continence service can assess the cause. Cutting back on caffeine and alcohol and avoiding constipation can also help.

myth: Blood in your poo is just piles, so there's no need to see a doctor.
fact: Piles are a common cause of bright red blood after going to the toilet, but blood in your poo can also be a sign of other conditions, including bowel cancer. Health services advise seeing a GP if you have blood in your poo, especially if it keeps happening or comes with other changes.
explanation: Warning signs that make a check more important include a lasting change in bowel habits, tummy pain, unexplained weight loss, tiredness, or dark or black poo. Most people with these symptoms do not have cancer, but when bowel cancer is found early it is much more treatable. Doctors are used to these questions, so there is no need to feel embarrassed.

myth: Blood pressure tablets ruin your kidneys, so it's better not to take them.
fact: Uncontrolled high blood pressure is one of the leading causes of kidney damage. Treating it protects the kidneys, and some blood pressure medicines (ACE inhibitors and ARBs) are used specifically to slow kidney disease.
explanation: Some of these medicines can change kidney blood test results, so your doctor may check your kidney function when you start them or change the dose. This is routine monitoring, not a sign that the pills are damaging your kidneys. Do not stop them without talking to your doctor.

sources.label: NIDDK — High blood pressure and kidney disease

myth: Blood thinners make your blood thin and watery.
fact: So-called blood thinners do not thin the blood. Anticoagulants such as warfarin, apixaban and rivaroxaban, and antiplatelets such as aspirin and clopidogrel, make blood less likely to form harmful clots.
explanation: They are used to prevent strokes, heart attacks and clots in the legs and lungs. Because they increase bleeding, tell doctors and dentists you take them, and get urgent help for heavy bleeding, black stools or a head injury. Do not stop them without advice.

myth: Blue light from screens damages your eyes, so you need blue-light glasses.
fact: There is no good evidence that the blue light from screens damages the eyes, and eye doctors do not generally recommend blue-light-blocking glasses for eye health.
explanation: Screen discomfort is mainly due to eye strain and reduced blinking, which blue-light glasses do not fix. Light from screens at night may affect sleep, which is a separate issue.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Brain-training games and puzzles will prevent dementia.
fact: Brain-training games improve performance on the tasks practised, but there is no strong evidence that they prevent dementia.
explanation: Staying mentally and socially active is linked to better brain health and is worth doing. The strongest evidence for lowering dementia risk involves physical activity, not smoking, managing blood pressure and diabetes, limiting alcohol and treating hearing loss.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Breast swelling in men ('man boobs') is always just fat that dieting will fix.
fact: Being overweight is one cause, but enlarged breast tissue in men (gynaecomastia) can also be caused by hormone changes in puberty or older age, certain medicines, conditions such as kidney or liver disease or an overactive thyroid, and drug use including anabolic steroids.
explanation: Gynaecomastia is often harmless and may settle on its own, especially in teenage boys. See a GP if it is painful, getting bigger, affects only one side or there is a lump, nipple discharge or skin change, as men can rarely get breast cancer.

myth: Breastfed babies don't need vaccines because breast milk protects them.
fact: Breast milk gives babies some protection against infections, but it does not protect them from serious diseases such as measles, whooping cough, polio or meningitis. Breastfed babies need the same vaccines as other babies.
explanation: Antibodies passed on in breast milk and during pregnancy are short-lived and do not cover all infections. Breastfeeding and vaccination work well together. Vaccines given during pregnancy, such as the whooping cough vaccine, help protect babies in their first weeks of life.

sources.label: NHS — NHS vaccinations and when to have them
WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: Breastfed babies may need a vitamin D supplement.
fact: Health authorities in the UK and US recommend vitamin D drops for breastfed babies, because breast milk alone usually does not provide enough.
explanation: Formula is already fortified, so babies drinking enough formula may not need extra. Vitamin D supports healthy bones and helps prevent rickets. Ask a health visitor, pharmacist or paediatrician about the right product.

sources.label: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamin D

myth: Breastfeeding lowers a mother's risk of breast cancer.
fact: Breastfeeding is linked to a lower risk of breast cancer for the mother, and the protective effect is greater the longer a person breastfeeds in total. It is also linked to a lower risk of ovarian cancer.
explanation: This is one of several health benefits of breastfeeding for both mother and baby. It does not mean that people who could not or chose not to breastfeed will get breast cancer; many factors affect risk. Any amount of breastfeeding has benefits, and support is available if it is difficult.

myth: Breathing hot steam or using a hairdryer kills cold and flu viruses in your nose.
fact: Inhaling steam or hot air does not kill viruses inside your body. Steam may temporarily ease a blocked nose, but it does not shorten or cure an infection, and very hot steam can cause burns.
explanation: These claims circulated widely during the COVID-19 pandemic, sometimes with videos of people breathing hot air. Body temperature is tightly controlled, and inhaled heat cannot reach the levels needed to destroy viruses without harming tissue. Scalds from bowls of boiling water are a real risk, especially for children.

myth: Breathing into a paper bag helps someone having an asthma attack.
fact: An asthma attack needs the person's reliever inhaler, usually blue, not a paper bag. Health services advise sitting up straight, staying calm and taking one puff of the reliever every 30 to 60 seconds, up to 10 puffs, and calling emergency services if they are not improving or get worse.
explanation: Breathing into a bag can reduce the oxygen someone gets, which is dangerous when their airways are already narrowed. If symptoms improve, the person should still get an urgent appointment with a doctor or nurse the same day. If no inhaler is available or the person is very breathless, call for help immediately.

myth: Briefly shaking a baby to stop them crying doesn't do any harm.
fact: Shaking a baby, even for a few seconds, can cause bleeding and swelling in the brain, blindness, lasting disability or death. Babies' heads are heavy and their neck muscles weak, so the brain moves back and forth inside the skull.
explanation: This is different from normal play: gentle bouncing or swinging does not cause these injuries. Constant crying can be overwhelming for any parent. If you feel frustrated, put the baby safely on their back in the cot, leave the room for a few minutes to calm down and ask someone for help.

myth: Brown sugar, honey and coconut sugar are much healthier than white sugar.
fact: Brown sugar, honey, syrups and coconut sugar are all forms of free sugars and have similar effects on teeth and calories as white sugar. WHO advises limiting all free sugars, including honey and syrups.
explanation: These sugars are often marketed as natural or unrefined, and some contain tiny amounts of minerals. The amounts are too small to make a real difference to health. Honey should not be given to babies under one year old because of the risk of infant botulism.

myth: Brushing harder gets your teeth cleaner.
fact: Brushing too hard can wear down enamel and damage gums. Gentle brushing with a soft brush for two minutes is enough.
explanation: Plaque is soft and comes off with gentle technique. Electric toothbrushes with pressure sensors can help people who brush too hard.

myth: Brushing your teeth once a day is enough.
fact: Dental and health organisations recommend brushing twice a day for about 2 minutes with fluoride toothpaste, including last thing at night before bed.
explanation: Plaque builds up throughout the day, and saliva flow drops at night, so night-time brushing is especially important. Spit out after brushing rather than rinsing, to leave fluoride on the teeth. Cleaning between the teeth helps remove plaque the brush misses.

sources.label: NHS — How to keep your teeth clean

myth: Bunions are only caused by wearing high heels or tight shoes.
fact: Tight or narrow shoes can make bunions worse and more painful, but bunions often run in families and can also be linked to foot shape and conditions such as arthritis. Men and people who never wear heels can get them too.
explanation: Wide, comfortable shoes, bunion pads and painkillers can ease symptoms. Surgery is the only way to remove a bunion and is considered if pain is severe. See a GP or podiatrist if a bunion is painful or affecting your walking.

myth: Bystanders can help save a life with hands-only CPR, even without training in rescue breaths.
fact: If an adult collapses and is not breathing normally, calling emergency services and giving hard, fast chest compressions in the centre of the chest can keep blood flowing to the brain until help arrives. Hands-only CPR is recommended for untrained bystanders.
explanation: Many people do nothing because they fear doing CPR wrong or giving mouth-to-mouth. Starting compressions quickly makes a big difference to survival. Use a defibrillator (AED) if one is available; the device gives spoken instructions.

myth: Calories don't matter as long as you eat 'clean' or the right kind of food.
fact: Eating more energy than your body uses leads to weight gain, even if the food is healthy. Food quality matters a lot for health, and some foods are more filling than others, but quantity still counts.
explanation: Healthy foods such as nuts, avocados, olive oil and smoothies can be high in calories. Focusing on whole, minimally processed foods often helps people eat less without counting, which may be why the idea feels true. Both quality and quantity matter.

myth: Cancer is really a fungus, and baking soda (bicarbonate) can cure it.
fact: Cancer is not a fungus; it is a disease in which the body's own cells grow out of control because of changes in their genes. Baking soda does not cure cancer.
explanation: Injecting or swallowing large amounts of bicarbonate can dangerously upset the body's chemistry and has caused deaths. People who promote this idea have no evidence from clinical studies. Delaying proven treatment can allow a curable cancer to spread.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — What is cancer?
National Cancer Institute — Complementary and alternative medicine

myth: Cannabis is natural, so it's harmless for your mental health.
fact: Regular cannabis use, especially of strong (high-THC) types and starting in the teenage years, is linked to a higher risk of psychosis and schizophrenia. It can also worsen anxiety and lead to dependence in some people.
explanation: Being 'natural' does not make something safe. Not everyone who uses cannabis develops problems, but the risks are higher for people with a family history of psychosis. If you're worried about your cannabis use or have unusual experiences such as paranoia, talk to a GP.

myth: Cannabis oil cures cancer.
fact: There is no reliable evidence from human studies that cannabis or cannabis oil cures cancer. Some cannabinoid medicines can help with side effects such as nausea and vomiting from chemotherapy.
explanation: Laboratory and animal studies showing cannabinoids affecting cancer cells are often presented online as proof of a cure. Many substances kill cancer cells in a dish but do not work in people. Products sold online may contain unknown amounts of THC or CBD, and relying on them instead of proven treatment can be dangerous.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Cannabis and cannabinoids (PDQ)

myth: Carbohydrates are bad for you and should be cut out.
fact: Carbohydrates are a main source of energy, and whole grains, vegetables, fruit and pulses are linked to better health. Health bodies recommend choosing high-fibre, wholegrain carbohydrates and limiting refined carbs and added sugars, not avoiding all carbs.
explanation: Low-carb diets became popular and some people do lose weight on them, mainly because they eat fewer calories overall. Cutting out whole groups of foods can mean missing out on fibre, which supports digestion and lowers the risk of bowel cancer and heart disease. The type and amount of carbohydrate matter most.

myth: Carpal tunnel syndrome is caused by typing on a computer.
fact: Carpal tunnel syndrome is pressure on a nerve in the wrist. Repetitive hand and wrist movements may contribute, but it is also linked with pregnancy, family history, wrist injuries and conditions such as diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis, and often has no single clear cause.
explanation: It causes tingling, numbness and pain in the hand and fingers, often at night. Wearing a wrist splint at night and resting the hand can help, and it sometimes improves on its own, particularly after pregnancy. See a GP if symptoms persist or your hand feels weak.

myth: Cataracts have to be 'ripe' before they can be removed.
fact: Modern cataract surgery does not need the cataract to 'ripen'. Surgery is usually considered when the cataract affects your daily life.
explanation: The idea dates from older surgical techniques. Today's procedure is common and usually done under local anaesthetic.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Celery and other 'negative-calorie' foods burn more calories to digest than they contain.
fact: Digesting food uses only a small share of the energy it provides, roughly a tenth on average. No ordinary food takes more energy to digest than it supplies, so 'negative-calorie' foods do not exist.
explanation: Celery, cucumber and leafy greens are very low in calories and high in water and fibre, so they are a filling, healthy part of a diet. They simply do not cause weight loss on their own. Diets built only around such foods can leave people short of protein and other nutrients.

sources.label: Harvard Health Publishing — The truth about metabolism

myth: Cellulite is caused by toxins and only happens if you're overweight.
fact: Cellulite is very common, especially in women, and is related to how fat and connective tissue are arranged under the skin, as well as genes, hormones, age and skin thickness. Lean people can have it too, and it is not caused by toxins.
explanation: Cellulite is harmless. Creams, detox products and 'anti-cellulite' massages have little lasting effect. Exercise and weight changes can alter its appearance somewhat, but having cellulite is normal.

myth: Charcoal toothpaste or powder is a safe, natural way to whiten teeth.
fact: There is no good evidence that charcoal products whiten teeth effectively, and they can be abrasive. One study reviewed by the American Dental Association found a charcoal and salt mixture wore away enamel, which can make teeth look more yellow over time.
explanation: Most charcoal toothpastes contain little or no fluoride, so using them instead of regular toothpaste may raise the risk of decay. Surface stains can be reduced with regular brushing and professional cleaning. If you want whitening, ask a dentist about safe options.

myth: Chelation therapy clears blocked arteries and replaces heart surgery.
fact: Chelation therapy, which uses a chemical such as EDTA to bind metals in the blood, has not been shown to clear blocked arteries. It is approved for treating heavy-metal poisoning, not heart disease.
explanation: A large US trial found at most a small and uncertain benefit in some people who had had a heart attack, and further research did not confirm chelation as a treatment. Chelation can cause serious side effects, including dangerously low calcium levels.

sources.label: NCCIH — Chelation for coronary heart disease

myth: Chemotherapy kills more people than it saves; it's just poison.
fact: Chemotherapy cures some cancers, such as many testicular cancers, lymphomas and childhood leukaemias, and helps many other people live longer or reduces the chance of cancer returning after surgery.
explanation: Chemotherapy can cause serious side effects, and whether it is worthwhile depends on the type and stage of cancer, so it is important to discuss the benefits and risks with your cancer team. Treatments to prevent sickness and other side effects have improved a lot.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Chemotherapy to treat cancer

myth: Chewing an aspirin while waiting for help during a suspected heart attack can help.
fact: Health services advise calling emergency services first, then, if the person is not allergic to aspirin and has not been told not to take it, having them slowly chew an adult aspirin tablet. Aspirin helps thin the blood and can improve blood flow to the heart.
explanation: Aspirin is not a replacement for emergency care, and calling for an ambulance comes first. The person should sit and rest while waiting. Emergency call handlers can advise whether aspirin is suitable, for example for people with bleeding problems or already on blood thinners.

myth: Chewing betel nut, paan or gutka is a harmless habit.
fact: Chewing areca (betel) nut, paan with tobacco, gutka and other smokeless tobacco products causes mouth cancer and other cancers. They also damage the gums and can cause a condition that stiffens the mouth (oral submucous fibrosis).
explanation: Mouth cancer is common in parts of South and Southeast Asia where these products are widely used. Warning signs include mouth ulcers that do not heal within three weeks, red or white patches and lumps. Stopping chewing lowers the risk, and dentists can check for early changes.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Definition: betel quid

myth: Chewing sugar-free gum after meals can help protect your teeth.
fact: Chewing sugar-free gum increases the flow of saliva, which helps neutralise acids and wash away food after eating. As an extra to brushing twice a day and cleaning between teeth, it may help lower the risk of tooth decay.
explanation: It is not a replacement for brushing. Gum sweetened with sugar has the opposite effect. People with jaw problems may find chewing gum makes them worse.

myth: Chicken soup cures a cold.
fact: Nothing cures the common cold; it usually gets better on its own within one to two weeks. Warm drinks and soup can be soothing and help you stay hydrated, which is helpful, but they do not kill the virus.
explanation: Rest, fluids and simple painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease symptoms. See a doctor if symptoms last more than three weeks, get suddenly worse, or you have trouble breathing or chest pain.

myth: Chickenpox is always a harmless childhood illness.
fact: Chickenpox is usually mild in children, but it can cause serious complications such as skin infections, pneumonia and brain inflammation. It is more likely to be severe in babies, adults, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems.
explanation: Seek medical advice if a child with chickenpox has skin that becomes hot, painful and red around the spots, has difficulty breathing, or seems very unwell. Do not give ibuprofen to someone with chickenpox unless a doctor advises it, as it may increase the risk of serious skin infections.
