A chickenpox vaccine is available and is part of routine childhood schedules in many countries.

myth: Children always grow out of asthma.
fact: Some children's asthma symptoms improve or disappear as they get older, but many continue to have asthma, and symptoms can return in adulthood. Asthma that seems to have gone may come back after infections or exposure to triggers.
explanation: It is true that childhood wheezing often settles, which is why this belief is common. Stopping treatment because a child seems to have outgrown asthma can lead to serious attacks. Review medicines with a doctor or asthma nurse rather than stopping on your own.

myth: Children always grow out of their food allergies.
fact: Many children outgrow allergies to milk and eggs, but allergies to peanuts and tree nuts are more likely to last into adulthood. Whether an allergy has gone should be checked with an allergy specialist, not by testing at home.
explanation: A specialist may use tests and, when safe, a supervised food challenge to see whether a child can now eat a food. Trying the food at home without advice can be dangerous for some allergies.

myth: Children and teenagers can't really get depression; it's just a phase.
fact: Children and adolescents can develop depression, and it is one of the leading causes of illness in young people. It can look like irritability, withdrawal or falling school performance rather than sadness.
explanation: Moodiness is normal in adolescence, which is why depression in young people is often missed. Persistent changes lasting more than a couple of weeks are worth discussing with a doctor. Young people in crisis should be helped to reach urgent support.

myth: Children and teenagers under 16 shouldn't be given aspirin.
fact: Aspirin should not be given to children under 16 unless a doctor prescribes it, because it is linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious condition that can damage the liver and brain.
explanation: For pain or fever in children, paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose for the child's age are the usual choices. Check labels, as some cold remedies and gels contain aspirin-like ingredients (salicylates). Some children with specific conditions are prescribed aspirin by specialists, and that is different.

myth: Children don't need to see a dentist until they start school.
fact: Health services advise taking children to the dentist as soon as their first teeth appear, or by their first birthday. Early visits help find problems and get children used to the dentist.
explanation: Tooth decay is common in young children and can start soon after teeth come through. Regular check-ups let the dentist give advice on brushing, diet and fluoride. In the UK, NHS dental care is free for children.
keywords: when to take child to dentist

sources.label: NHS — Taking care of children's teeth

myth: Children get worms from eating too many sweets or sugar.
fact: Sugar does not cause worms. Threadworms (pinworms), the most common worms in children in many countries, are caught by swallowing tiny eggs picked up on fingers, food or surfaces.
explanation: The eggs are laid around the bottom at night, causing itching, and can be passed on when children scratch and then touch their mouths or other things. Treatment is a medicine from the pharmacy for the whole household, plus hand washing, short nails and washing bedding. Other kinds of worm infection are spread through contaminated soil, food or water, not sugar.

myth: Children grow out of type 1 diabetes.
fact: Type 1 diabetes is lifelong. The immune system destroys the cells that make insulin, and they do not grow back, so insulin is always needed.
explanation: Soon after diagnosis some children need less insulin for a while, called the "honeymoon phase", which can make it seem the diabetes is going away, but it returns. Research into new treatments continues. Stopping insulin causes diabetic ketoacidosis, which can be fatal.

myth: Children only need an eye test if they complain about their sight.
fact: Children rarely complain about poor vision because they assume everyone sees the way they do. Eye checks are offered to newborns and young children, and regular sight tests help find problems such as a lazy eye or short-sightedness early, when treatment works best.
explanation: Signs to look out for include squinting, sitting very close to screens, rubbing eyes, headaches or one eye turning in or out. In the UK, sight tests are free for children under 16. A lazy eye is much easier to treat when found before about age 7.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye screening for children

myth: Children who wet the bed are being lazy or doing it on purpose.
fact: Bedwetting is common in children and is not their fault. It usually happens because the body makes a lot of urine at night, the bladder is small or overactive, or the child does not wake when the bladder is full, and it often runs in families.
explanation: Punishing or shaming a child does not help and can make things worse. Most children grow out of it, but help is available, including bedwetting alarms and medicines. See a GP if a child over 5 is wetting the bed often, or if bedwetting starts again after being dry for months.

myth: Children will grow out of a lazy eye or squint on their own.
fact: A lazy eye usually needs treatment, such as glasses or patching, and treatment works best when started early in childhood.
explanation: If untreated, reduced vision in the affected eye can become permanent. Children's eye checks help pick up problems early.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Children with flat feet need special shoes or insoles to build their arches.
fact: Flat feet are normal in babies and young children, and arches usually develop gradually through childhood. Special shoes or insoles are not needed if the child has no pain or problems walking.
explanation: Some people keep flat feet as adults without any trouble. See a GP if your child has foot pain, stiff feet, walks unusually, or if only one foot is flat. Well-fitting ordinary shoes and plenty of active play are what children's feet need.

myth: Chocolate and greasy food cause acne.
fact: Acne is mainly driven by hormones, oil production, clogged pores and bacteria. Greasy food does not cause acne, though some studies suggest high-glycaemic diets and possibly dairy may worsen it in some people.
explanation: The evidence on diet and acne is still developing and effects seem modest. Effective treatments are available, so persistent or scarring acne is worth seeing a doctor or pharmacist about.

myth: Chromium supplements can control diabetes so you don't need medicine.
fact: There is only weak evidence that chromium might help with blood sugar, and it has not been shown to replace diabetes medicines. Most studies of supplements for diabetes are small or of low quality.
explanation: Taking supplements instead of prescribed treatment can let blood sugar rise and increase the risk of complications. Some supplements can also interact with diabetes medicines. Talk to your diabetes team before trying any supplement.

myth: Cinnamon can cure diabetes or replace diabetes medicine.
fact: Studies of cinnamon for blood sugar control have given inconsistent results, and there is no evidence that it cures diabetes. It should not replace prescribed treatment.
explanation: Cinnamon is often recommended online as a natural blood sugar fix. Cassia cinnamon, the common type in supermarkets, contains coumarin, which in large amounts can harm the liver. Using cinnamon as a spice in food is fine.

myth: Circumcised men can't get HIV or other sexually transmitted infections.
fact: Medical male circumcision lowers a man's risk of getting HIV through vaginal sex by about 60%, but it does not give full protection. Circumcised men can still get and pass on HIV and other STIs.
explanation: The WHO recommends voluntary medical male circumcision as one part of HIV prevention in some countries with high HIV rates, alongside condoms, testing and other measures. It does not protect partners directly, and it has not been shown to protect against HIV during anal sex.

myth: Clove oil cures toothache, so you don't need a dentist.
fact: Clove oil has a mild numbing effect and may ease toothache for a short time, but it does not treat the cause, such as decay, a cracked tooth or an abscess. Toothache lasting more than 2 days should be seen by a dentist.
explanation: Undiluted clove oil can irritate or burn the gums. Over-the-counter painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen can help while you wait for an appointment. Get urgent help if you have facial swelling, a high temperature or difficulty swallowing or breathing.

myth: Coconut oil is good for your heart.
fact: Coconut oil is very high in saturated fat, which raises LDL ('bad') cholesterol. Heart health organisations advise replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats such as olive, rapeseed or sunflower oil.
explanation: Coconut oil has been marketed as a superfood, partly based on studies of a special type of fat (MCT oil) that differs from ordinary coconut oil. It raises LDL cholesterol more than unsaturated vegetable oils in trials. Using it occasionally for flavour is fine, but it is not a heart-healthy choice.

myth: Coconut oil, raspberry seed oil or other natural oils work as a natural sunscreen.
fact: Plant oils offer little or no reliable protection against UV rays. Sunscreens are tested and labelled with an SPF and broad-spectrum protection, and homemade or 'natural' alternatives have not been shown to protect the skin.
explanation: Recipes for DIY sunscreen spread widely online, but people using them can get badly sunburnt. If you have concerns about particular sunscreen ingredients, mineral sunscreens based on zinc oxide or titanium dioxide are an alternative. Shade and clothing also give good protection.

sources.label: US FDA — Sunscreen: how to help protect your skin from the sun
American Academy of Dermatology — Understand sunscreen labels

myth: Coffee dehydrates you, so it doesn't count towards your fluid intake.
fact: Caffeine has a mild diuretic effect, but in usual amounts coffee and tea still provide more fluid than they cause you to lose. They count towards daily fluid intake.
explanation: People who rarely drink caffeine may notice they urinate more after a coffee, which led to this belief. Regular drinkers develop tolerance to this effect. Very high caffeine intake can cause problems such as poor sleep, anxiety and a fast heartbeat, so moderation is still wise.

myth: Coffee in the afternoon doesn't affect my sleep, as long as I can still fall asleep.
fact: Caffeine stays in the body for hours, and having it in the afternoon or evening can reduce total sleep time and deep sleep even in people who fall asleep easily. Sleep experts generally advise avoiding caffeine for several hours before bed.
explanation: Caffeine is found in coffee, tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate, and people vary in how sensitive they are. If you're tired during the day despite seemingly sleeping fine, cutting back on afternoon caffeine is a simple experiment.

myth: Cold plunges and ice baths are proven to burn fat, boost immunity and speed up recovery.
fact: Cold water immersion is popular, and some people find it helps with muscle soreness or feel energised afterwards, but scientific evidence for its wider health claims remains inconclusive. It also carries real risks.
explanation: Sudden immersion in cold water can trigger gasping, rapid breathing and spikes in heart rate and blood pressure, and hypothermia can start within minutes. People with heart problems, high blood pressure or circulation problems should check with a doctor first, and nobody should take an ice bath alone.

sources.label: Harvard Health Publishing — Can ice baths improve your health?

myth: Cold, damp weather causes arthritis.
fact: Weather does not cause arthritis. Osteoarthritis is linked to age, joint injury, genetics and weight, and rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease.
explanation: Many people with arthritis feel their pain changes with the weather. Studies on this are mixed, and any effect seems to be on how symptoms feel rather than on the disease itself. Keeping warm and active can help comfort.

myth: Colloidal silver cures infections and boosts the immune system.
fact: There is no reliable evidence that taking colloidal silver by mouth treats or prevents any disease. It can cause argyria, a permanent blue-grey discolouration of the skin, and can interfere with some medicines.
explanation: Silver has antibacterial uses in some medical dressings, which lends the idea credibility. Swallowed silver products are different and have not been shown to work. US regulators have taken action against companies making false claims about silver products.

myth: Colon cleanses and colonic irrigation remove built-up toxins and waste.
fact: There is no evidence that colon cleansing removes toxins or improves health. The bowel clears itself naturally, and colon cleansing can cause dehydration, mineral imbalances, infections and, rarely, bowel injury.
explanation: The idea that waste 'builds up' and poisons the body is an old theory that has been disproven. Bowel preparation before a colonoscopy is a different, medically supervised procedure. Fibre, fluids and activity support healthy bowel function.

myth: Colour-blind people see only in black and white.
fact: Most people with colour vision deficiency see colours but have trouble telling certain colours apart, most often red and green.
explanation: Seeing no colour at all is very rare. Colour vision deficiency is usually inherited and is much more common in males.

myth: Compounded 'bioidentical' hormones are a natural, safer alternative to regular HRT.
fact: Custom-mixed (compounded) 'bioidentical' hormones are not regulated in the same way as licensed HRT, so their safety, strength and purity are not checked. Licensed 'body-identical' HRT, such as oestradiol and micronised progesterone, is available on prescription and has been studied.
explanation: The word 'bioidentical' is often used in marketing to suggest a product is safer, but there is no good evidence that compounded products are safer or more effective. Saliva tests sometimes used to tailor them are not reliable. A GP or menopause specialist can discuss licensed options.

myth: Cot bumpers, pillows and soft toys make a baby's cot safer and cosier.
fact: Safe sleep advice is to keep the cot clear: a firm, flat mattress with no bumpers, pillows, duvets or soft toys. Soft items raise the risk of suffocation and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
explanation: Babies can get their faces pressed against soft padding or become trapped. Place your baby on their back with their feet at the foot of the cot, and use a baby sleeping bag or firmly tucked-in blankets no higher than the shoulders. Babies do not need a pillow until well after their first birthday.

myth: Cough and cold medicines are safe and helpful for toddlers.
fact: Over-the-counter cough and cold medicines are not recommended for young children because they have not been shown to work in this age group and can cause side effects.
explanation: Rules differ by country, but many advise against these medicines under six years. Fluids, rest and, for children over one, a little honey can ease coughs. Always check dosing with a pharmacist.

myth: Cough syrup cures a cough.
fact: Most coughs are caused by viral infections and get better on their own within three to four weeks. There is little evidence that cough medicines speed recovery, though some people find them soothing.
explanation: Honey and lemon in warm water may help adults and children over 1. Many cough and cold medicines are not suitable for young children. See a doctor if a cough lasts more than three weeks, you cough up blood, or you have chest pain, breathlessness or weight loss.

myth: COVID-19 vaccines are making large numbers of healthy young people "die suddenly".
fact: Safety monitoring of billions of COVID-19 vaccine doses has not shown that the vaccines cause large numbers of sudden deaths. Serious side effects are rare, and they are tracked by safety systems in many countries.
explanation: Sudden deaths in young people have always happened, often from undiagnosed heart conditions, and viral social media videos rarely give the real cause. A rare side effect of mRNA vaccines is inflammation of the heart (myocarditis), mostly in young men, and most people recover. COVID-19 infection itself can also damage the heart.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: vaccine safety

myth: COVID-19 vaccines cause "turbo cancer" or make cancers grow faster.
fact: There is no evidence that COVID-19 vaccines cause cancer or make existing cancers grow or spread faster. Cancer organisations recommend COVID-19 vaccination for many people with cancer, who are at higher risk from the infection.
explanation: "Turbo cancer" is not a medical term; it spread through social media posts and anecdotes. The mRNA in some COVID-19 vaccines does not enter the cell nucleus or alter DNA, and it is broken down quickly. Delays in screening and diagnosis during the pandemic may mean some cancers were found later, which is a different issue from vaccines.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: vaccine safety

myth: COVID-19 vaccines cause infertility.
fact: There is no evidence that COVID-19 vaccines affect fertility in women or men. Studies of couples trying to conceive found similar pregnancy rates in vaccinated and unvaccinated people.
explanation: This rumour started from a misreading of how the spike protein relates to a placental protein, which was not supported by evidence. Some people noticed small, temporary changes in their period after vaccination, which resolve and do not affect fertility. COVID-19 infection itself during pregnancy carries extra risks, which is why vaccination has been recommended for pregnant people in many countries.

myth: COVID-19 vaccines contain metal or graphene that makes your arm magnetic.
fact: COVID-19 vaccines do not contain metals, magnets or graphene, and they cannot make your arm magnetic. Their ingredients are publicly listed.
explanation: Videos of magnets or coins sticking to people's arms are explained by skin oils, sweat and the shape of the arm, and the same trick works on unvaccinated people. A vaccine dose is less than a millilitre, far too little to hold a magnet even if it contained metal.

myth: Cow's milk can replace breast milk or formula as a baby's main drink before their first birthday.
fact: Cow's milk should not be given as a main drink until a baby is 12 months old, because it does not contain enough iron and other nutrients for babies. Small amounts can be used in cooking or with food from around 6 months.
explanation: Before 12 months, breast milk or first infant formula should be the main drink. After 12 months, whole (full-fat) cow's milk can be given as a drink. Other plant 'milks' are not suitable replacements for babies, and rice drinks should not be given to young children.

sources.label: NHS — Drinks and cups for babies and young children

myth: Cracking your knuckles causes arthritis.
fact: Research has found no link between habitual knuckle cracking and arthritis. The sound comes from gas bubbles in the joint fluid, not damage.
explanation: The popping sound comes from gas bubbles forming in the fluid that lubricates the joint. Studies comparing habitual knuckle crackers with non-crackers have not found more arthritis, although pain or swelling in a joint should be checked.

myth: Crash diets are the best way to lose weight for good.
fact: Very restrictive diets can cause fast initial weight loss, but the weight is often regained once normal eating resumes. Gradual changes to eating and activity that you can keep up are more likely to lead to lasting results.
explanation: Rapid results are motivating, which is why crash diets are popular. Severe restriction can cause tiredness, nutrient shortfalls and gallstones. Medically supervised very low-calorie programmes exist for specific situations, such as type 2 diabetes remission, but these include support and monitoring.

myth: Craving sweet foods means you're having a girl, and craving salty or sour foods means a boy.
fact: Food cravings are common in pregnancy but they do not tell you the baby's sex. The sex of the baby is fixed by chromosomes at conception.
explanation: Why cravings happen is not fully understood; hormones, changes in taste and smell, and habit may all play a part. Cravings are harmless as long as your overall diet stays balanced. Tell your midwife if you crave non-food items such as soil or ice, as this can sometimes be linked to low iron.

sources.label: NHS — Have a healthy diet in pregnancy

myth: Cut and suck out the venom after a snake bite, or use a tourniquet.
fact: Cutting the wound, sucking out venom and applying a tight tourniquet do not help and can cause more harm. Keep the person calm and still, keep the bitten limb still, and get emergency medical help, where antivenom can be given if needed.
explanation: These methods are often shown in films and old survival guides. Remove rings or tight items near the bite in case of swelling, and do not apply ice. Advice on pressure bandaging differs by region and snake type, so follow local emergency guidance.

myth: Cuts and grazes heal best if you leave them uncovered to dry out and scab.
fact: Dermatologists advise keeping a clean wound moist, for example with petroleum jelly, and covered with a dressing. Moist wounds tend to heal well and may scar less than wounds left to dry out and form thick scabs.
explanation: First, stop any bleeding with pressure and rinse the wound with clean water. Change the dressing regularly. Seek help for deep or gaping cuts, wounds that won't stop bleeding, bites, or signs of infection such as spreading redness, swelling, pus or fever.

sources.label: American Academy of Dermatology — Proper wound care

myth: Cutting down to a few cigarettes a day in pregnancy is as good as quitting, and a smaller baby means an easier birth.
fact: Any smoking in pregnancy harms the baby: it raises the risk of miscarriage, premature birth, stillbirth, low birth weight and sudden infant death. Stopping completely, at any stage of pregnancy, is the best thing you can do for your baby.
explanation: Babies who are small because of smoking are not easier to deliver; they are more likely to be unwell. Free stop-smoking support is available through maternity services, and nicotine replacement products are much safer than smoking. Second-hand smoke also affects the baby, so support for partners to quit helps too.

myth: Cutting your hair often makes it grow faster.
fact: Hair grows from the follicle in the scalp, so trimming the ends does not change how fast it grows.
explanation: Regular trims remove split ends, which can stop hair from breaking and help it look longer and healthier over time. The growth rate itself stays the same.

myth: Dabbing toothpaste on a spot overnight dries it out.
fact: Toothpaste is not designed for skin, and ingredients in it can irritate the skin and make redness worse. Proven spot treatments, such as products containing benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid, are available from pharmacies.
explanation: Dermatologists advise using gentle skin care, not scrubbing, and not picking or squeezing spots, which can lead to scarring and dark marks. Acne treatments usually take several weeks to work. Severe or scarring acne should be seen by a GP.

sources.label: American Academy of Dermatology — Tips for managing acne

myth: Dandruff means you have a dirty or dry scalp.
fact: Dandruff is not caused by poor hygiene, though it can be more noticeable if hair isn't washed regularly. It is often linked to a type of yeast that naturally lives on the scalp, and it is harmless and not catching.
explanation: Anti-dandruff shampoos containing ingredients such as zinc pyrithione, salicylic acid, selenium sulphide or ketoconazole usually help. Rubbing oil into the scalp for 'dryness' does not usually fix dandruff. See a GP if the scalp is very itchy, red or swollen, or if there are flaky patches elsewhere on the body.

myth: Dangling a ring or needle on a thread over the bump or wrist shows whether you're having a boy or a girl.
fact: The way a ring or needle swings cannot detect a baby's sex. The baby's sex is set by chromosomes at conception and can only be found reliably by an ultrasound scan later in pregnancy or by medical genetic tests.
explanation: The ring test gets the answer right about half the time, which is what you would expect from guessing. Small, unconscious movements of the hand decide which way it swings. In many places the 20-week scan can show the baby's sex if you want to know, although some hospitals do not tell parents.

myth: Dementia is a normal part of getting old.
fact: Dementia is not a normal part of ageing. It is caused by diseases such as Alzheimer's disease and vascular disease that damage the brain.
explanation: The risk of dementia rises with age, and most older people do not develop it. Some mild slowing of memory is common with age, but problems that affect daily life should be checked by a doctor.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Dementia only affects memory.
fact: Memory loss is a common symptom, but dementia can also affect thinking speed, language, understanding, judgement, mood, behaviour and the ability to carry out everyday tasks.
explanation: In some types, such as frontotemporal dementia, changes in personality or behaviour may come before memory problems. Recognising these signs can lead to earlier diagnosis and support. Talk to a GP if you notice changes in yourself or someone close to you.

myth: Dental X-rays expose you to dangerous amounts of radiation.
fact: Dental X-rays use very low doses of radiation. Dentists follow the principle of keeping doses as low as reasonably achievable and only take X-rays when the benefit justifies it.
explanation: X-rays help find problems that cannot be seen during an exam, such as decay between teeth, infections and bone loss. Modern digital X-rays use even lower doses. If you are unsure why an X-ray is needed, ask your dentist.

myth: Depression is just a sign of weakness and people should snap out of it.
fact: Depression is a common medical condition involving changes in mood, thinking, sleep and energy. It is not a character flaw, and people cannot simply will themselves out of it.
explanation: Depression can come from a mix of genetic, biological, psychological and life-event factors, and it can affect anyone. Telling someone to snap out of it can make them feel worse and less likely to seek help. Effective treatments include talking therapies and medication. If you are struggling, talking to a GP, a doctor or a mental health helpline is a good first step.

myth: Depression is simply caused by a chemical imbalance, like low serotonin.
fact: Depression does not have one single cause. It is thought to result from a combination of genetic, biological, psychological and life factors, such as stressful events, loneliness, illness and substance use.
explanation: The 'low serotonin' explanation is an oversimplification that research has not confirmed. This does not mean antidepressants don't help: they are an effective treatment for many people, even though the way they work is more complex than once thought. Talking therapies, social support and physical activity also play important roles.

myth: Detox teas flush toxins out of your body.
fact: Your liver and kidneys already remove waste efficiently. "Detox" products are not proven to remove toxins and some can cause dehydration or digestive harm.
explanation: Your liver and kidneys remove waste products continuously. Many detox teas contain laxatives or diuretics, which cause water loss rather than removing toxins, and can lead to dehydration or interact with medicines.

myth: Diabetes can damage your eyes before you notice any change in your vision.
fact: Diabetic retinopathy often causes no symptoms in its early stages, even when damage is building up at the back of the eye. Regular eye screening can find it early, when treatment can prevent sight loss.
explanation: People with diabetes are advised to have eye screening regularly, usually every one to two years. Keeping blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol under control lowers the risk. Get seen quickly if your vision suddenly worsens or you notice new floaters or dark patches.

myth: Diabetes greatly increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes.
fact: Yes. Over time, high blood sugar damages blood vessels and the nerves that control the heart, and people with diabetes are more likely to develop heart disease and stroke, often at a younger age.
explanation: Heart disease is a leading cause of death in people with diabetes. Controlling blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol, not smoking and staying active lower this risk, and some diabetes medicines also protect the heart.

sources.label: NIDDK — Diabetes, heart disease, and stroke

myth: Dietary supplements are tested and approved for safety and effectiveness like medicines.
fact: In the US, the FDA does not approve dietary supplements for safety or effectiveness before they are sold. Manufacturers are responsible for their products, and some supplements have been found to contain undeclared drugs or different amounts of ingredients than labelled.
explanation: Supplements are sold next to medicines in pharmacies, so people assume they are regulated in the same way. Rules vary between countries, but in many places they are regulated more like foods. Products for weight loss, bodybuilding and sexual performance are most often found to be contaminated.

myth: Diseases went away because of clean water and better food, not because of vaccines.
fact: Clean water, sanitation and better nutrition did greatly reduce diseases such as cholera and typhoid. But diseases like measles, polio and diphtheria fell sharply only after vaccines were introduced, and they come back when vaccination rates drop.
explanation: Measles spreads through the air, so clean water does not stop it. Countries with modern sanitation still see measles and whooping cough outbreaks when vaccine coverage falls. Vaccines and public health measures work together.

myth: Double-jointed people have extra joints.
fact: Nobody has double joints. People described as double-jointed have joint hypermobility, meaning their joints move further than usual, often because of looser connective tissue.
explanation: Hypermobility is common in children and often becomes less marked with age. For many it causes no problems, but some people have pain, frequent sprains or dislocations, and may be diagnosed with joint hypermobility syndrome. Exercises to strengthen muscles around the joints can help.

myth: Drinking "food-grade" hydrogen peroxide oxygenates your body and cures diseases.
fact: Drinking hydrogen peroxide does not cure any disease and can be very dangerous. Concentrated "food-grade" solutions can burn the mouth, throat and stomach and cause gas bubbles in the blood vessels, leading to stroke-like injuries or death.
explanation: Hydrogen peroxide is sometimes promoted online as an oxygen therapy for cancer, infections and other illnesses, with no evidence. If someone swallows it, get emergency medical help or contact a poison centre.

myth: Drinking a glass of water at bedtime prevents heart attacks and strokes.
fact: There is no evidence that drinking water at particular times of day prevents heart attacks or strokes.
explanation: This advice spreads widely in forwarded messages. Staying hydrated is sensible, but the proven ways to lower heart attack and stroke risk are not smoking, controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes, being active, eating a healthy diet and keeping a healthy weight.

myth: Drinking alcohol in moderation doesn't raise your cancer risk.
fact: Alcohol is a cause of several cancers, including mouth, throat, oesophagus, liver, bowel and breast cancer. Risk rises with the amount drunk, and even light to moderate drinking is linked to a higher risk of some cancers, particularly breast cancer.
explanation: Messages about red wine being good for the heart have made alcohol seem harmless in small amounts. The type of drink does not matter; the alcohol itself is the problem. Drinking less lowers risk, and many health bodies now say there is no completely safe level for cancer.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Alcohol and cancer risk

myth: Drinking apple cider vinegar cures heartburn and acid reflux.
fact: There is no good scientific evidence that apple cider vinegar treats heartburn or acid reflux, and its acidity may make symptoms worse for some people. Proven measures include eating smaller meals, avoiding trigger foods, losing excess weight, raising the head of the bed and pharmacy remedies.
explanation: The idea comes from the theory that reflux is caused by too little stomach acid, which is not true for most people with reflux. Undiluted vinegar can also damage tooth enamel and irritate the throat. Heartburn that happens most days, or comes with difficulty swallowing, weight loss or vomiting, should be checked by a doctor.

sources.label: NIDDK — Acid reflux (GER & GERD) in adults

myth: Drinking apple cider vinegar melts away fat.
fact: There is no good evidence that apple cider vinegar causes meaningful fat loss. Studies have been small and short, with at most very modest effects.
explanation: Apple cider vinegar is one of the most popular weight-loss tips on social media. Drinking it neat can damage teeth and the throat, and large amounts may lower potassium levels. Diluting it in food, such as a salad dressing, is a safer way to enjoy it.

sources.label: NIH ODS — Dietary supplements for weight loss

myth: Drinking beer or stout helps you make more breast milk.
fact: Alcohol does not increase milk supply. It passes into breast milk and can reduce the amount of milk the baby gets and affect the baby's feeding and sleep.
explanation: This is an old tradition in several countries, but the evidence points the other way. Milk supply is mainly driven by how often and how well the baby feeds. An occasional drink is unlikely to harm a breastfed baby, but avoid feeding for 2 to 3 hours after a drink, and never share a bed or sofa with your baby after drinking.

myth: Drinking borax in water is a healthy supplement that cures arthritis and removes toxins.
fact: Borax (sodium borate) is a cleaning and laundry product, not a dietary supplement. Swallowing boron compounds such as borax or boric acid can cause poisoning, with vomiting, diarrhoea, skin rashes and, in larger amounts, kidney damage and collapse.
explanation: Social media videos promote "borax water" for joint pain, inflammation and to "remove fluoride" or "detox", with no evidence. Small amounts of boron are naturally present in fruit, vegetables and nuts. If someone swallows borax, contact a poison centre.

myth: Drinking castor oil, or putting it in your belly button or on castor oil packs, detoxes your liver and dissolves cysts and tumours.
fact: There is no evidence that castor oil detoxes the liver, removes toxins or shrinks cysts, fibroids or tumours, whether swallowed, applied to the navel or used in packs. Swallowed castor oil is a strong laxative.
explanation: Taking too much by mouth can cause cramping, severe diarrhoea, dehydration and salt imbalances. It should not be used to try to start labour except under medical advice. The liver and kidneys clear waste from the body without the need for "detox" products.

sources.label: NCCIH — "Detoxes" and "cleanses": what you need to know

myth: Drinking cayenne pepper in water can stop a heart attack.
fact: Cayenne pepper cannot stop a heart attack. A heart attack is a medical emergency that needs urgent treatment to restore blood flow to the heart.
explanation: If you think someone is having a heart attack, call emergency services immediately. While waiting, they should rest; emergency services may advise chewing an aspirin if they are not allergic. Every minute matters, so do not delay calling for help to try home remedies.

myth: Drinking cold water after a meal turns the oil in your food solid, which builds up in your gut and causes heart attacks or cancer.
fact: Your stomach and intestines are kept at body temperature, so a cold drink warms up quickly and cannot set fats into solid lumps. Fats are broken down by bile and enzymes and absorbed regardless of what you drink.
explanation: This claim has circulated widely in chain messages, often alongside advice to drink only warm water. Choosing warm drinks because you like them is fine, but cold water does not cause heart attacks, cancer or blocked intestines. Heart disease risk depends on factors such as smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes and overall diet.

sources.label: NIDDK — Your digestive system & how it works

myth: Drinking cranberry juice cures a urine infection.
fact: There is no evidence that cranberry products ease symptoms or treat a urinary tract infection once it has started. Some evidence suggests that taking cranberry products regularly may help prevent repeat infections in some people.
explanation: Mild bladder infections sometimes clear on their own, but many need antibiotics, especially if symptoms are severe, you are pregnant or you have a fever or back pain, which can mean a kidney infection. Cranberry juice can be high in sugar. Speak to a pharmacist or GP about symptoms, and check with a doctor before using cranberry if you take warfarin.

myth: Drinking diluted bleach or disinfectant can kill viruses inside your body.
fact: Drinking or injecting bleach or disinfectant does not treat any infection and can cause serious poisoning, damage to the mouth, throat and stomach, and death.
explanation: Disinfectants are meant for cleaning surfaces only. If someone swallows bleach or a cleaning product, contact a poison centre or emergency services straight away and do not try to make them vomit.

myth: Drinking green tea or taking green tea extract burns belly fat.
fact: Research suggests green tea and green tea extract have, at most, a very small effect on weight that is unlikely to matter in practice. Concentrated green tea extract supplements have been linked to rare cases of liver injury.
explanation: Plain green tea is a fine drink and a better choice than sugary drinks, which can help indirectly. Pills sold as 'fat burners' often contain concentrated extracts and caffeine, which can cause side effects. Weight change still depends mainly on overall diet and activity.

myth: Drinking lemon water cures cancer.
fact: A healthy diet supports overall wellbeing, but there is no scientific evidence that lemon water cures or prevents cancer. Cancer requires diagnosis and treatment guided by qualified oncologists.
explanation: Lemon water can be part of a healthy diet and helps with hydration, but no food or drink has been shown to cure cancer. Delaying proven treatment in favour of unproven remedies can let cancer grow and spread.

myth: Drinking lots of milk is all you need to prevent osteoporosis.
fact: Getting enough calcium and vitamin D is important for bones, but extra milk alone does not prevent osteoporosis. Exercise, not smoking, limiting alcohol and genetics also play a big role.
explanation: Calcium can come from many foods besides dairy. Vitamin D mostly comes from sunlight on skin, and supplements are recommended for some people. Weight-bearing and strength exercises help build and keep bone.

sources.label: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Calcium

myth: Drinking milk soothes and heals stomach ulcers.
fact: Milk may briefly coat the stomach, but it then stimulates more acid production and does not heal ulcers. Ulcers are treated by addressing the cause, such as H. pylori infection or painkiller use, often with acid-reducing medicine.
explanation: Milk-based diets were once a standard treatment for ulcers, so the advice lingers in many families. Short-term comfort from milk can make it feel helpful. Anyone with ongoing stomach pain should see a doctor rather than self-treating.

myth: Drinking strong coffee can stop an asthma attack if you don't have your inhaler.
fact: Caffeine has a weak, slow effect on the airways and is no substitute for a reliever inhaler. An asthma attack without access to an inhaler is an emergency, and you should call emergency services.
explanation: Relying on coffee or other home remedies can cost valuable time. People with asthma should always carry their reliever inhaler and have a written asthma action plan. Needing your reliever more often than usual is a sign to get your asthma reviewed.

myth: Drinking turpentine or kerosene kills parasites and cleans out the body.
fact: Turpentine and kerosene are poisons. Swallowing them can damage the lungs, stomach, kidneys and nervous system and can be fatal; they do not treat parasites or "candida".
explanation: These remedies are promoted online and in some folk traditions. Small amounts can be breathed into the lungs while swallowing, causing a severe chemical pneumonia. If someone has swallowed them, get emergency help and do not make them vomit. Proven medicines exist for confirmed parasite infections.

myth: Drinking warm lemon water in the morning burns fat.
fact: Lemon water does not burn fat or boost metabolism in any meaningful way. It can be a pleasant low-calorie drink and help you stay hydrated.
explanation: Replacing sugary drinks with water, with or without lemon, can reduce calorie intake, which may be where the idea came from. Frequent acidic drinks can wear down tooth enamel, so drinking through a straw or rinsing with plain water afterwards can help.

myth: Drinking water with meals dilutes your stomach acid and ruins digestion.
fact: Drinking water with food does not stop you digesting it. The stomach adjusts the acid and enzymes it releases, and fluids actually help break down food and move it through the gut.
explanation: Water also helps soften stools and prevent constipation. If large drinks with meals make you feel uncomfortably full or worsen reflux, it is fine to sip more slowly, but there is no need to avoid water at mealtimes.

sources.label: NIDDK — Your digestive system & how it works

myth: Driving when you're very tired can be as dangerous as driving drunk.
fact: Research shows that after about 18 to 24 hours without sleep, reaction times and alertness are impaired to a similar degree as having a blood alcohol level around or above many legal driving limits. Drowsy drivers can also have 'microsleeps' without realising.
explanation: Opening a window, turning up the music or drinking coffee are not reliable fixes. If you feel sleepy while driving, stop somewhere safe and rest. Shift workers and people with untreated sleep apnoea are at higher risk.

sources.label: Sleep Foundation — Drowsy driving vs. drunk driving

myth: During long exercise like a marathon, you can never drink too much water.
fact: Drinking much more water than you lose in sweat during long endurance events can dilute the sodium in your blood, a condition called hyponatraemia. It can cause nausea, headache, confusion, seizures and, rarely, death.
explanation: A sensible approach for most people is to drink according to thirst during long exercise rather than forcing down large amounts. Slower runners in long races are at higher risk because they have more time to drink. Confusion or vomiting during or after an endurance event needs urgent medical help.

myth: Dyeing your hair gives you cancer.
fact: Studies of personal hair dye use have not shown a clear link with cancer. Some studies have found small possible increases in certain cancers, but the results are inconsistent.
explanation: Some chemicals in hair dyes made before the 1980s were found to cause cancer in animals, and manufacturers changed their formulas. Hairdressers who work with dyes every day may have a slightly higher risk of some cancers. Following the product instructions and wearing gloves reduces exposure.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Hair dyes and cancer risk

myth: Early gum disease can be reversed with good brushing and cleaning between your teeth.
fact: Gingivitis, the early stage of gum disease, can usually be reversed by removing plaque with careful brushing twice a day, cleaning between teeth and professional cleaning if needed.
explanation: If it is left untreated, it can progress to periodontitis, which damages the bone supporting the teeth and cannot be fully reversed, although it can be managed. Bleeding gums are a common early sign; keep brushing gently rather than stopping.

myth: Eating a big meal shortly before bed can make heartburn worse.
fact: Lying down with a full stomach makes it easier for stomach acid to flow back up into the food pipe. Health services advise avoiding eating for a few hours before going to bed if you get heartburn or acid reflux.
explanation: Other helpful steps include eating smaller meals, raising the head end of your bed, keeping to a healthy weight and noticing which foods or drinks, such as alcohol, coffee or fatty foods, trigger your symptoms. This advice is about reflux; late eating does not cause heartburn in everyone.

sources.label: NIDDK — Acid reflux (GER & GERD) in adults

myth: Eating a lot of ultra-processed food is linked to poorer health.
fact: Studies have linked diets high in ultra-processed foods with higher risks of obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease and early death. Many of these foods are high in salt, sugar and saturated fat and low in fibre.
explanation: Most of this evidence comes from observational studies, so it is still debated whether processing itself causes harm or the nutrients these foods contain. Not all processed foods are unhealthy: frozen vegetables, tinned beans and wholemeal bread can all be part of a healthy diet.

myth: Eating after 8pm makes you put on weight.
fact: Weight gain depends mainly on how much you eat and drink overall compared with how much energy you use, not on the clock. However, late-night eating is often linked to snacking on high-calorie foods, and some research suggests meal timing may have small effects.
explanation: People who eat late often do so while tired or watching screens, which can lead to eating more. Shift workers have to eat at unusual times and can still manage their weight. Eating a large meal right before bed can also worsen heartburn for some people.

myth: Eating bananas, curd or other "cold" foods gives you a cold.
fact: Colds are caused by viruses that spread from person to person. Bananas, yoghurt, curd and other foods do not cause colds.
explanation: The idea of "cold" and "hot" foods comes from traditional systems of medicine in many cultures, but foods cannot give you a viral infection. Bananas and curd are nutritious and can be eaten when you have a cold. Handwashing and avoiding close contact with sick people are what reduce the spread of colds.

myth: Eating burnt toast or crispy chips will give you cancer.
fact: Browning starchy foods at high temperatures forms acrylamide, which causes cancer in animals at high doses. Studies in people have not found a consistent link between acrylamide in food and cancer.
explanation: Because the evidence in animals exists, experts suggest aiming for a golden colour rather than dark brown or burnt when toasting, frying or roasting starchy foods. Not smoking, limiting alcohol and keeping a healthy weight have far larger effects on cancer risk.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Acrylamide and cancer risk

myth: Eating cheese before bed gives you nightmares.
fact: There is no good scientific evidence that cheese causes nightmares.
explanation: Heavy or rich meals close to bedtime can cause indigestion that disturbs sleep, which may explain the belief. Stress, some medicines and poor sleep are more common causes of bad dreams.

myth: Eating disorders are a lifestyle choice or about vanity.
fact: Eating disorders are serious mental illnesses with biological, psychological and social causes. They are not a choice and have one of the highest risks of serious complications of any mental illness.
explanation: People cannot simply decide to 'just eat normally', and blame can make it harder to ask for help. Recovery is possible with specialist treatment, which usually includes talking therapy and support from family and friends. If you are struggling, please reach out to a GP or an eating disorder helpline.

myth: Eating fish and milk together causes white patches on the skin (vitiligo).
fact: Vitiligo happens when the skin loses pigment cells, most often because the immune system attacks them. It is not caused by food combinations such as fish with milk or yoghurt.
explanation: This belief is widespread in South Asia and the Middle East and can lead to unnecessary food restrictions and blame. Vitiligo tends to run in families and is linked to some other autoimmune conditions. Treatments may help restore colour in some people, and sun protection for the pale patches is important.

sources.label: American Academy of Dermatology — Vitiligo: causes

myth: Eating fruit after a meal makes it rot or ferment in your stomach.
fact: Fruit does not rot or ferment in the stomach when eaten with or after a meal. Stomach acid and digestive enzymes break down all foods together, and the stomach's acidity prevents rotting.
explanation: This claim is popular in WhatsApp messages and food-combining diets. Some people do feel bloated after certain fruits or large meals, which is a matter of individual tolerance. Fruit can be eaten at any time of day.

myth: Eating local honey cures hay fever.
fact: There is no good evidence that local honey prevents or treats hay fever. Hay fever is mostly caused by wind-borne pollen from grasses and trees, while bees mainly collect pollen from flowers.
explanation: The idea is based on gradual exposure, similar to proper allergen immunotherapy, which uses measured doses under medical supervision. Honey contains unpredictable amounts of pollen and can occasionally cause allergic reactions. Antihistamines, steroid nasal sprays and reducing pollen exposure are proven options; honey must never be given to babies under one.

myth: Eating lots of carrots gives you better night vision.
fact: Carrots contain beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A, and vitamin A deficiency can cause night blindness. But for people who already get enough vitamin A, eating extra carrots does not improve vision.
explanation: The idea is often traced to Second World War stories used to explain pilots' success at night. A balanced diet supports eye health, but it will not give better-than-normal sight.

sources.label: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamin A
American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Eating more fibre and drinking enough fluids helps prevent constipation.
fact: Increasing fibre from foods such as fruit, vegetables, whole grains and pulses, drinking enough fluids and staying active are first-line ways to prevent and ease constipation.
explanation: People often reach for laxatives first. Fibre should be increased gradually to avoid wind and bloating. If constipation persists despite these changes, or comes with blood, weight loss or severe pain, see a doctor.

myth: Eating peanuts while pregnant will give your baby a nut allergy.
fact: There is no clear evidence that eating peanuts in pregnancy causes peanut allergy in the baby. You can eat peanuts and foods containing them as part of a healthy diet, unless you are allergic to them yourself or a health professional advises otherwise.
explanation: Advice to avoid peanuts in pregnancy was withdrawn once studies did not support it. Separately, research shows that introducing peanut foods to babies early, in a safe form, can lower the chance of peanut allergy. Whole nuts should never be given to young children because of choking.

sources.label: NHS — Foods to avoid in pregnancy

myth: Eating pineapple or a hot curry will bring on labour.
fact: There is no good evidence that pineapple, spicy food or other home remedies start labour. When labour needs to be started for medical reasons, it is done in hospital with methods such as a membrane sweep, medicines or breaking the waters.
explanation: Most babies arrive within two weeks either side of the due date, so whatever someone tried last often gets the credit. Spicy food can cause heartburn or an upset stomach, and some remedies such as castor oil can cause diarrhoea and dehydration. If you are overdue, your midwife will talk to you about your options.

sources.label: ACOG — When pregnancy goes past your due date

myth: Eating plenty of fruit and vegetables lowers your risk of heart disease and some cancers.
fact: Diets rich in fruit and vegetables are linked to lower risks of heart disease, stroke and some cancers. WHO recommends eating at least 400 grams, about five portions, of fruit and vegetables a day.
explanation: This advice is repeated so often that some people doubt it makes a real difference. Fruit and vegetables provide fibre, vitamins, minerals and other plant compounds, and help replace less healthy foods. Variety matters, and potatoes and other starchy roots do not count towards the five portions in WHO's guidance.

myth: Eating processed meat increases the risk of bowel cancer.
fact: The International Agency for Research on Cancer has classified processed meat, such as bacon, ham and sausages, as a cause of colorectal cancer, and red meat as a probable cause. The risk rises with the amount eaten.
explanation: This is sometimes dismissed because processed meat sits in the same 'group' as tobacco, which led to headlines that it is equally dangerous. The group reflects how strong the evidence is, not how big the risk is; smoking is far more harmful. Eating less processed meat and more fibre-rich foods is a reasonable step.

sources.label: WHO — Q&A on the carcinogenicity of red and processed meat

myth: Eating raw garlic cures infections and replaces antibiotics.
fact: Garlic contains compounds that affect bacteria in the laboratory, but there is no good evidence that eating it cures infections in people. It is not a substitute for antibiotics or other treatments when they are needed.
explanation: Garlic has a long history in folk medicine, and lab studies on its compound allicin are often quoted online. Effects seen in a dish do not translate into curing infections in the body. Large amounts of raw garlic can upset the stomach, and garlic supplements can increase bleeding risk with blood thinners.

myth: Eating rice gives you diabetes.
fact: No single food causes diabetes. Eating large amounts of white rice and other refined starches has been linked with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, especially alongside inactivity and weight gain, but rice can be part of a healthy diet.
explanation: Choosing brown or wholegrain rice more often, watching portion sizes and filling half the plate with vegetables can help. The overall pattern of diet, body weight and physical activity matters more than any one food.

myth: Eating six small meals a day 'stokes your metabolism' and helps you burn more fat.
fact: The energy your body uses to digest food depends mainly on how much you eat in total, not on how many meals you split it into. Studies comparing frequent small meals with fewer larger meals at the same calorie intake find no meaningful difference in weight loss.
explanation: Some people find smaller, regular meals help them manage hunger, and that is a perfectly good reason to eat that way. Others do better with three meals and fewer snacks. What matters most for weight is the overall amount and quality of food across the day.

sources.label: Harvard Health Publishing — The truth about metabolism

myth: Eating soy foods like tofu raises your risk of breast cancer.
fact: Eating soy foods as part of a normal diet does not raise breast cancer risk. Studies in women, including breast cancer survivors, have not found harm, and some suggest a possible lower risk.
explanation: Soy contains plant compounds called isoflavones that are weakly similar to oestrogen, which led to concern. The effects of concentrated soy isoflavone supplements are less clear, so women with a history of breast cancer may want to discuss those with their doctor.

myth: Eating sugar makes cancer grow faster, so cutting out sugar cures cancer.
fact: All cells, including healthy ones, use glucose for energy, and the body makes glucose even if you eat no sugar. Research has not shown that eating sugar makes cancer grow faster or that cutting it out shrinks tumours.
explanation: The idea comes from the fact that cancer cells use a lot of glucose, which is how some scans detect them. Indirectly, a diet high in sugar can contribute to weight gain, and obesity raises the risk of several cancers. People having cancer treatment often need enough energy to keep their weight up, so strict diets should be discussed with the care team.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Common cancer myths and misconceptions

myth: Eating too little puts your body into 'starvation mode' so you gain weight.
fact: When you eat less and lose weight, your body does burn somewhat less energy, which can slow weight loss over time. But eating too little does not cause weight gain on its own.
explanation: This idea is used to explain why weight loss stalls. The slowdown is real but modest, and stalls are often due to eating more than people realise or being less active. Very low intakes are still unwise without medical supervision because of nutrient shortfalls and muscle loss.

myth: Eating too much sugar directly causes diabetes.
fact: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition and is not caused by sugar or diet. Type 2 diabetes is linked to excess weight, inactivity, age and family history; sugary drinks and foods can contribute through weight gain, and sugary drinks in particular are linked to higher risk.
explanation: Because diabetes involves high blood sugar, it seems logical that eating sugar causes it. The relationship is indirect: a diet high in calories from any source, including sugar, raises the risk of type 2 diabetes. Cutting down on sugary drinks is still a sensible step.

myth: Echinacea reliably prevents and cures colds.
fact: Research on echinacea for colds has produced mixed results. Some studies suggest a small benefit in preventing colds, but there is no strong evidence that it cures them or shortens them substantially.
explanation: Echinacea products vary widely in the plant species, parts used and preparation, which makes results hard to compare. It may cause allergic reactions, especially in people allergic to plants in the daisy family. Rest, fluids and time remain the mainstays of cold care.

myth: Eczema and psoriasis are contagious.
fact: Eczema and psoriasis cannot be caught from another person. They are related to the immune system, genetics and skin barrier, not infection.
explanation: Visible rashes can lead to stigma, which affects quality of life. Eczema skin can sometimes become infected, and that infection may need treatment, but the condition itself does not spread.

myth: Eczema is caused by food, so cutting out foods like dairy or wheat will cure it.
fact: Atopic eczema is a long-term skin condition that often runs in families alongside asthma and hay fever. Certain foods can make it worse in some people, especially some babies with food allergies, but food is not the main cause for most people.
explanation: Cutting out food groups without medical advice can lead to poor nutrition, particularly in children. The mainstay of treatment is using emollients regularly, avoiding irritants such as soap, and using prescribed treatments like steroid creams during flare-ups. If you suspect a food trigger, talk to a GP before changing your diet.

myth: Educational videos and apps help babies learn to talk faster.
fact: Babies and toddlers learn language mainly through live, back-and-forth interaction with people, such as talking, reading and playing together. The WHO recommends no sedentary screen time for children under 2.
explanation: Studies have found that very young children learn far less from screens than from real conversation. Occasional video calls with family are different, because they involve real interaction. Reading aloud, singing and talking about what you are doing all help language develop.

sources.label: WHO — To grow up healthy, children need to sit less and play more

myth: Eggs are bad for your heart because of their cholesterol.
fact: For most people, cholesterol in food has a smaller effect on blood cholesterol than saturated and trans fats do. Eggs can be part of a healthy, balanced diet, although people with certain conditions may be advised to limit them.
explanation: Egg yolks are high in dietary cholesterol, which is why eggs were long seen as a heart risk. Research suggests moderate egg eating is not strongly linked to heart disease in healthy people, though findings vary and some people respond more strongly. How eggs are cooked and served, such as with bacon, sausages or butter, often matters more than the eggs.

myth: Elderberry syrup cures flu and prevents COVID-19.
fact: Some small studies suggest elderberry may ease cold and flu symptoms, but the evidence is limited and it is not a cure. There is no good evidence that it prevents or treats COVID-19.
explanation: Raw or unripe elderberries, and the leaves and stems, can cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea if not properly prepared. Flu vaccination and, for people at high risk, antiviral medicines prescribed by a doctor are the proven ways to prevent and treat flu.

myth: Electric ab belts give you a six-pack without exercise.
fact: The US Food and Drug Administration states that electrical muscle stimulators alone will not give you 'six-pack' abs. Repeated stimulation may strengthen muscles somewhat, but it does not remove the fat that covers them.
explanation: Visible abdominal muscles depend mostly on overall body fat, which changes through diet and activity. Many of these devices have not been cleared by regulators, and poorly made ones can cause shocks, burns or skin irritation. People with pacemakers or other implanted devices should not use them.

myth: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a barbaric treatment that fries your brain.
fact: Modern ECT is given under general anaesthetic with a muscle relaxant and is used mainly for severe depression and some other serious conditions when other treatments have not worked or rapid help is needed. It is one of the most effective treatments for severe depression.
explanation: Its image comes partly from older practices and films. ECT does have side effects, most notably short-term confusion and memory problems, and some people report longer-lasting memory gaps, so its risks and benefits need careful discussion. It is only given with consent, except in specific legal circumstances.

myth: Erectile dysfunction can be an early warning sign of heart disease.
fact: Erectile dysfunction is often caused by reduced blood flow, and it can appear before other signs of narrowed arteries. Doctors may check blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar.
explanation: Not everyone with ED has heart disease, and there are many other causes. It is a good reason to have a health check rather than a cause for alarm.

myth: Erectile dysfunction is just a normal part of getting old that you have to accept.
fact: Erectile dysfunction becomes more common with age, but it is not inevitable and it is often treatable at any age.
explanation: Causes include reduced blood flow, diabetes, medicines, stress and relationship issues. Treatments include lifestyle changes, medicines and talking therapies, so it is worth speaking to a doctor.

myth: Erection problems are mainly caused by low testosterone.
fact: Hormone problems are one possible cause, but erectile dysfunction is more often linked to conditions affecting blood flow, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes, or to stress, anxiety, alcohol and some medicines.
explanation: Taking testosterone will not fix erection problems that have other causes and has its own risks. Occasional problems are common and usually caused by tiredness, stress or alcohol. If it happens often, a GP can look for the cause and discuss treatments.

myth: Every bout of diarrhoea needs antibiotics to stop it.
fact: Most diarrhoea is caused by viruses or clears up on its own, and antibiotics do not help. The most important treatment is replacing lost fluids, ideally with oral rehydration solution (ORS); for children, zinc tablets are also recommended in many countries.
explanation: Antibiotics are only needed for certain bacterial infections, such as cholera or severe bloody diarrhoea, and using them unnecessarily causes side effects and resistance. Get medical help quickly for signs of dehydration, blood in the stool, high fever, or diarrhoea in a young baby.

myth: Everyone has hidden parasites and should do a parasite cleanse.
fact: Most people in countries with clean water and sanitation do not have intestinal parasites. Real parasite infections are diagnosed with tests, such as stool samples, and treated with specific medicines, not general 'cleanse' kits.
explanation: Social media videos often show strands of gut lining, mucus or undigested food passed after a cleanse and claim they are worms. Herbal parasite cleanses are not proven to work and some can cause side effects or interact with medicines. If you think you or your child has worms, such as itching around the bottom at night, a pharmacist or doctor can advise on proper treatment.

myth: Everyone is a little bit autistic.
fact: Many people share some traits seen in autism, such as liking routine or finding loud places tiring. Autism is diagnosed when differences in social communication and repetitive behaviours or sensory sensitivities are present from early childhood and have a significant effect on daily life.
explanation: The phrase is often meant kindly, but it can downplay the real challenges autistic people face. Autism is a lifelong difference in how people experience the world, not a scale everyone sits on. Anyone who thinks they may be autistic can ask a GP about an assessment.

myth: Everyone must drink exactly eight glasses of water a day.
fact: Fluid needs vary with body size, activity, climate and health. Guidance such as the NHS's suggestion of 6 to 8 glasses of fluid a day is a rough guide, and all drinks, including tea, coffee and milk, plus water in food, count towards it.
explanation: The 'eight glasses' rule is easy to remember but was never a strict scientific requirement. Thirst and pale yellow urine are useful guides for most healthy people. Some people, such as those with certain heart or kidney conditions, may be told to limit fluids.

myth: Everyone needs exactly eight hours of sleep a night.
fact: Most adults need around 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night, but individual needs vary. Children and teenagers need more.
explanation: Eight hours is a reasonable average, not a strict rule. A good sign you're getting enough is that you wake feeling refreshed and don't feel sleepy during the day. Regularly getting less than 7 hours is linked to health problems, so it's worth protecting your sleep time.

sources.label: NHLBI — How much sleep is enough?
Sleep Foundation — How much sleep do you need?

myth: Everyone needs to have their wisdom teeth taken out.
fact: Wisdom teeth only need removing if they are causing problems, such as repeated infection, decay, gum disease or damage to nearby teeth, often because there is not enough room for them to come through.
explanation: Many people keep their wisdom teeth without trouble. Removing healthy teeth 'just in case' carries the risks of surgery without clear benefit. Your dentist can check them and advise.

myth: Everyone on statins should take CoQ10 to stop muscle pain.
fact: The overall evidence does not show that coenzyme Q10 supplements reduce muscle pain caused by statins.
explanation: Most people who take statins do not get muscle side effects. If you do have muscle pain, talk to your doctor, who may check for other causes, change the dose or try a different statin. Do not stop a statin without advice, as it protects against heart attacks and strokes.

myth: Everyone over 50 should take a daily aspirin to prevent heart attacks.
fact: Low-dose aspirin is recommended for many people who have already had a heart attack or stroke. For people without heart disease, current guidance generally advises against routine daily aspirin because the bleeding risk can outweigh the benefit.
explanation: Advice on aspirin has changed as newer trials showed smaller benefits and real risks of stomach and brain bleeding. Whether aspirin is right depends on your personal risk. Do not start or stop daily aspirin without speaking to a doctor.

myth: Exercise will wear out arthritic joints faster.
fact: Regular, appropriate exercise is one of the main treatments for osteoarthritis. It reduces pain, improves function and strengthens muscles that support the joints.
explanation: Low-impact activities such as walking, swimming and cycling, plus strengthening exercises, are often recommended. A physiotherapist can tailor a plan, and some discomfort while starting is normal.

myth: Exercising in the evening will ruin your sleep.
fact: Regular exercise generally improves sleep quality, and evening exercise is fine for most people. Very vigorous workouts close to bedtime may make it harder for some people to fall asleep.
explanation: If you find late workouts keep you awake, try finishing intense exercise an hour or more before bed or switching to gentler activity in the evening. Getting active at whatever time you can manage is better than not exercising.

sources.label: Sleep Foundation — Best time of day to exercise for sleep

myth: Eye exercises can cure short-sightedness so you don't need glasses.
fact: Eye exercises cannot correct refractive errors such as short-sightedness, long-sightedness or astigmatism, which are due to the shape of the eye.
explanation: Some specific exercises are used for certain eye-muscle or focusing problems under specialist supervision. Glasses, contact lenses and laser surgery are the proven ways to correct refractive errors.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Fake tan or bronzer protects your skin from the sun.
fact: Self-tanning products colour the outer layer of the skin but do not protect it from UV rays unless they also contain sunscreen. In the US, tanning products without sunscreen must carry a warning saying so.
explanation: Fake tan is a much safer way to look tanned than sunbathing or sunbeds, but you still need sunscreen, shade and clothing. Tanning pills and injections sold online are not approved and can be harmful.

myth: Falls are just a normal part of getting older and can't be prevented.
fact: Falls are common in older age but many can be prevented. Strength and balance exercises, reviewing medicines, eyesight checks, safer homes and suitable footwear all reduce the risk.
explanation: Falls are a leading cause of injury in older people, and fear of falling can lead to less activity, which weakens muscles further. A GP can arrange a falls risk assessment. If someone falls and may have hurt their head, neck, back or hip, or cannot get up, call an ambulance.

myth: Fat around your waist is more harmful to health than fat elsewhere on your body.
fact: Fat stored deep around the abdominal organs (visceral fat) is more strongly linked to type 2 diabetes, heart disease and some other conditions than fat on the hips or thighs. That is why waist size is used alongside BMI to judge health risk.
explanation: You can carry extra visceral fat even if your weight is in the 'healthy' BMI range. A simple check is your waist measurement: as a general guide, your waist should be less than half your height. Regular activity, a balanced diet, enough sleep and limiting alcohol all help reduce visceral fat; sit-ups alone do not target it.

sources.label: Harvard Health Publishing — Taking aim at belly fat

myth: Fat-burning pills and slimming teas help you lose weight safely.
fact: There is little good evidence that over-the-counter weight-loss supplements or slimming teas lead to meaningful, lasting weight loss. Some have been found to contain hidden drugs or ingredients that can cause serious harm.
explanation: These products are heavily advertised on social media, often with before-and-after photos. Many slimming teas act as laxatives, so any quick weight drop is mostly water, not fat. Products containing stimulants can raise blood pressure and heart rate.

sources.label: NIH ODS — Dietary supplements for weight loss

myth: Feed a cold, starve a fever.
fact: There is no evidence that eating more helps a cold or that going without food helps a fever. With either illness, the main advice is to rest, drink plenty of fluids and eat as your appetite allows.
explanation: This saying is centuries old and was based on ideas about body heat rather than evidence. A fever increases fluid loss, so staying hydrated matters more than food. Not feeling hungry when unwell is normal, but avoiding food deliberately is not helpful.
keywords: should i eat with a fever

myth: Feeling depressed is just part of getting old.
fact: Depression is not a normal part of ageing. It is treatable at any age, and older adults respond to treatment much like younger people.
explanation: Loss, illness and isolation can raise the risk, and depression in older people is often missed or mistaken for physical illness or dementia. If you or someone you know is struggling, talking to a doctor is a good first step; anyone in crisis should get urgent help.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Female genital cutting (FGM) is cleaner and has health benefits.
fact: FGM has no health benefits. It can cause severe pain, bleeding, infections, problems passing urine, pain during sex, complications in childbirth and lasting psychological harm.
explanation: The WHO considers FGM a violation of the rights of girls and women, and it is illegal in many countries. It is sometimes justified by beliefs about hygiene, religion or marriage, but no religious text requires it. Specialist health services can support people who have had FGM, including with pregnancy and birth.

myth: Fertility falls off a cliff on your 35th birthday.
fact: Female fertility declines gradually with age, faster after about 35, but there is no sudden drop on a particular birthday. Many people conceive naturally after 35.
explanation: Age does increase the time to conceive and the risk of miscarriage and some complications. People over 35 are often advised to seek help sooner if they have not conceived after six months of trying.

myth: Fibroids are a type of cancer.
fact: Fibroids are non-cancerous growths in or around the womb. They are very common, and many people with fibroids have no symptoms at all.
explanation: When they do cause symptoms, these can include heavy or painful periods, tummy pain or needing to pee often. Treatment depends on symptoms and may include medicines or surgery; fibroids that cause no problems often need no treatment. They tend to shrink after the menopause.

myth: Fibromyalgia isn't a real condition; it's all in people's heads.
fact: Fibromyalgia is a recognised long-term condition that causes widespread pain, increased sensitivity to pain, tiredness, sleep problems and difficulty concentrating. It is thought to involve changes in how the nervous system processes pain.
explanation: There is no single test for it, which has led to doubt, but it is diagnosed from symptoms and by ruling out other conditions. There is no cure, but exercise, talking therapies, some medicines and good sleep habits can help manage symptoms.

myth: Fish contains too much mercury to be worth eating.
fact: For most people the benefits of eating fish outweigh the risks. Health services recommend about two portions of fish a week, including one of oily fish, but advise limiting certain large predatory fish such as shark, swordfish and marlin, which contain more mercury.
explanation: Pregnant women, women planning pregnancy and children have specific limits on some fish. Smaller fish such as sardines, salmon and mackerel are generally low in mercury and rich in omega-3 fats.

myth: Fish oil capsules prevent heart attacks.
fact: Most large trials have found that standard fish oil supplements do not prevent heart attacks or strokes in the general population. Eating oily fish as part of a healthy diet is linked to better heart health, and some prescription omega-3 medicines are used for specific people with high triglycerides.
explanation: The link between fish-eating populations and lower heart disease led to supplement popularity. Some studies have linked omega-3 supplements to a higher risk of atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm. Speak to a doctor if you are considering omega-3 for a heart condition.

myth: Fish oil supplements cure dry eyes.
fact: Some small studies suggested omega-3 supplements might ease dry eye symptoms, but a large year-long NIH-funded trial (the DREAM study) found them no better than a placebo. The evidence is mixed and they are not a cure.
explanation: Dry eye can have many causes, including screen use, ageing, hormonal changes, blepharitis and some medicines. Lubricating drops, warm compresses and lid hygiene help many people. See an optometrist if symptoms persist.

sources.label: NCCIH — Omega-3 supplements: what you need to know

myth: Flat cola or sports drinks are the best treatment for diarrhoea and vomiting.
fact: Fizzy drinks and fruit juices contain a lot of sugar and too little salt, and can make diarrhoea worse, especially in children. Oral rehydration solutions are designed to replace lost fluid and salts and are recommended for people at risk of dehydration.
explanation: Flat cola is a common home remedy, and for a healthy adult with mild illness small sips of any fluid are better than none. Babies and young children are at higher risk of dehydration and should keep feeding, with oral rehydration solution if advised. Seek help for signs of dehydration such as very little urine, drowsiness or a dry mouth.

myth: Flossing is pointless.
fact: The research evidence for flossing specifically is limited, but cleaning between the teeth with floss or interdental brushes is still recommended because a toothbrush cannot reach those surfaces.
explanation: Headlines about weak flossing studies led some people to stop. Many dentists find interdental brushes easier and effective. Ask your dentist which method suits you.

myth: Flu is just a bad cold.
fact: Flu is caused by different viruses from the common cold and is usually more severe, often with sudden fever, body aches and exhaustion. Seasonal flu causes hundreds of thousands of deaths worldwide each year, according to WHO.
