fact: Strength training builds strength and bone health in women, but large increases in muscle size are difficult to achieve and usually need specific, intensive training and diet.
explanation: Women typically have lower testosterone levels than men, which limits muscle growth. Guidelines recommend muscle-strengthening activities for all adults at least two days a week.

myth: Liver detox supplements and teas cleanse your liver after drinking or unhealthy eating.
fact: A healthy liver clears waste and alcohol by itself, and no supplement has been shown to 'detox' it. Some herbal and dietary supplements can actually damage the liver.
explanation: The best ways to protect your liver are to drink less alcohol, keep to a healthy weight and get vaccinated against hepatitis B if advised. Liver disease often causes no symptoms until it is advanced, so people with heavy drinking or other risk factors may need blood tests rather than detox products.

sources.label: NCCIH — "Detoxes" and "cleanses": what you need to know

myth: Living near power lines gives you cancer.
fact: Most studies have not found that the electric and magnetic fields from power lines cause cancer. Some studies found a weak link with childhood leukaemia at the highest exposures, but it has not been shown that power lines are the cause.
explanation: The fields from power lines and household wiring are low-energy and do not damage DNA in the way that X-rays or UV light can. Research continues, but the evidence is weak and inconsistent.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Electromagnetic fields and cancer

myth: Loneliness and social isolation can harm your physical health, not just your mood.
fact: The WHO describes social isolation and loneliness as serious risks to health. They are linked with a higher risk of stroke, heart disease, diabetes, cognitive decline, depression and early death.
explanation: Older adults are at particular risk because of bereavement, retirement, health problems or hearing loss. Staying in touch with others, joining groups or volunteering can help. If you or someone you know is struggling with loneliness, a GP or local community services can suggest support.

sources.label: WHO — Social connection linked to improved health and reduced risk of early death (June 2025)

myth: Long COVID isn't real; it's just anxiety or people being lazy.
fact: Long COVID (post COVID-19 condition) is recognised by the WHO and health services. It describes symptoms such as fatigue, breathlessness and problems with memory and concentration that last for months after infection and cannot be explained by another cause.
explanation: It can affect people who had a mild infection. Symptoms can come and go and may affect the ability to work or study. Support services and rehabilitation can help, and many people improve over time.

myth: Losing even a small amount of weight can improve your health.
fact: For people living with overweight or obesity, losing around 5 to 10% of body weight can improve blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar and lower the risk of type 2 diabetes.
explanation: Many people feel discouraged because they are far from their 'ideal' weight. Health benefits start well before that point. Being more active and eating better can also improve health independently of weight change.

myth: Losing weight can ease knee and hip arthritis.
fact: Being overweight puts extra strain on weight-bearing joints such as the knees and hips. Losing weight if you are overweight is one of the recommended ways to ease osteoarthritis symptoms, alongside regular exercise.
explanation: Even a modest weight loss can reduce pain and improve how well the joints work for many people. Exercise strengthens the muscles that support the joints. A GP or physiotherapist can help plan activity that suits your joints.

myth: Losing weight slowly and steadily is more likely to last than losing it fast.
fact: Health services generally advise aiming to lose about 0.5 to 1 kg (1 to 2 lb) a week through lasting changes to eating and activity. Habits you can keep up are the key to keeping weight off.
explanation: Very rapid weight loss from extreme diets tends to include water and muscle, can cause gallstones, and is often regained. That said, some medically supervised low-calorie programmes produce faster early loss and can work well for some people with support. The overall message is to choose a plan you can maintain.

myth: Losing your teeth is a normal part of getting old.
fact: Tooth loss is mainly caused by tooth decay and gum disease, which are largely preventable, not by ageing itself. With good care, many people keep their natural teeth for life.
explanation: Older adults may face extra risks, such as dry mouth from medicines and receding gums, so regular dental check-ups remain important. Brushing with fluoride toothpaste, cleaning between teeth, limiting sugar and not smoking all help. Dentures and implants can replace missing teeth if needed.

myth: Low-fat or 'light' products are always healthier and help you lose weight.
fact: Some low-fat products have extra sugar or other ingredients added to improve taste, so they may not be lower in calories. Reading nutrition labels gives a better picture than the 'low-fat' claim alone.
explanation: Choosing lower-fat versions of some foods, like milk or cooking methods, can reduce saturated fat and calories. But a 'light' label can encourage eating larger amounts. Unsaturated fats from foods like nuts, olive oil and oily fish are part of a healthy diet.

myth: Lying with your legs up in the air after sex helps you get pregnant.
fact: There is no good evidence that lying with your legs raised, or any particular sex position, makes pregnancy more likely. Sperm reach the cervix within minutes of ejaculation, whatever position you are in.
explanation: What makes the biggest difference is having regular sex, every two to three days, throughout the cycle. Some semen leaking out afterwards is normal and does not reduce your chances. If you enjoy lying down for a while, it does no harm.

myth: Lymphatic drainage massage flushes out toxins, de-bloats you and helps you lose weight.
fact: Manual lymphatic drainage is a specialised massage used, with compression and exercise, to help manage lymphoedema, a condition where fluid builds up because the lymphatic system is damaged. There is no good evidence that it removes 'toxins' or reduces body fat in healthy people.
explanation: Any slimmer look after a session is temporary fluid movement. Massage can feel relaxing, which is a perfectly good reason to have one, but it is not a weight-loss treatment. Swelling in one limb or that does not go away should be checked by a doctor rather than treated with home massage.

sources.label: NCCIH — Massage therapy: what you need to know

myth: Magnesium supplements or a 'sleepy girl mocktail' will cure your insomnia.
fact: Research suggests magnesium may help sleep in some people, particularly those with low magnesium levels, but the evidence is limited and it is not a proven treatment for insomnia. Drinks combining magnesium powder with tart cherry juice have not been properly studied.
explanation: A calming bedtime drink can be part of a relaxing routine, and most people get enough magnesium from foods like nuts, leafy greens and whole grains. Magnesium supplements can cause diarrhoea and may not be suitable for people with kidney disease. Long-term insomnia is best treated with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I).

myth: Magnetic or copper bracelets ease arthritis pain.
fact: Research has not found conclusive evidence that static magnets, including magnetic bracelets, relieve pain. Copper bracelets have not been shown to work better than placebo bracelets in studies.
explanation: Arthritis pain naturally goes up and down, so improvement after buying a bracelet can feel convincing. Magnets can interfere with pacemakers and some other medical devices. Exercise, weight loss if needed, and pain relief advised by a doctor or pharmacist have better evidence.

sources.label: NCCIH — Magnets for pain: what you need to know

myth: Mammograms cause breast cancer or make it spread because of the radiation and squeezing.
fact: Mammograms use a very low dose of radiation, and for women of screening age the benefit of finding cancer early is considered to outweigh this small risk. Compressing the breast during a mammogram does not cause cancer to spread.
explanation: Screening does have downsides that are worth knowing: it can miss some cancers and can find cancers that would never have caused harm, leading to treatment that was not needed. Screening programmes explain these trade-offs so you can choose. Report any breast changes to a GP even if you had a normal mammogram recently.

myth: Many people need a vitamin D supplement in winter.
fact: In countries with little winter sunshine, such as the UK, health authorities advise considering a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter, because the body cannot make enough from sunlight then. Some groups are advised to take it all year.
explanation: Advice varies by country, skin colour, age and lifestyle, so this does not apply to everyone everywhere. People with darker skin, those who cover their skin or rarely go outdoors, and some older adults are at higher risk of low vitamin D. Taking very high doses for long periods can be harmful.

sources.label: NIH ODS — Vitamin D fact sheet

myth: Measles is a mild childhood illness that everyone used to get.
fact: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases and can cause pneumonia, brain inflammation (encephalitis), blindness and death. WHO estimates that it still kills more than 100,000 people a year worldwide, mostly young children.
explanation: Older generations often remember measles as a normal part of childhood, and many children did recover. But the deaths and disabilities it caused were also common before vaccination. Measles can also weaken the immune system for months or years afterwards.

myth: Measles outbreaks are caused by vaccinated people spreading the virus.
fact: Measles outbreaks happen when the virus reaches groups where too few people are vaccinated. The weakened virus in the MMR vaccine is not known to spread from a vaccinated person to others.
explanation: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known, so very high vaccination coverage is needed to stop it spreading. Most people who catch measles in outbreaks are unvaccinated. Two doses of MMR vaccine give strong, long-lasting protection.

sources.label: NHS — MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine

myth: Medicines sold cheaply at markets, roadside stalls or on social media are just as good as those from a pharmacy.
fact: Medicines from unregulated sellers are much more likely to be substandard or falsified. They may contain the wrong amount of the active ingredient, the wrong ingredient, or toxic substances.
explanation: Falsified medicines can fail to treat serious illnesses such as malaria and infections, contribute to drug resistance, and cause poisoning. Buy medicines from licensed pharmacies, check packaging, and report anything that looks suspicious or does not work as expected.

sources.label: WHO — Substandard and falsified medical products

myth: Melatonin is a natural, harmless sleeping pill everyone can take.
fact: Melatonin can help with some sleep problems, such as jet lag or certain body clock disorders, but its effect on general insomnia is modest. It can cause side effects and interact with medicines.
explanation: In some countries melatonin is prescription-only; in others it is sold as a supplement whose actual content can differ from the label. Children and pregnant people should only use it on medical advice.

myth: Men can't get breast cancer.
fact: Men have breast tissue and can get breast cancer, although it is much rarer than in women.
explanation: It usually affects older men. A lump, nipple changes or discharge should be checked by a doctor rather than ignored.

myth: Men don't really get depression; real men just tough it out.
fact: Men do get depression, but they are less likely to be diagnosed or to seek help. In many countries men die by suicide at higher rates than women.
explanation: In men, depression may show as anger, irritability, risk-taking, heavy drinking or overworking. Asking for help is a strength. Talking to a GP, doctor or helpline is a good first step, and anyone in crisis should contact emergency services or a crisis line.

myth: Men go through a menopause just like women.
fact: Testosterone falls gradually in men, by a small amount each year from around 30 to 40, rather than dropping suddenly as oestrogen does at menopause. True testosterone deficiency is uncommon.
explanation: Symptoms often blamed on a 'male menopause', such as low mood, tiredness or low sex drive, are frequently linked to stress, lifestyle, depression or other health problems. A doctor can check what is going on.

myth: Menopause is just hot flushes and periods stopping.
fact: Menopause can bring a wide range of symptoms, including sleep problems, low mood, anxiety, brain fog, joint aches, vaginal dryness and reduced sex drive, as well as hot flushes.
explanation: Lower oestrogen after menopause also increases the risk of osteoporosis. Symptoms vary a lot between people; treatments including hormone replacement therapy and non-hormonal options can help.

myth: Menopause only happens in your fifties.
fact: The average age of menopause is around 51, but it can happen earlier. Menopause before 45 is called early menopause and before 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency.
explanation: Perimenopause symptoms can start several years before periods stop. Early menopause can also follow surgery or cancer treatment. Anyone with symptoms at a younger age should see a doctor, as treatment may protect bones and heart.

myth: Metformin damages your kidneys.
fact: Metformin does not damage the kidneys. Because it is cleared by the kidneys, doctors check kidney function and may lower the dose or stop it if the kidneys are not working well.
explanation: High blood sugar from untreated or poorly controlled diabetes is a major cause of kidney damage, so stopping metformin out of fear can do more harm. Common side effects are stomach upset and diarrhoea, which often settle or improve with slow-release tablets.

myth: Microwaving destroys all the nutrients in food.
fact: All cooking methods change nutrients to some degree. Microwaving often keeps nutrients as well as or better than boiling, because it uses shorter cooking times and less water.
explanation: Some vitamins, such as vitamin C and some B vitamins, are sensitive to heat and leak into cooking water. Because microwaving is quick and uses little water, vegetables can keep more of these vitamins. Steaming is another good option.

myth: Microwaving food makes it radioactive or causes cancer.
fact: Microwave ovens heat food using non-ionising radiation that makes water molecules vibrate. This does not make food radioactive or change it in a way that causes cancer, and ovens are built to keep microwaves inside.
explanation: The word 'radiation' makes many people think of nuclear radiation, which is a different, high-energy type. A real safety point is to use microwave-safe containers, because some plastics not designed for heating can warp or leach chemicals. Damaged ovens with doors that do not close properly should be repaired or replaced.

myth: Miracle Mineral Solution (MMS, chlorine dioxide) cures autism, COVID-19 and other diseases.
fact: MMS becomes chlorine dioxide, a type of industrial bleach, when mixed as instructed. It has no proven health benefits and can cause severe vomiting, diarrhoea, dangerously low blood pressure and life-threatening reactions.
explanation: MMS has been promoted online and in private groups as a cure for autism, cancer, HIV and COVID-19. US regulators have warned consumers not to buy or drink it, and sellers have been prosecuted. If someone has swallowed it and is unwell, contact a poison centre or emergency services.

myth: Miscarriage is rare and usually happens because the mother did something wrong.
fact: Miscarriage is common: about 1 in 8 known pregnancies ends in miscarriage, and many more happen before a person knows they are pregnant. Most early miscarriages are caused by chromosome problems in the baby and are not caused by anything the mother did.
explanation: Normal activities such as work, exercise, sex or a fall or shock are not usually the cause. Having one miscarriage does not mean you will not have a successful pregnancy next time. If you have had three or more in a row, doctors may offer tests to look for a cause.

myth: Mobile phones and 5G cause brain cancer.
fact: Large studies have not found consistent evidence that mobile phone use causes brain tumours or other cancers. Mobile phones and 5G networks use non-ionising radio waves, which do not damage DNA the way X-rays or UV light can.
explanation: In 2011 the International Agency for Research on Cancer classed radiofrequency fields as 'possibly carcinogenic', a category meaning evidence is limited and inconclusive, which is often misreported. Brain cancer rates have not risen in line with the huge growth in phone use. Using a headset or speaker reduces exposure for anyone who wants to be cautious.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Cell phones and cancer risk
National Cancer Institute — Common cancer myths and misconceptions

myth: Morning sickness only happens in the morning.
fact: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy can happen at any time of day or night.
explanation: It usually eases by around 16 to 20 weeks. Severe vomiting where you cannot keep fluids down may be hyperemesis gravidarum, which needs prompt medical care.

myth: Mpox only affects gay men.
fact: Anyone can catch mpox through close contact with an infected person, including skin-to-skin and sexual contact, contact with contaminated items, or from infected animals. It affects people of any sex or sexuality.
explanation: During the 2022 global outbreak most cases were in men who have sex with men, but outbreaks in parts of Africa have affected children and whole households. Vaccines are available for people at higher risk. Stigma can stop people from getting tested and treated.

myth: mRNA COVID-19 vaccines can, rarely, cause inflammation of the heart.
fact: Yes. Myocarditis and pericarditis are rare side effects of mRNA COVID-19 vaccines, seen mostly in young males, usually within days of a dose. Most cases are mild and people recover with treatment and rest.
explanation: Health agencies identified this risk through safety monitoring and updated their advice, for example on which vaccines to offer to which age groups. COVID-19 infection can also cause heart inflammation. Seek medical help after vaccination if you have chest pain, shortness of breath or a fast, fluttering or pounding heartbeat.

myth: mRNA COVID-19 vaccines change your DNA.
fact: mRNA vaccines never enter the cell nucleus, where DNA is kept, and cannot alter your genes. The mRNA gives cells temporary instructions to make a harmless protein, and it is broken down by the body within days.
explanation: The word 'genetic' in descriptions of mRNA technology led many people to assume it edits genes. Human cells read mRNA all the time as a normal part of making proteins. The vaccine mRNA is fragile, which is why some of these vaccines had to be kept very cold.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: MSG (monosodium glutamate) is dangerous and causes 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'.
fact: MSG is considered safe to eat by food safety agencies, including the US FDA. Studies have not consistently shown that MSG causes headaches or other symptoms in normal amounts eaten with food.
explanation: The term 'Chinese restaurant syndrome' came from a 1968 letter and spread with little evidence, and it has been criticised as reflecting bias. Glutamate occurs naturally in foods such as tomatoes, cheese and mushrooms. A small number of people may report short-lived mild symptoms after large amounts of MSG without food.

sources.label: FDA — Questions and answers on monosodium glutamate (MSG)

myth: Muscle cramps mean you're low on potassium, so eat a banana.
fact: Most leg cramps have no clear cause and are not due to low potassium. They are usually harmless and short-lived, and stretching and massaging the muscle can ease them.
explanation: Cramps can be linked to exercise, pregnancy, getting older, some medicines and some health conditions. Bananas are a healthy snack, but there is little evidence they prevent cramps. See a GP if cramps are frequent, severe, disrupt your sleep, or come with swelling, numbness or muscle weakness.

myth: My smartwatch or sleep app tells me exactly how much deep and REM sleep I get.
fact: Consumer sleep trackers can give a useful rough picture of sleep timing and patterns, but they are not perfectly accurate, especially at telling sleep stages apart. A formal sleep study is needed to measure sleep stages reliably.
explanation: Some people become anxious about their sleep scores, which can itself make sleep worse. Use trackers to spot trends, but pay more attention to how you feel during the day. If you're concerned about your sleep, talk to a doctor.

sources.label: Sleep Foundation — Sleep trackers: are they accurate?

myth: Napping during the day always ruins your night's sleep.
fact: Short naps of around 20 to 30 minutes early in the afternoon can improve alertness without harming night sleep for most people.
explanation: Long or late naps can make it harder to fall asleep at night, so people with insomnia are often advised to avoid them. A strong need to nap every day can also be a sign of poor night sleep worth looking into.

myth: Needing your blue reliever inhaler several times a week is normal if you have asthma.
fact: When asthma is well controlled, most people rarely need their reliever inhaler. Needing it 3 or more times a week is a sign that asthma is not well controlled and should be reviewed by a doctor or asthma nurse.
explanation: Often the answer is a regular preventer inhaler, a different treatment or a better inhaler technique. Relying on a reliever alone leaves the underlying inflammation untreated and raises the risk of a serious attack.

myth: Night owls are just undisciplined; anyone can become a morning person if they try.
fact: People have different natural sleep-timing preferences, called chronotypes, which are partly genetic and change with age. Habits can shift sleep timing somewhat, but not everyone can comfortably become an early riser.
explanation: Getting bright light in the morning, dimming lights in the evening and keeping a consistent schedule, even at weekends, can help move your body clock earlier. Being a night owl is not a character flaw, though it can be harder in a world built around early starts.

myth: No pain, no gain: exercise only works if it hurts.
fact: Exercise does not need to be painful to be beneficial. Moderate activity that makes you breathe harder but still lets you talk brings major health benefits.
explanation: Some muscle soreness a day or two after new or harder exercise is normal. Sharp pain, joint pain or chest pain during exercise is a signal to stop and get it checked.

myth: Nobody in my family has diabetes, so I can't get it.
fact: Family history raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, but many people develop it without any affected relatives. Other risk factors include being overweight, physical inactivity, age, ethnicity and a history of gestational diabetes.
explanation: People of South Asian, Black African, African Caribbean and some other backgrounds have a higher risk and may develop type 2 diabetes at a younger age and a lower weight. Type 2 diabetes often has no symptoms at first, so a blood test is the only way to be sure.

sources.label: NIDDK — Risk factors for type 2 diabetes

myth: Noni juice cures cancer, diabetes and high blood pressure.
fact: Noni has not been shown to have a beneficial effect on any health condition in studies of people.
explanation: Several cases of liver damage have been reported in people drinking noni juice or tea, although it is not certain noni was the cause. Noni is high in potassium, which can be risky for people with kidney disease or taking some blood pressure medicines.

myth: Not getting enough sleep can make it harder to manage your weight.
fact: Regularly sleeping too little is linked to a higher risk of weight gain and obesity. Short sleep can affect hormones that control hunger and fullness and tends to increase snacking and cravings for high-calorie food.
explanation: Most of the evidence comes from observational studies and short experiments, so sleep is one factor among many rather than the main cause of weight gain. Still, aiming for enough regular sleep is a useful part of any plan to manage weight. Ongoing sleep problems, such as loud snoring with pauses in breathing, are worth discussing with a doctor.

sources.label: NHLBI — Sleep deprivation and deficiency: health effects

myth: Nothing can be done for macular degeneration.
fact: Wet age-related macular degeneration can often be treated with injections into the eye that slow or stop vision loss, especially if started early. For dry AMD there is no cure yet, but certain vitamin supplements can slow progression in people with intermediate disease.
explanation: Sudden changes such as straight lines looking wavy or a dark patch in central vision should be checked urgently, because wet AMD can progress quickly. Low-vision aids, good lighting and support services help people make the most of their sight. Not smoking lowers the risk.

sources.label: National Eye Institute — Age-related macular degeneration

myth: Nothing can be done for osteoarthritis, so you just have to live with the pain.
fact: Although osteoarthritis cannot be cured, its symptoms can often be eased. Regular exercise, losing weight if needed, suitable footwear, pain relief, physiotherapy and, for severe cases, joint replacement surgery can all help.
explanation: Staying active is one of the most effective treatments, even though it may feel counterintuitive when joints hurt. Many people find their symptoms vary and do not always get worse. A GP can help put together a plan and refer to physiotherapy if needed.

myth: Numbing gels from the pharmacy are the safest go-to for a teething baby.
fact: Gels containing benzocaine or lidocaine offer little benefit for teething and have been linked to serious side effects in young children, including a rare blood disorder (methaemoglobinaemia) with benzocaine. The US FDA advises against using them for teething.
explanation: Products sold for teething vary by country, so always check the ingredients and age guidance and ask a pharmacist. Homeopathic teething tablets are also not recommended. A chilled teething ring, gum massage and, if needed, infant paracetamol or ibuprofen at the right dose are the usual advice.

sources.label: FDA — Safely soothing teething pain in infants and children

myth: Nuts are unhealthy because they are high in fat.
fact: Most of the fat in nuts is unsaturated, and nuts also provide protein, fibre, vitamins and minerals. Eating a small handful of unsalted nuts regularly is linked to better heart health.
explanation: Nuts are high in calories, so portion size matters if you are watching your weight. Choose plain, unsalted nuts rather than salted, sugar-coated or chocolate-covered ones.

sources.label: NHLBI — Heart-healthy living: choose heart-healthy foods

myth: OCD just means being very neat and tidy.
fact: Obsessive-compulsive disorder is a mental health condition with unwanted, distressing thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours (compulsions) that take up a lot of time and interfere with life.
explanation: Liking things orderly is a personality trait, not OCD. Obsessions in OCD can be about contamination, harm, doubt or many other themes, and treatments such as CBT with exposure and response prevention help.

myth: Okra water, bitter gourd (karela) juice or fenugreek can cure diabetes.
fact: There is no good evidence that okra water, bitter melon, fenugreek or similar home remedies cure diabetes. Some may have small effects on blood sugar, but they are not a substitute for proven treatment.
explanation: These remedies are widely shared on WhatsApp and in family traditions. Combining them with diabetes medicines can sometimes lower blood sugar too much. Eating these vegetables as part of a balanced diet is fine, but talk to your diabetes team before relying on them.

myth: Older people can't learn new things because the brain stops changing after childhood.
fact: The brain stays able to change and form new connections throughout life. Older adults can learn new skills, languages and habits.
explanation: Learning may take a little longer with age, but practice, motivation and staying active all help. Learning new things is also thought to support brain health.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Older people need less sleep.
fact: Older adults need about the same amount of sleep as younger adults, around seven to nine hours. Sleep tends to become lighter and more broken with age, which can make it harder to get.
explanation: Changes in body clock, health conditions, medicines and needing the toilet at night can reduce sleep in later life. Ongoing poor sleep is not something to accept as normal and can often be improved.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Once an adult tooth is knocked out, it can't be saved.
fact: A knocked-out adult tooth can often be saved if it is put back in its socket, or kept in milk, and a dentist is seen as soon as possible, ideally within an hour. Hold it by the crown, not the root, and rinse briefly in milk or saline if dirty.
explanation: Do not scrub the tooth or let it dry out. Baby teeth should never be put back in, as this can damage the adult tooth underneath, but the child should still see a dentist. Speed matters, so treat it as a dental emergency.

myth: Once you have a mental illness you never get better.
fact: Many people recover fully or manage their symptoms well with treatment and support. Recovery is common, though it can take time and may involve setbacks.
explanation: Some conditions are long-term, but treatment, therapy, medication and social support can let people live full lives. Getting help early generally improves outcomes. If you are struggling, talking to a GP, a doctor or a mental health helpline is a good first step.

myth: Once you have osteoporosis, nothing can be done about it.
fact: Osteoporosis can be treated. Medicines can strengthen bones and lower the risk of fractures, and exercise, enough calcium and vitamin D, and steps to prevent falls also help.
explanation: Treatment depends on your fracture risk, age and other health conditions. Stopping smoking and drinking less alcohol help protect bones. A GP can explain the options and whether a bone density scan is needed.

myth: Once you start insulin, you become addicted to it.
fact: Insulin is not addictive. It is a hormone the body needs; people with type 1 diabetes cannot make it, and many people with type 2 diabetes make too little as the condition progresses.
explanation: Needing insulin is a sign of how diabetes changes over time, not a personal failure or an addiction. Some people with type 2 diabetes use insulin for a while and later reduce or stop it under medical guidance, for example after weight loss.

sources.label: NIDDK — Insulin, medicines, and other diabetes treatments

myth: Once you're an adult your bones are fixed, so nothing you do changes them.
fact: Bone is living tissue that is constantly being broken down and rebuilt throughout life. Most people build their maximum bone mass by early adulthood, and after that bone is slowly lost with age, faster after the menopause.
explanation: Physical activity, especially weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercise, a diet with enough calcium and vitamin D, not smoking and limiting alcohol help keep bones strong at any age. Building strong bones in childhood and young adulthood lowers the risk of osteoporosis later.

myth: Once you've had a caesarean, all your future babies have to be born by caesarean.
fact: Many people who have had a caesarean can safely have a vaginal birth next time, known as VBAC (vaginal birth after caesarean). Most of those who plan a VBAC give birth vaginally.
explanation: Whether VBAC is a good option depends on the reason for the previous caesarean, the type of cut in the womb, how many caesareans you have had and your current pregnancy. There is a small risk of the scar opening during labour, so labour is monitored in hospital. Your midwife or obstetrician can help you weigh up the choices.

sources.label: ACOG — Vaginal birth after cesarean delivery

myth: Once you've had dengue, a second infection will be milder.
fact: A second dengue infection with a different type of the virus raises the risk of severe dengue. There are four types of dengue virus, and having one gives lasting protection only against that type.
explanation: Severe dengue can cause bleeding, organ damage and dangerously low blood pressure. Anyone who has had dengue before should be especially careful to avoid mosquito bites and should seek care quickly for warning signs such as severe stomach pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums or extreme tiredness.

myth: Once you've lost weight on injections like Wegovy or Ozempic, you can stop them and the weight will stay off.
fact: Medicines such as semaglutide can help people with obesity lose a meaningful amount of weight when used alongside changes to diet and activity. In studies, many people regained much of the lost weight within a year of stopping the medicine.
explanation: These medicines work by reducing appetite, and appetite tends to return when they are stopped. They can also cause side effects such as nausea, vomiting and constipation, and should only be used under medical supervision, not bought from unregulated online sellers. Building eating and activity habits during treatment gives the best chance of keeping weight off.

sources.label: NIDDK — Prescription medications to treat overweight & obesity

myth: Once your blood pressure is normal, you can stop taking your tablets.
fact: Blood pressure is often normal because the medicine is working. Stopping without medical advice usually lets it rise again, increasing the risk of stroke and heart attack.
explanation: People often feel well and see a normal reading, so assume they are cured. Some people can reduce or stop medication after lasting lifestyle changes, but this should be done with a doctor and with monitoring. Never stop suddenly without advice, as some medicines need to be reduced gradually.

sources.label: American Heart Association — High blood pressure

myth: One application of sunscreen in the morning protects you all day.
fact: Sunscreen wears off. Health services recommend reapplying it at least every 2 hours, and straight after swimming, towel drying or sweating, even if it is labelled water-resistant or 'once a day'.
explanation: Most people also apply too little sunscreen, which lowers its protection. Use it generously, and combine it with shade, especially around midday, and protective clothing and sunglasses.

sources.label: American Academy of Dermatology — How to apply sunscreen

myth: One high blood pressure reading means you have high blood pressure for life.
fact: A single high reading is not enough to diagnose high blood pressure. Blood pressure changes during the day and can rise with stress, activity, caffeine or being at the doctor's surgery, so the diagnosis is confirmed with repeated readings, often using home or 24-hour monitoring.
explanation: Equally, one normal reading does not rule it out. If you are told your blood pressure is high, follow up with repeat checks. Home monitors can help; sit quietly for a few minutes before measuring and use a correctly sized cuff.

myth: Only dirty people get scabies.
fact: Scabies is an itchy rash caused by tiny mites that spread through close skin-to-skin contact, and anyone can get it, regardless of how clean they are. Washing does not prevent or cure it.
explanation: Scabies often spreads within households, care homes and between sexual partners. It is treated with creams or lotions from a pharmacy, and everyone in the household should be treated at the same time, even without symptoms. Washing bedding and clothes on a hot wash helps prevent reinfection.

myth: Only elderly people get dementia.
fact: Dementia mostly affects older people, but it can begin before 65. This is called young-onset dementia.
explanation: Young-onset dementia can be missed because symptoms are blamed on stress, depression or menopause. Anyone with ongoing changes in memory, behaviour or thinking should see a doctor.

myth: Only heavy drinkers get fatty liver disease.
fact: Fatty liver disease that is not caused by alcohol is very common and is mainly linked to being overweight, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol. It often causes no symptoms in its early stages.
explanation: This condition is now often called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), previously non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Early stages can improve with weight loss, regular activity and a healthy diet. Without changes, it can progress to scarring of the liver in some people.

myth: Only men can be colour-blind.
fact: Colour vision deficiency is much more common in men because the genes for the most common type are on the X chromosome, but women can have it too. Red-green colour blindness, the most common type, affects many times more men than women.
explanation: Women who carry the gene can pass it to their sons. Colour vision problems can also develop later in life because of eye diseases, some medicines or injury, in both men and women. Simple tests at an optician can check colour vision.

myth: Only mothers can get depression after a baby is born; fathers can't.
fact: Fathers and partners can also develop depression after having a baby. Changes in sleep, relationships, money and responsibilities, and a partner's own mental health, can all play a part.
explanation: Men may be less likely to talk about how they feel or to recognise symptoms such as low mood, irritability, withdrawing or drinking more. Depression after a baby is treatable. Speaking to a GP or a health visitor is a good first step.

myth: Only old people get arthritis.
fact: Arthritis can affect people of any age, including children. Rheumatoid arthritis often starts between 30 and 50, and juvenile arthritis affects children.
explanation: Osteoarthritis does become more common with age. Joint pain, swelling or stiffness that lasts should be checked at any age, because early treatment of inflammatory arthritis can prevent damage.

myth: Only older people get high blood pressure.
fact: High blood pressure becomes more common with age, but young adults and even children can have it. It often causes no symptoms at any age.
explanation: Risk factors include being overweight, eating a lot of salt, drinking too much alcohol, not being active, a family history, and some kidney and hormone conditions. Adults should have their blood pressure checked regularly, for example every five years, and more often if it is borderline or high.

myth: Only older people have strokes.
fact: The risk of stroke rises with age, but strokes can happen at any age, including in young adults and, rarely, in children and babies.
explanation: High blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol and atrial fibrillation are major risk factors at any age. Remember FAST: face drooping, arm weakness, speech problems, time to call an emergency number. Fast treatment can greatly improve recovery.

myth: Only overweight people get type 2 diabetes.
fact: Excess weight is a major risk factor, but people of a healthy weight can also get type 2 diabetes. Age, family history, ethnicity and where fat is stored on the body also affect risk.
explanation: People of South Asian, Black African and Black Caribbean backgrounds, for example, can develop type 2 diabetes at a lower body weight. Fat stored around the waist and organs raises risk even when overall weight looks normal. Anyone with symptoms like excess thirst, frequent urination or unexplained tiredness should get checked.

myth: Only overweight, older men get sleep apnoea.
fact: Obstructive sleep apnoea is more common in men, older people and people who are overweight, but it can affect anyone, including women, slim people and children. In women it may be missed because symptoms can be less typical, such as tiredness, headaches or insomnia.
explanation: Signs include loud snoring, pauses in breathing or gasping during sleep noticed by a partner, waking often, and feeling very sleepy during the day. Untreated sleep apnoea raises the risk of high blood pressure, heart problems and accidents. It is diagnosed with a sleep study and is often treated with a CPAP machine.

myth: Only people who inject insulin can get dangerously low blood sugar.
fact: Some diabetes tablets, especially sulfonylureas such as gliclazide and glimepiride, can also cause low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia). Skipping meals, alcohol and extra exercise make it more likely.
explanation: Symptoms include sweating, shaking, hunger, a fast heartbeat and confusion. Treat a hypo with a fast-acting sugar such as juice or glucose tablets, then recheck. Ask your doctor or pharmacist whether your medicines can cause hypos.

myth: Only smokers get mouth cancer.
fact: Smoking and other tobacco use, including chewing tobacco, betel quid and paan, are major causes of mouth cancer, but it also affects non-smokers. Drinking alcohol and infection with HPV (for cancers at the back of the throat) also raise the risk.
explanation: Mouth cancer can appear as an ulcer that does not heal, a red or white patch, or a lump in the mouth or neck. Dentists check for signs of it at routine check-ups. Cutting down on alcohol, avoiding all forms of tobacco and HPV vaccination lower the risk.

myth: Only soldiers get PTSD.
fact: Post-traumatic stress disorder can follow any traumatic event, such as an assault, accident, disaster, sudden loss or difficult childbirth.
explanation: PTSD was first widely studied in veterans, which is why the link persists. Not everyone exposed to trauma develops PTSD, and effective therapies exist.

myth: Only teenagers get acne.
fact: Acne is most common in teenagers, but many adults, especially women, have acne in their 20s, 30s, 40s and beyond. Hormonal changes, such as around periods, pregnancy and menopause, can play a part.
explanation: Adult acne can be treated, though some treatments are not suitable in pregnancy. Some medicines and skin or hair products can also trigger spots. See a GP if over-the-counter treatments have not helped after a couple of months, or if acne is affecting your confidence.

sources.label: American Academy of Dermatology — Adult acne

myth: Only tennis players get tennis elbow.
fact: Tennis elbow is caused by overusing the muscles and tendons of the forearm, and most people who get it do not play tennis. Repetitive activities such as painting, using tools, typing or lifting can cause it.
explanation: It causes pain around the outside of the elbow and usually gets better with rest from the activity that caused it, although it can sometimes last more than a year. Painkillers, physiotherapy and changing how you do tasks can help.

myth: Only trained medical staff should use a defibrillator, because you could shock someone who doesn't need it.
fact: Public-access defibrillators (AEDs) are designed for anyone to use. They give spoken instructions and analyse the heart rhythm, delivering a shock only if it is needed.
explanation: If someone collapses and is not breathing normally, call emergency services, start CPR and ask someone to fetch the nearest AED. Using an AED quickly, alongside CPR, greatly improves the chance of survival from cardiac arrest.

sources.label: American Red Cross — Using an AED

myth: Only very old men need to think about prostate cancer.
fact: Prostate cancer is most common in men over 50 and risk rises with age, but it can occur earlier, particularly in men with a family history or of Black ethnicity.
explanation: Men in higher-risk groups are often advised to talk to a doctor about testing from a younger age. Many prostate cancers grow slowly, so decisions about testing and treatment are individual.

myth: Only women get osteoporosis.
fact: Osteoporosis is more common in women, especially after menopause, but men get it too, and men with hip fractures have a high risk of complications.
explanation: Risk factors in men include older age, low testosterone, smoking, heavy drinking, long-term steroid use and some medical conditions. Many men are never tested.

myth: Only women get thrush; men can't get it.
fact: Men can get thrush, a yeast infection that can affect the head of the penis and foreskin, causing redness, irritation, itching or a discharge. It is treated with antifungal creams or tablets.
explanation: Thrush is more likely in men with diabetes, a weakened immune system or after antibiotics. It is not classed as a sexually transmitted infection. If it keeps coming back, see a GP, as it can sometimes be a sign of undiagnosed diabetes.

sources.label: NHS — Thrush in men and women

myth: Only women who sleep around get cervical cancer.
fact: Almost all cervical cancers are caused by HPV, a very common infection that almost all sexually active people catch at some point, usually without symptoms. Someone can be infected by their only partner.
explanation: Most HPV infections clear on their own, but some persist and can lead to cervical cancer years later. The HPV vaccine and regular cervical screening prevent most cervical cancers. Stigma about this cancer can stop women from going for screening.

myth: Only young women get eating disorders.
fact: Eating disorders affect people of all genders, ages, body sizes and backgrounds. Men and older adults are often under-diagnosed.
explanation: The stereotype can stop people from recognising a problem or seeking help. A person does not have to look underweight to have a serious eating disorder. Early treatment improves recovery.

myth: Opioid painkillers can't be addictive if a doctor prescribed them.
fact: Prescribed opioids, such as codeine, tramadol, oxycodone and morphine, can cause dependence and addiction, especially when taken for longer than a few days or at higher doses.
explanation: Opioids are important for some kinds of pain, such as after surgery or for cancer pain, and are safest when used at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Do not stop suddenly after long-term use, as this can cause withdrawal; ask your doctor for a plan. Never mix opioids with alcohol or sleeping pills.

sources.label: MedlinePlus — Opioids and opioid use disorder

myth: Organic food is much more nutritious than non-organic food.
fact: Studies have not found consistent, meaningful differences in vitamins and minerals between organic and conventionally grown foods. Organic produce tends to have lower pesticide residues, but residues on conventional food are generally within safety limits.
explanation: People choose organic for many reasons, including environmental and animal welfare concerns, which are valid personal choices. From a nutrition point of view, eating plenty of fruit and vegetables matters more than whether they are organic. Washing produce under running water is sensible either way.

myth: Over-the-counter sleep aids like Nytol or ZzzQuil are fine to take every night.
fact: Many over-the-counter sleep aids contain sedating antihistamines such as diphenhydramine. They may help occasionally, but their benefit is uncertain, they can leave you groggy the next day, and they are meant for short-term use only.
explanation: Side effects can include dry mouth, constipation and confusion, and older adults are at higher risk of falls and memory problems. These products can also interact with other medicines and alcohol. If you need help sleeping for more than a couple of weeks, talk to a GP or pharmacist about the cause.

myth: Over-the-counter testosterone booster supplements reliably raise testosterone and build muscle.
fact: There is little good evidence that most testosterone booster supplements meaningfully raise testosterone or build muscle in healthy men.
explanation: Supplements are not tested like medicines, and some have been found to contain undeclared ingredients. Men worried about low testosterone should see a doctor, who can test levels and look for underlying causes.

myth: Painkillers you can buy without a prescription are completely safe in any situation.
fact: Over-the-counter painkillers are safe for most people when used as directed, but they can cause harm. Ibuprofen and aspirin can cause stomach bleeding and kidney problems and affect blood pressure, and too much paracetamol can cause serious liver damage.
explanation: Check the label for the maximum dose, avoid taking two products with the same ingredient (many cold remedies contain paracetamol) and ask a pharmacist if you have stomach, kidney, liver or heart problems, are pregnant, or take other medicines.

myth: Papaya leaf juice cures dengue.
fact: There is no cure or specific antiviral medicine for dengue. Treatment is rest, plenty of fluids, paracetamol for fever and pain, and close medical monitoring for warning signs.
explanation: Papaya leaf extract has been tested in small studies to see whether it raises platelet counts, but it has not been shown to prevent severe dengue or replace medical care. Avoid ibuprofen and aspirin with dengue because they can increase the risk of bleeding. Relying on home remedies can delay treatment when warning signs appear.

myth: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is so safe you can't take too much.
fact: Paracetamol is safe at recommended doses, but taking too much, even a little over the limit for several days, can cause serious liver damage. Many cold and flu remedies also contain paracetamol, making accidental overdose easy.
explanation: Because it is sold everywhere, many people assume paracetamol is harmless at any dose. Early overdose may cause no symptoms, so anyone who has taken too much should get urgent medical advice even if they feel well. Check labels to avoid taking two products that both contain it.

myth: Parkinson's disease is just a shaking hand.
fact: Tremor is one of the main symptoms, but not everyone with Parkinson's has it. The condition also causes slow movement and stiff muscles, and often other symptoms such as balance problems, loss of smell, sleep problems, depression, anxiety and memory problems.
explanation: Some non-movement symptoms, such as loss of smell or acting out dreams in sleep, can appear years before diagnosis. There is no cure yet, but medicines, physiotherapy and other support help manage symptoms. See a GP if you are worried about possible signs.

myth: Passing wind many times a day means something is wrong with your digestion.
fact: Passing gas is a normal part of digestion, and most people pass wind several times or more each day. Gas comes from swallowed air and from gut bacteria breaking down food, especially fibre-rich foods such as beans and vegetables.
explanation: More wind after eating healthy, high-fibre food is common and usually harmless. It is worth seeing a doctor if gas comes with tummy pain, ongoing diarrhoea or constipation, weight loss or blood in your poo. Eating more slowly and adjusting trigger foods can help if wind is bothersome.

sources.label: NIDDK — Gas in the digestive tract

myth: Peeing on a jellyfish sting relieves the pain.
fact: Urine does not help jellyfish stings and may make the stinging cells release more venom. Rinse the area with seawater rather than fresh water, remove any tentacles carefully, and soak the area in hot (not scalding) water if possible.
explanation: This myth was popularised by a television sitcom and spread widely. Some advice, such as using vinegar, depends on the type of jellyfish, so follow local lifeguard guidance. Severe pain, breathing difficulty or stings to a large area need urgent medical help.

sources.label: NHS — Jellyfish and other sea creature stings

myth: Peeing, washing or douching straight after sex stops you getting pregnant.
fact: None of these prevent pregnancy. Sperm can reach the cervix within minutes, urine comes out of a different opening (the urethra), and douching does not remove sperm that have already entered the womb.
explanation: If you have had sex without contraception, or contraception failed, emergency contraception can prevent pregnancy if used soon enough. The copper IUD is the most effective option and works up to 5 days after sex. Peeing after sex may help reduce urine infections, but it is not contraception.

myth: People are either left-brained (logical) or right-brained (creative).
fact: Although some functions are more concentrated on one side of the brain, people do not have a dominant hemisphere that defines their personality or thinking style.
explanation: Large brain-imaging studies have found no evidence for left-brained or right-brained people. Both sides work together for most tasks, including logic and creativity.

myth: People on a vegan diet need a reliable source of vitamin B12, such as fortified foods or a supplement.
fact: Yes. Vitamin B12 is found naturally almost only in animal foods, so people who eat no animal products need fortified foods (such as some plant milks, cereals and yeast extracts) or a B12 supplement.
explanation: Lack of B12 can cause anaemia, tiredness and, if not treated, nerve damage, which may not be fully reversible. Plant foods such as seaweed and spirulina are not reliable sources. This is especially important during pregnancy and breastfeeding and for vegan children.

sources.label: NHS — Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia

myth: People who are overweight have a slow metabolism.
fact: People with a larger body usually burn more energy at rest, not less, because there is more body tissue to maintain. Differences in metabolism between people of similar size are generally small.
explanation: Metabolism is often blamed for weight gain because it feels outside our control. Some medical conditions, such as an underactive thyroid, and some medicines can affect weight. Appetite, food environment, sleep, stress and activity levels all play a larger role for most people.

myth: People who had a COVID-19 vaccine 'shed' it and make others sick.
fact: None of the widely used COVID-19 vaccines contain live virus, so there is nothing that can be shed and passed to other people. The spike protein made after vaccination stays in the body and is cleared over time.
explanation: The idea of 'shedding' comes from some live vaccines, such as oral polio vaccine, where weakened virus can be passed on in rare cases. That does not apply to mRNA or protein-based vaccines. Claims that vaccinated people affect others' periods or health have not been supported by evidence.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: People who self-harm are just seeking attention.
fact: Self-harm is usually a way of coping with overwhelming emotions, distress or trauma, and many people who self-harm hide it. It is a sign that someone needs support, not something to dismiss.
explanation: Responding calmly and without judgement makes it easier for someone to open up. If you are self-harming, or worried about someone who is, please talk to a GP, a trusted person or a mental health helpline. If someone is seriously injured or at immediate risk, call emergency services.

myth: People who talk about suicide won't actually do it; they just want attention.
fact: Many people who die by suicide have spoken about it beforehand. Talk of suicide should always be taken seriously.
explanation: Talking about wanting to die or being a burden are recognised warning signs. Responding with care, listening and helping the person reach support can save a life. If there is immediate danger, contact emergency services or a crisis line.

myth: People with asthma shouldn't exercise.
fact: Regular exercise is good for people with asthma and can improve fitness and lung health. With asthma well controlled and the right preparation, most people with asthma can exercise fully, and many elite athletes have asthma.
explanation: Exercise can trigger symptoms in some people, which leads them to avoid it. A doctor or asthma nurse can help adjust treatment, which may include using a reliever inhaler before exercise. Warming up and avoiding very cold, dry air can also help.

myth: People with dark skin don't need sun protection.
fact: Darker skin has more natural protection against burning, but it can still be damaged by UV and people with dark skin can get skin cancer.
explanation: Skin cancer in people with darker skin is often found later, when it is harder to treat, and can appear in less sun-exposed places such as the palms, soles or under nails. Sun protection is still advised when UV is high.

myth: People with diabetes can never eat any sugar or sweets.
fact: People with diabetes can include small amounts of sugar as part of a balanced diet, planned around their meals, activity and medication. The overall pattern of eating matters more than avoiding sugar completely.
explanation: Diabetes eating advice used to be very strict, and many people still believe sugar is completely banned. Carbohydrates in general, including bread, rice and pasta, affect blood sugar, not just sweets. People who use insulin or some tablets may actually need fast-acting sugar to treat a low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia).

sources.label: NIDDK — Diabetes diet, eating and physical activity

myth: People with diabetes need to buy special 'diabetic' foods.
fact: There is no need for special 'diabetic' foods. People with diabetes are advised to eat the same healthy, balanced diet recommended for everyone.
explanation: Products labelled 'diabetic' or 'suitable for diabetics' are often expensive and can still be high in fat and calories. Some contain sugar alcohols that can cause bloating and diarrhoea. Reading normal food labels is usually more helpful.

sources.label: NIDDK — Diabetes diet, eating and physical activity

myth: People with diabetes should check their feet every day.
fact: Yes. Diabetes can reduce feeling in the feet and slow healing, so small cuts, blisters or sores may go unnoticed and turn into serious infections or ulcers. Checking your feet daily helps catch problems early.
explanation: Look for cuts, redness, swelling, blisters and changes in colour or temperature, and use a mirror or ask someone to help if needed. Wear well-fitting shoes, avoid walking barefoot and have your feet checked at diabetes reviews. See a health professional quickly about any wound that is not healing.

myth: People with diabetes shouldn't eat fruit because it has sugar.
fact: Whole fruit contains fibre, vitamins and minerals and can be part of a healthy diet for people with diabetes. Portion size and spreading fruit through the day matter more than avoiding it.
explanation: The natural sugar in fruit leads many people to cut it out. Whole fruit is a better choice than fruit juice or dried fruit, which raise blood sugar more quickly. A dietitian or diabetes team can help plan portions.

sources.label: NIDDK — Diabetes diet, eating and physical activity

myth: People with diabetes shouldn't exercise or play sports.
fact: Regular physical activity helps people with diabetes control blood sugar, lower blood pressure and cholesterol, and improve heart health. People with diabetes compete at every level of sport.
explanation: People who use insulin or some tablets may need to check blood sugar before and after exercise and carry a quick sugar source in case of a low. Those with eye, foot or heart complications should ask their care team which activities suit them.

myth: People with HIV who take treatment and have an undetectable viral load cannot pass HIV on through sex.
fact: Yes. People living with HIV who take antiretroviral treatment and keep an undetectable viral load do not transmit HIV to their sexual partners. This is often called "undetectable = untransmittable" (U=U).
explanation: Treatment needs to be taken every day as prescribed, with regular blood tests to check the virus stays undetectable. With effective treatment, people with HIV can expect a near-normal life expectancy. Condoms still protect against other sexually transmitted infections.

myth: People with mental illness are usually violent and dangerous.
fact: Most people with mental health conditions are not violent. They are more likely to be victims of violence than to commit it.
explanation: Media stories often link violence with mental illness, which feeds stigma. Factors such as substance misuse and past violence are stronger predictors of violence than a mental health diagnosis alone.

myth: People with narcolepsy are just lazy or don't sleep enough at night.
fact: Narcolepsy is a rare long-term brain condition that causes sleepiness people cannot control, sudden sleep attacks and, in many cases, sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotions such as laughter (cataplexy). It is not caused by laziness or poor sleep habits.
explanation: Other symptoms can include sleep paralysis, vivid dreams and waking often at night. Symptoms usually start in children and young adults and can take years to diagnose. There is no cure, but medicines and planned naps can help people manage it.

myth: Peppermint oil capsules can ease the symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome.
fact: Studies suggest enteric-coated peppermint oil capsules can help relieve tummy pain and bloating in some people with IBS. It is one of the options health services suggest trying.
explanation: Peppermint oil can cause heartburn in some people, which is why coated capsules are used. It does not work for everyone, and IBS symptoms such as unexplained weight loss or bleeding should be checked by a doctor before assuming it is IBS. Other helpful steps include adjusting fibre, regular meals and managing stress.

myth: Picking up a crying baby too often will spoil them.
fact: Young babies cannot be spoiled by being comforted. Responding to their needs helps them feel secure.
explanation: Crying is how babies communicate hunger, discomfort or the need for closeness. If crying is constant or you feel overwhelmed, it is fine to put the baby down safely and take a short break, and to seek help from a health visitor or doctor.

myth: Pink eye (conjunctivitis) always needs antibiotic eye drops.
fact: Most conjunctivitis is caused by viruses or allergies, and antibiotics do not help these. Bacterial conjunctivitis often clears on its own within a week or two, although antibiotics are sometimes prescribed.
explanation: Cleaning the eyelids with cooled boiled water, avoiding contact lenses and not sharing towels help while it clears. See a doctor urgently if the eye is painful, sensitive to light, vision changes, or if a newborn has red, sticky eyes.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Pink eye (conjunctivitis)

myth: Pink Himalayan salt or sea salt is healthier than table salt and doesn't raise blood pressure.
fact: Pink salt, rock salt and sea salt are mostly sodium chloride, just like table salt, and they affect blood pressure in the same way. The trace minerals they contain are present in amounts too small to matter for health.
explanation: Most adults eat more salt than recommended, which raises blood pressure and the risk of heart disease and stroke. Cutting down on salt of any kind helps; using herbs, spices, lemon or vinegar for flavour can make this easier. Ordinary table salt is often iodised, which helps prevent iodine deficiency.

myth: Plant milks like oat, almond or rice milk are nutritionally the same as cow's milk.
fact: Plant milks vary widely. Many are low in protein compared with cow's or soya milk, and unless they are fortified they may lack calcium, iodine and vitamin B12. Unsweetened, calcium-fortified versions are the best choice.
explanation: Soya drinks are the closest to cow's milk in protein. Rice drinks are not recommended for children under 5 because of their arsenic content. Children under 2 should not have plant drinks as their main milk unless advised by a health professional.

myth: PMS is all in women's heads.
fact: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) is a recognised condition linked to hormone changes during the menstrual cycle. Symptoms such as mood swings, bloating, breast tenderness and tiredness are real and vary from person to person.
explanation: A severe form, premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), can seriously affect mental health. Lifestyle changes, some contraceptive pills and certain antidepressants can help. Keeping a symptom diary for a few months can help a GP make a diagnosis.

myth: Polio vaccine drops are a secret plan to make children infertile.
fact: Polio vaccines protect children against polio, a virus that can cause permanent paralysis. They do not affect fertility, and billions of doses have been given worldwide with close safety monitoring.
explanation: Rumours that polio drops cause sterility have led some communities to refuse vaccination, which has allowed polio to return and paralyse children. Polio has been eliminated from most of the world thanks to vaccination, and it remains only in a small number of places where vaccination coverage is low.

myth: Polycystic ovary syndrome means you have cysts growing on your ovaries.
fact: Despite the old name, PCOS is a hormonal condition, and the 'cysts' seen on scans are small fluid-filled follicles, not true cysts. Some people with the condition do not have these follicles at all. The NHS now calls it polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS).
explanation: It is diagnosed from a combination of irregular periods, signs of raised androgen hormones such as extra hair growth or acne, and sometimes the ovary appearance on a scan. It is also linked with insulin resistance and a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. There is no cure, but treatments and lifestyle changes help manage symptoms.

myth: Popping pimples helps them heal faster.
fact: Squeezing spots can push bacteria deeper, increase inflammation and lead to scarring. It is better to leave them alone.
explanation: Popping can seem to give a quick fix, but it often makes the spot last longer. Persistent or painful acne can be treated with products from a pharmacist or prescriptions from a doctor.

myth: Postnatal depression is just the 'baby blues' and goes away on its own.
fact: The baby blues, with tearfulness and low mood, are common in the first two weeks after birth and usually pass. Postnatal depression lasts longer, can start any time in the first year, and is a real illness that usually needs support and treatment.
explanation: Signs include persistent sadness, loss of interest, difficulty bonding with the baby, and frightening thoughts. Partners can be affected too. Having postnatal depression does not mean someone is a bad parent. Speak to a midwife, health visitor or GP; if anyone has thoughts of harming themselves or the baby, get urgent help.

myth: Potatoes count towards your 5 A Day.
fact: Potatoes, yams, cassava and plantain are starchy foods and do not count towards your 5 A Day of fruit and vegetables in UK guidance. Sweet potatoes, parsnips and swedes do count, because they are usually eaten in addition to the starchy part of a meal.
explanation: Potatoes are still a useful food, especially with the skins on, which add fibre. Boiled, baked or mashed potatoes are healthier choices than chips or crisps.

myth: Pregnancy can make your gums more likely to swell and bleed.
fact: Hormonal changes in pregnancy can exaggerate the gums' response to plaque bacteria, making gingivitis (swollen, bleeding gums) more common. Tooth decay can also become more likely because of snacking or vomiting.
explanation: Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, cleaning between teeth and keeping up dental check-ups help. After vomiting, rinse with water (or a little baking soda in water) rather than brushing straight away, to protect enamel from stomach acid. Dental treatment is safe during pregnancy.

myth: Pregnant women should avoid all vaccines because they could harm the baby.
fact: Some vaccines are specifically recommended in pregnancy, including whooping cough (pertussis), flu and, in many countries, RSV and COVID-19 vaccines. They protect the mother and pass antibodies to the baby, protecting it in the first weeks of life before it can be vaccinated.
explanation: These vaccines have been given to very large numbers of pregnant people and are closely monitored for safety. Live vaccines, such as MMR, are usually avoided in pregnancy as a precaution, which is why it helps to check your vaccinations before trying to conceive. Your midwife or GP can tell you which vaccines are due and when.

myth: Pricking a stroke victim's fingertips or earlobes with a needle to let out blood can save them.
fact: There is no evidence that bloodletting from the fingers or ears helps someone having a stroke. The only effective first aid is to call emergency services immediately so the person can get hospital treatment quickly.
explanation: This advice has circulated for years in chain messages. Strokes caused by a clot can sometimes be treated with clot-busting medicines or a procedure to remove the clot, but only within hours, so every minute matters. Don't give the person anything to eat or drink while waiting for help.

myth: Probiotic supplements improve everyone's health.
fact: Some specific probiotic strains may help with certain problems, such as reducing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea. But benefits depend on the strain and the condition, and there is little evidence that healthy people gain general health benefits from taking them.
explanation: Interest in the gut microbiome has led to many bold marketing claims. Probiotics are generally safe for healthy people but have caused serious infections in rare cases in very ill or immunocompromised patients, including premature babies. Foods like yoghurt and kefir can be part of a varied diet.

myth: Products labelled 'hypoallergenic' can't cause skin reactions.
fact: There is no official standard for the term 'hypoallergenic' on cosmetics; in the US, the FDA says it means whatever a company wants it to mean. Products labelled this way can still cause allergic or irritant reactions.
explanation: People with sensitive skin or known allergies should check the full ingredients list rather than relying on marketing terms like 'hypoallergenic', 'natural' or 'dermatologist tested'. Patch-testing a small area first can help. A dermatologist can arrange patch tests to identify specific allergies.

myth: Prostate cancer always grows so slowly that it never needs treating.
fact: Many prostate cancers grow very slowly and may never cause harm, and these can often be safely monitored instead of treated straight away. But some prostate cancers are aggressive and spread, and these need treatment.
explanation: Doctors use tests such as PSA levels, MRI scans and biopsies to judge how likely a cancer is to grow. Monitoring (active surveillance) includes regular check-ups, with treatment offered if the cancer changes. Prostate cancer can often be cured when found early.

myth: Put a hot water bottle or heat pad on a fresh sprain to help it heal.
fact: For the first few days after a sprain or strain, health services advise rest, ice (wrapped in a towel), compression and raising the injured area. Heat, along with alcohol, running and massage, should be avoided early on because it can increase swelling.
explanation: After the first few days, gentle movement helps recovery. See a doctor if you can't put weight on the injury, if it looks deformed, or if the pain and swelling do not start to improve.

myth: Put a raw steak on a black eye.
fact: A black eye is best treated with a cold compress, such as an ice pack or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel, held gently on the area for a few minutes at a time. Raw meat is not recommended, as it can carry bacteria that may cause infection.
explanation: The cold reduces swelling, and any cold object would do the same job as the steak once did. Get urgent help if there are vision changes, blood in the eye, severe pain, or a head injury with vomiting or drowsiness.

myth: Put butter, oil or toothpaste on a burn.
fact: Butter, oil, toothpaste and similar home remedies should not be put on burns. They can trap heat, delay cooling and increase the risk of infection. The recommended first step is to cool the burn under cool or lukewarm running water.
explanation: These remedies are passed down in families and may feel soothing at first. After cooling, a burn can be loosely covered with cling film or a clean plastic bag. Get medical help for large or deep burns, burns on the face, hands, feet or genitals, and burns in children.

myth: Put something in a person's mouth during a seizure so they don't swallow their tongue.
fact: It is impossible to swallow your tongue. Never put anything in the mouth of someone having a seizure, as it can break teeth, injure the jaw or cause choking. Protect their head, move hazards away and time the seizure.
explanation: Seizures can be frightening to watch, and people want to do something to help. Once the jerking stops, put the person on their side in the recovery position. Call an ambulance if a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, it is their first seizure, or they are injured or do not wake up.

myth: Putting a jaundiced newborn in direct sunlight by a window will cure the jaundice.
fact: Newborn jaundice that needs treatment is treated with phototherapy: special blue lights used in a controlled setting with the baby's temperature and eyes protected. Direct sunlight is not a safe or reliable treatment and can cause sunburn or overheating.
explanation: Mild jaundice is common in the first week and often clears on its own with good feeding. Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life, a very yellow or drowsy baby, pale poo or jaundice lasting more than 2 weeks needs to be checked by a midwife or doctor. A simple blood test shows whether treatment is needed.

myth: Putting a newborn to sleep in their own room from the start is safest and teaches independence.
fact: Health services advise that babies sleep in a cot or Moses basket in the same room as a parent or carer for at least the first 6 months, for day and night sleeps. This lowers the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
explanation: Room-sharing is different from bed-sharing: the baby sleeps on their own separate surface next to you. Sleeping in a separate room in the early months has no proven benefit for independence. Talk to your health visitor if you have questions about safe sleep arrangements.

myth: Putting an aspirin directly on a sore tooth helps toothache.
fact: Placing aspirin against the gum or tooth does not work better than swallowing it and can cause a painful chemical burn to the gum.
explanation: Painkillers work when taken by mouth as directed. Toothache often means decay or infection, so see a dentist. Facial swelling with fever or trouble swallowing needs urgent care.

myth: Putting an unconscious person who is breathing on their side (the recovery position) helps keep their airway clear.
fact: Placing an unresponsive person who is breathing normally on their side helps keep the airway open and lets vomit or fluid drain out of the mouth rather than being breathed in.
explanation: Call emergency services and keep checking their breathing. If they stop breathing normally, roll them onto their back and start CPR. If you suspect a spinal injury, try to keep the head and neck in line when moving them.

sources.label: American Red Cross — Unresponsive and breathing person

myth: Putting breast milk in a baby's eye cures conjunctivitis or a sticky eye.
fact: There is no good evidence that breast milk treats eye infections, and it is not sterile, so it could introduce bacteria. Sticky eyes in babies are often caused by a blocked tear duct and are usually cleaned with cooled boiled water.
explanation: Red, swollen or sticky eyes in a newborn in the first few weeks of life can be a sign of a serious infection and need to be checked by a doctor urgently. Older babies and children with conjunctivitis usually get better on their own.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Pink eye (conjunctivitis)

myth: Putting coffee powder, turmeric or ash on a cut stops the bleeding and prevents infection.
fact: The recommended way to stop bleeding is to press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or dressing and, if possible, raise it. Powders and household substances are not sterile and can make infection more likely and wound cleaning harder.
explanation: Once bleeding stops, rinse the cut under clean running water and cover it with a plaster or dressing. Seek medical help if bleeding is heavy or won't stop, the cut is deep or gaping, or there is something stuck in it.

myth: Putting ice on a burn is the best way to cool it down.
fact: Ice, iced water and very cold packs can damage the skin further. Burns should be cooled with cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible.
explanation: After cooling, keep the person warm so they don't get too cold, remove jewellery or clothing near the burn unless it is stuck, and cover the burn loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag. Large, deep or facial burns, chemical or electrical burns, and burns in babies and young children need medical help.

myth: Putting onions in your socks or rubbing Vicks on your feet draws out a cold or stops a cough.
fact: There is no evidence that onions in socks or vapour rub on the feet treat colds, flu or coughs. Viruses are not "drawn out" through the feet.
explanation: Most colds and coughs clear up on their own. Rest, fluids, honey in warm water (not for babies under 1) and simple painkillers can help. Menthol vapour rubs should not be used on young children unless the label says they are suitable, and should never be put in or near the nose of a baby.

myth: Rabies treatment means 14 painful injections in the stomach.
fact: Modern rabies treatment after a bite is a short course of vaccine doses given in the arm, sometimes with rabies immunoglobulin around the wound. The old painful injections into the stomach are no longer used.
explanation: Fear of the old treatment can stop people seeking care after an animal bite or scratch. Once rabies symptoms appear it is almost always fatal, but prompt washing of the wound and vaccination after exposure is very effective at preventing it.

myth: Raising a child with two languages causes speech delay.
fact: Learning two languages does not cause language delay. Bilingual children reach language milestones within the normal range, though they may mix languages for a while.
explanation: A child who is not reaching milestones in either language should be assessed like any other child, rather than the delay being blamed on bilingualism.
