explanation: COVID-19 vaccines were developed quickly, which made many people uneasy. The speed came from earlier research on similar viruses, large funding, running trial phases in parallel and fast regulatory review, not from skipping steps. Like all medicines, vaccines can have side effects, and these are published openly.

myth: Vaccines cause sudden infant death syndrome (cot death).
fact: Studies have not found that vaccines cause sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Babies are vaccinated in the same months when SIDS is most common, so some deaths will happen after vaccination by coincidence.
explanation: Losing a baby is devastating and families naturally look for a cause. Known ways to lower SIDS risk include placing babies on their back to sleep, keeping the cot clear and avoiding smoke exposure. Some research suggests vaccinated babies are not at higher risk of SIDS than unvaccinated babies.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: Vaccines contain microchips used to track people.
fact: Vaccines do not contain microchips, tracking devices or any electronics. Their ingredients are listed publicly and consist of the active component plus small amounts of stabilisers, salts and sometimes adjuvants.
explanation: This claim spread widely during the COVID-19 pandemic, often mixed with conspiracy theories about governments or billionaires. A working tracking chip would need a power source and antenna and could not pass through a standard vaccine needle. Ingredient lists for licensed vaccines are published by regulators and manufacturers.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: Vaccines weaken your immune system.
fact: Vaccines train your immune system to recognise specific pathogens. They strengthen your body’s defences rather than weakening them, and are among the most studied medical interventions in history.
explanation: Vaccines contain weakened, inactivated or partial pieces of a germ, or instructions to make a harmless piece, that teach the immune system to respond quickly. Mild side effects like a sore arm or brief fever are signs the immune system is responding, not being damaged.

myth: Vaginal douching or special washes keep the vagina clean and healthy.
fact: The vagina cleans itself. Douching and perfumed washes can upset its natural balance and increase the risk of infections such as bacterial vaginosis.
explanation: Washing the outside area (vulva) with water or a mild unperfumed soap is enough. Changes in discharge, smell or itching are worth checking with a doctor or sexual health clinic.

myth: Vaginal steaming (yoni steaming) cleanses the womb and balances hormones.
fact: There is no evidence that steaming the vagina with herbs cleanses the womb, balances hormones or improves fertility. The vagina keeps itself clean with natural discharge, and steam can burn delicate skin.
explanation: Steam cannot reach the womb through the cervix, and hormones are not affected by heat applied to the vulva. Like douching, steaming may also upset the natural balance of bacteria and lead to infections. If you are worried about discharge, smell, periods or fertility, a GP or sexual health clinic can help.

myth: Vaginal thrush is a sexually transmitted infection caused by being unclean.
fact: Thrush is a common yeast infection and is not classed as a sexually transmitted infection. It is caused by an overgrowth of yeast that normally lives on the body and is not caused by poor hygiene.
explanation: It is more likely after antibiotics, in pregnancy, with poorly controlled diabetes, or when the skin is irritated. Over-washing and perfumed products can make it worse. Antifungal treatments are available from pharmacies; see a GP if it is your first time, if it keeps coming back or if treatment does not work.

sources.label: NHS — Thrush in men and women

myth: Valerian or chamomile tea is a proven cure for insomnia.
fact: Studies of valerian and chamomile for sleep have had mixed or inconclusive results, and neither is a proven treatment for insomnia. They are generally considered low-risk for short-term use, though they can cause side effects or interact with some medicines.
explanation: A warm, caffeine-free drink can be a pleasant part of a bedtime routine. Chamomile may cause reactions in people allergic to plants such as ragweed or daisies. Insomnia lasting months is better treated with CBT for insomnia, so talk to a GP if poor sleep is affecting your life.

myth: Vaping is just as harmful as smoking cigarettes.
fact: Vapes are not risk-free, and long-term effects are still being studied, but UK health services say vaping is much less harmful than smoking for adult smokers who switch completely. The WHO warns that e-cigarettes are harmful and should not be used by children or non-smokers.
explanation: Cigarette smoke contains thousands of chemicals, many of which cause cancer and are produced by burning tobacco, which vapes do not do. Vaping still exposes users to nicotine, which is addictive, and other chemicals. Advice differs between countries, so check the guidance where you live.

sources.label: NHS — Using e-cigarettes to stop smoking

myth: Vegetarians and vegans can't get enough protein.
fact: Well-planned vegetarian and vegan diets can provide all the protein people need. Good sources include beans, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, soya, nuts, seeds and whole grains, and for vegetarians also eggs and dairy.
explanation: Eating a variety of plant proteins over the day provides all the essential amino acids, so careful "combining" at each meal is not necessary. People on vegan diets do need to pay attention to nutrients such as vitamin B12, iodine, iron, calcium and omega-3 fats.

myth: Very dark brown urine and severe muscle pain after a hard workout are just dehydration.
fact: Dark, tea- or cola-coloured urine with severe muscle pain, swelling or weakness after extreme exercise can be a sign of rhabdomyolysis, where damaged muscle releases substances that can harm the kidneys. It needs urgent medical attention.
explanation: Rhabdomyolysis is uncommon but has been linked to very intense or unaccustomed workouts, especially in heat or when dehydrated. Building up intensity gradually, particularly when starting a new class or programme, lowers the risk. Ordinary dark yellow urine is usually a sign of needing more fluids.

myth: Viagra gives you an erection automatically, even if you're not aroused.
fact: Sildenafil (Viagra) and similar medicines increase blood flow to the penis, but they only work when a man is sexually aroused. They do not cause an erection on their own and do not increase sex drive.
explanation: These medicines are not suitable for everyone, particularly people taking nitrate medicines for angina or with some heart conditions. Erection problems can be a sign of other health conditions, so it is worth speaking to a GP or pharmacist.

myth: Vitamin B12 injections give everyone an energy boost.
fact: Vitamin B12 injections treat B12 deficiency, which can cause tiredness and anaemia. In people with normal B12 levels, extra B12 has not been shown to increase energy.
explanation: B12 shots are sold at clinics and wellness centres as energy or weight-loss boosters. People at risk of deficiency include those with pernicious anaemia, older adults, vegans, and people taking certain medicines such as metformin. A blood test can show whether you need treatment.

sources.label: NIH ODS — Vitamin B12 fact sheet

myth: Vitiligo is contagious, so you should avoid touching someone who has it.
fact: Vitiligo cannot be caught from another person. It is a long-term condition in which pale patches develop because the skin lacks the pigment melanin.
explanation: People with vitiligo often face stigma, which can affect their mental health more than the condition itself. It does not cause physical harm, though the pale patches burn easily in the sun. Support groups and talking therapies can help people who feel distressed by how their skin looks.

sources.label: American Academy of Dermatology — Vitiligo: causes

myth: Waking a sleepwalker can harm them or give them a heart attack.
fact: Waking a sleepwalker is not dangerous, although they may be confused or startled. It is usually best to guide them gently back to bed.
explanation: The bigger risk is injury while sleepwalking, such as falls or wandering outside. Securing doors and windows and removing hazards helps. Frequent episodes or risky behaviour are worth discussing with a doctor.

myth: Walking doesn't count as real exercise.
fact: Brisk walking is moderate-intensity aerobic activity and counts towards the recommended 150 minutes a week. Regular walking is linked to a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, some cancers and depression.
explanation: Walking fast enough to raise your heart rate and make you breathe faster, while still being able to talk, is a good guide to moderate intensity. It is free, low-impact and easy to fit into daily life, which makes it one of the most practical ways to get active. Adding hills or a faster pace increases the challenge.

myth: Washing your hands with soap and water prevents infections.
fact: Handwashing with soap and water is one of the most effective ways to prevent the spread of many infections, including diarrhoeal illnesses and respiratory infections such as colds and flu.
explanation: Some people doubt that something so simple makes a real difference. Soap helps lift germs off the skin so they rinse away, and washing for about 20 seconds covers all parts of the hands. Key times are after using the toilet, before eating or preparing food, and after coughing, sneezing or blowing your nose.

myth: We don't need vaccines anymore because these diseases have disappeared.
fact: Most vaccine-preventable diseases still circulate somewhere in the world and return quickly when vaccination rates fall. Measles outbreaks in recent years have occurred in many countries where coverage dropped.
explanation: Diseases like polio and diphtheria seem distant precisely because vaccines have kept them rare. Travel means an infection can arrive from anywhere within a day. Smallpox is the only human disease that has been fully eradicated, and only through vaccination.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: We only use 10% of our brains.
fact: Brain imaging shows that we use virtually all of our brain, though not every area is active at the same moment. Even simple tasks involve many regions.
explanation: The myth has no clear scientific origin and is popular in films and self-help marketing. Damage to almost any part of the brain causes some effect, which would not happen if most of it were unused.

myth: Wearing a face mask lowers your oxygen levels and poisons you with carbon dioxide.
fact: Properly worn face masks do not cause oxygen shortage or carbon dioxide poisoning in healthy people. Oxygen and carbon dioxide molecules pass easily through mask material.
explanation: Health workers wear masks for long shifts without harm. Masks can feel uncomfortable, and people with severe breathing problems or young children may not be advised to wear them. Change a mask if it becomes damp or dirty.

myth: Wearing an underwire bra causes breast cancer.
fact: There is no evidence that wearing a bra, underwired or not, causes breast cancer. A large study found no link between bra wearing and breast cancer risk.
explanation: The claim suggests bras block lymph drainage and trap toxins, but this is not how breast cancer develops. Known risk factors include age, inherited genes, alcohol, excess weight after menopause and some hormone treatments. Wear whatever bra is comfortable.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Common cancer myths and misconceptions

myth: Wearing glasses makes your eyes weaker and dependent on them.
fact: Glasses correct blurry vision but do not weaken the eyes or make the underlying condition worse.
explanation: Vision can change over time with age or as children grow, which people sometimes blame on their glasses. In children, not wearing prescribed glasses can actually harm visual development in some conditions, such as lazy eye.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Wearing hats makes you go bald.
fact: Wearing ordinary hats does not cause hair loss. The most common cause of baldness is inherited male- or female-pattern hair loss.
explanation: Very tight hairstyles or headwear worn constantly can pull on hair and cause traction alopecia, but a normal-fitting cap does not.

myth: Wearing hearing aids makes your hearing worse over time.
fact: Properly fitted hearing aids do not damage hearing. They make sounds louder so the remaining sensory cells in the ear can pick them up, helping with conversations and everyday life.
explanation: Some people feel their hearing is worse when they take aids out, because they have got used to hearing more clearly. Age-related hearing loss tends to progress slowly whether or not aids are used. Getting help early can also reduce isolation, and untreated hearing loss is linked with a higher risk of dementia.

myth: Wearing someone else's glasses or cheap ready-made reading glasses will damage your eyes.
fact: Wearing the wrong glasses may cause blurred vision, eye strain or a headache, but it does not damage the eyes. Ready-made reading glasses are fine for many people whose eyes need the same strength in both eyes and who have no astigmatism.
explanation: Discomfort goes away once you take the glasses off. Ready-made readers are not a substitute for an eye test, which also checks for eye diseases such as glaucoma. Children should wear glasses prescribed for them.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Reading glasses
American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye myths

myth: Wearing sunscreen will make you vitamin D deficient.
fact: In real-world use, people rarely apply enough sunscreen to block all the sunlight that makes vitamin D, and studies have not shown that normal sunscreen use causes deficiency. In the UK, most people can make enough vitamin D from short periods of sun from about April to September.
explanation: You don't need to burn, or skip sunscreen, to make vitamin D. In autumn and winter, when sunlight is too weak in many countries, health services advise considering a vitamin D supplement, and some groups are advised to take one all year. Skipping sun protection raises the risk of skin damage and skin cancer.

myth: Wearing tight underwear makes men infertile.
fact: Tight underwear does not make men infertile. Some research suggests looser underwear may be linked to slightly better sperm measures, because testicles work best a little cooler than body temperature.
explanation: Any effect appears small. Smoking, heavy drinking, obesity and some medicines have clearer effects on sperm. Men having trouble conceiving with a partner can ask a doctor for a semen test.

myth: Weight loss surgery is the easy way out.
fact: Weight loss (bariatric) surgery is a major treatment offered to people with severe obesity, usually after other approaches have been tried. It requires lifelong changes to eating, regular follow-up and often vitamin supplements.
explanation: Surgery can lead to large, lasting weight loss and can improve or even put conditions such as type 2 diabetes into remission. It also carries risks, and people need to adjust how much and how they eat for the rest of their lives. Calling it 'easy' adds stigma and can put people off a treatment that might help them.

myth: Weight-bearing exercise helps keep your bones strong.
fact: Weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercise helps build bone in young people and slows bone loss in adults.
explanation: Examples include walking, dancing, jogging, stair climbing and resistance exercises. People with osteoporosis can still exercise but may need advice on safe movements.

myth: When you have diarrhoea you should stop eating, or eat only plain toast and bananas.
fact: The most important thing with diarrhoea is to keep drinking fluids to avoid dehydration. You can eat as soon as you feel able to, and there is no need to stick to a special bland diet.
explanation: Starving yourself does not make diarrhoea stop sooner. Oral rehydration sachets from a pharmacy can help people at risk of dehydration, such as older people and young children. Babies should keep breastfeeding or having formula. Signs of severe dehydration, blood in diarrhoea, or symptoms lasting more than a week need medical advice.

myth: When you're pregnant you need to eat for two.
fact: Most people do not need extra calories in the first six months of pregnancy, and only a modest amount extra later on.
explanation: Eating much more than needed can lead to excess weight gain, which raises the risk of complications such as gestational diabetes. The focus should be on a balanced diet and recommended supplements.

myth: White teeth are healthy teeth.
fact: Tooth colour is not a reliable sign of dental health. Teeth naturally vary in shade, and white teeth can still have decay or gum disease.
explanation: Teeth can also darken with age, food, drinks and smoking. Whitening is cosmetic and is best done with dental advice.

myth: Wholegrain foods are healthier than refined white versions.
fact: Yes. Wholegrain foods such as brown rice, wholemeal bread, oats and whole wheat contain more fibre, vitamins and minerals than refined grains. Diets rich in whole grains are linked to lower risks of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and bowel cancer.
explanation: Fibre also helps digestion and keeps you feeling full. Swapping some refined starchy foods for wholegrain versions is an easy change; check labels, because "multigrain" or brown-coloured foods are not always wholegrain.

myth: Winter depression (seasonal affective disorder) is a real condition.
fact: Seasonal affective disorder is a recognised type of depression that comes and goes with the seasons, most often starting in autumn or winter.
explanation: Reduced daylight is thought to affect the body clock and mood-related brain chemistry. Treatments include light therapy, talking therapy and antidepressants. Feeling a bit low in winter is common; persistent symptoms deserve a check-up.

myth: Women who live together get their periods in sync.
fact: Larger and better-designed studies have not found that menstrual cycles synchronise when people live together.
explanation: Cycles vary in length, so periods of people living together will overlap by chance from time to time, which makes syncing seem real. The idea came from a 1970s study that later research could not reliably confirm.

myth: Women with PCOS can't get pregnant.
fact: Many people with polycystic ovary syndrome get pregnant, sometimes with help from lifestyle changes or fertility treatment.
explanation: PCOS can make ovulation irregular, which may make conceiving take longer. Treatments to encourage ovulation are often effective. PCOS does not mean you can't get pregnant, so contraception is still needed if you don't want a pregnancy.

myth: Women with small breasts can't make enough milk to breastfeed.
fact: Breast size mostly reflects the amount of fatty tissue, not the milk-producing tissue, so it does not determine how much milk you can make. Milk supply depends mainly on how often and how effectively the baby feeds.
explanation: Feeding responsively, with a good latch, tells the body to make more milk. A small number of people do have medical reasons for low supply, so if your baby is not gaining weight or has few wet nappies, ask a midwife, health visitor or breastfeeding specialist for help.

sources.label: NHS — Breastfeeding: the first few days

myth: You always need an X-ray or MRI scan for back pain.
fact: Most back pain does not need a scan. It usually improves within weeks, and scans often show age-related changes that are not the cause of the pain.
explanation: Scans are recommended when there are warning signs, such as suspected nerve damage, infection, cancer or a fracture. Unnecessary scans can lead to worry and treatments that do not help.

myth: You can burn belly fat by doing lots of sit-ups or crunches.
fact: You cannot choose where your body loses fat by exercising one area. Fat loss happens across the whole body through an overall energy deficit.
explanation: Sit-ups strengthen the abdominal muscles, but they do not specifically burn the fat over them. A combination of regular activity, strength training and a balanced diet reduces overall body fat, including around the waist.

myth: You can catch cancer from someone who has it.
fact: Cancer cannot be passed from person to person like a cold or flu. You can safely hug, kiss and care for someone with cancer.
explanation: Some viruses and bacteria that can be passed on, such as HPV, hepatitis B and C and H. pylori, raise the risk of certain cancers, but it is the infection that spreads, not the cancer. Vaccines against HPV and hepatitis B lower these risks.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Common cancer myths and misconceptions
National Cancer Institute — Infectious agents and cancer

myth: You can catch diabetes from someone else.
fact: Diabetes is not contagious. It cannot be passed on by touch, sharing food, kissing or any other contact.
explanation: Diabetes can run in families, partly because of shared genes and shared lifestyles, which may make it seem 'catching'. Sharing blood glucose meters, lancets or needles is unsafe because of blood-borne infections, not because of diabetes itself.

myth: You can catch hepatitis B by sharing food, cups or plates.
fact: Hepatitis B spreads through blood and other body fluids, for example from mother to baby at birth, through sex, or by sharing needles, razors or toothbrushes. It is not spread by sharing food, water, cutlery, hugging or kissing on the cheek.
explanation: Hepatitis A and E are the types that can spread through contaminated food and water, which may cause confusion. A safe and effective vaccine protects against hepatitis B, and people living with it do not need to be excluded from family meals.

myth: You can catch HIV from mosquito bites, sharing cups or hugging.
fact: HIV is not spread by mosquitoes, kissing, hugging, shaking hands or sharing cups, food, toilets or towels. It spreads through certain body fluids, mainly during sex without a condom, by sharing needles, or from mother to baby.
explanation: Fear of casual contact adds to the stigma faced by people living with HIV. Condoms, PrEP medicine, testing and treatment all prevent the spread of HIV.

myth: You can catch sexually transmitted infections from toilet seats.
fact: Sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea and HIV are spread through sexual contact, and some through blood or from mother to baby. They are not caught from toilet seats.
explanation: The bacteria and viruses that cause STIs survive poorly outside the body. If you have symptoms such as unusual discharge, pain when peeing or sores, or you are worried after sex, get tested; many STIs have no symptoms and are easily treated.

myth: You can catch shingles from someone who has it.
fact: You cannot catch shingles from another person. However, someone who has never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine can catch chickenpox from the fluid in shingles blisters.
explanation: Shingles happens when the chickenpox virus that has stayed dormant in your body since a past infection becomes active again. People with shingles should avoid pregnant women who have not had chickenpox, newborn babies and people with weakened immune systems until the blisters have crusted over.

myth: You can check for diabetes by seeing if ants are attracted to your urine.
fact: Diabetes is diagnosed with blood tests, such as fasting blood glucose or HbA1c, not by looking at urine or ants. Sugar only spills into the urine once blood sugar is already very high.
explanation: Ants may be drawn to many things, and the absence of ants does not rule out diabetes. Because type 2 diabetes often causes no symptoms early on, people at higher risk should ask for a blood test.
keywords: how to check diabetes at home

myth: You can die from a panic attack.
fact: Panic attacks can feel terrifying, with a racing heart, chest tightness, breathlessness and a feeling of doom, but they are not dangerous in themselves and pass, usually within 5 to 20 minutes.
explanation: Because symptoms can resemble a heart attack, anyone with chest pain they have not had checked before, or who is unsure, should get urgent medical help. Repeated panic attacks are treatable with talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy and sometimes medicine.

myth: You can eat whatever you want as long as you exercise enough.
fact: Physical activity has huge health benefits, but on its own it usually leads to only modest weight loss, because it is easy to eat back the calories burned. Lasting weight loss generally needs changes to eating as well as activity.
explanation: For example, it can take a long brisk walk to burn off the energy in a single large sugary snack or drink. Diet quality also matters for health independently of weight. Exercise is still very important for keeping weight off and for the heart, mood and bones, so the two work best together.

myth: You can fully catch up on lost sleep at the weekend.
fact: Extra sleep can ease some short-term sleepiness, but regularly sleeping too little during the week and catching up at weekends does not fully undo the effects on attention, metabolism and health.
explanation: A lie-in can help after a single short night. Irregular sleep times can also shift your body clock, making Monday harder. A consistent schedule with enough sleep each night works best.

myth: You can get by on a few 20-minute naps a day instead of a full night's sleep (polyphasic sleep).
fact: There is no good scientific evidence that polyphasic sleep schedules, such as the 'Uberman' pattern of short naps around the clock, are better than normal sleep. Schedules that cut total sleep this much lead to sleep deprivation.
explanation: Feeling more productive on such schedules may simply reflect having more waking hours, not better performance. Sleep deprivation affects concentration, mood, reaction times and long-term health. Short naps can be helpful alongside, not instead of, enough night-time sleep.

myth: You can never drink any alcohol with any antibiotic.
fact: Most common antibiotics do not interact seriously with moderate alcohol. However, some, such as metronidazole and tinidazole, can cause a severe reaction with alcohol, and alcohol can slow recovery from illness.
explanation: The blanket rule is simple to remember, which is why it spread. Check the leaflet or ask a pharmacist about your specific antibiotic. Avoiding alcohol while unwell is still sensible.

myth: You can only get tetanus from a rusty nail.
fact: Tetanus is caused by bacteria that live in soil and manure, not by rust. They can get into any wound, including cuts, puncture wounds, burns and animal bites, especially if the wound is dirty.
explanation: Rusty nails got the reputation because they are often dirty and cause deep puncture wounds. The tetanus vaccine is the best protection. If you have a dirty or deep wound and are not sure you're fully vaccinated, get medical advice promptly.

myth: You can only pass on a cold sore when there's a blister you can see.
fact: Cold sores are caused by the herpes simplex virus and are most contagious when blisters are present, but they can spread from the first tingling until they have completely healed. The virus can occasionally be passed on even without visible sores.
explanation: Avoid kissing, sharing cups or lip products, and oral sex while you have a cold sore, and don't kiss babies, who can become seriously ill. Antiviral creams from a pharmacy work best if used as soon as the tingling starts.

myth: You can only spread a cold or flu once you start feeling ill.
fact: People can spread cold and flu viruses before they notice symptoms, as well as while they are ill. With flu, you are usually most infectious in the first few days of symptoms.
explanation: This is one reason these viruses spread so easily. Washing hands, covering coughs and sneezes, and staying home when unwell help protect others, especially older people and those with long-term conditions.

myth: You can stop taking antibiotics as soon as you feel better.
fact: You should take antibiotics as directed by the prescriber. Stopping early can allow some infections to come back, although research is reviewing whether shorter courses work for some infections, and prescribers now often give shorter courses where evidence supports it.
explanation: The traditional rule was always to finish the course to prevent resistance, and some experts now question whether longer courses are always needed. That is a decision for the prescriber, not something to guess at home. If you have side effects or think you no longer need the antibiotic, speak to your doctor or pharmacist.

myth: You can stop taking antidepressants suddenly as soon as you feel better.
fact: Stopping antidepressants suddenly can cause withdrawal (discontinuation) symptoms such as dizziness, anxiety, irritability and flu-like feelings, and raises the chance of depression returning. Doctors usually advise continuing for at least several months after feeling better and then reducing the dose gradually.
explanation: Withdrawal symptoms are not the same as addiction, but they can be unpleasant and sometimes long-lasting. Planning when and how to stop with your doctor makes it safer. If symptoms return or you feel unwell while reducing, tell your doctor.

myth: You can tell someone has an eating disorder because they look very thin.
fact: Most people with eating disorders are not underweight. Conditions such as bulimia, binge eating disorder and other eating disorders often occur at an average or higher weight, and people with anorexia may hide weight loss.
explanation: Eating disorders are serious mental illnesses that can affect anyone, and they are best treated early. Signs can include strict dieting, secretive eating, making yourself sick, using laxatives, or excessive exercise. If you are worried about yourself or someone else, please talk to a GP or an eating disorder support service.

myth: You can tell the baby's sex from the shape of the bump.
fact: Bump shape depends on things like muscle tone, the baby's position and body build, not the baby's sex.
explanation: Old wives' tales about carrying high or low, cravings or heart rate are right about half the time, as a guess would be. An ultrasound scan or certain blood tests can determine sex.

myth: You can tell what your blood sugar is just by how you feel.
fact: Feelings are not a reliable guide to blood sugar. High blood sugar often causes no symptoms at all, and symptoms of low blood sugar can be missed, especially at night or in people who have had diabetes for many years.
explanation: Blood sugar meters, continuous glucose monitors and HbA1c blood tests give accurate information. Your diabetes team can tell you how often to check and what your targets should be.

myth: You can train your body to function well on five hours of sleep.
fact: Most adults need at least seven hours of sleep. People who regularly sleep less usually adapt to feeling tired but still show reduced attention, memory and reaction time.
explanation: Chronic short sleep is linked to higher risk of obesity, diabetes, heart disease and accidents. A very small number of people naturally need less sleep, but this cannot be learned.

myth: You can't develop new allergies as an adult.
fact: Allergies, including food allergies and hay fever, can start at any age. Some adults develop allergies to foods such as shellfish or tree nuts for the first time.
explanation: Many allergies begin in childhood, so adult-onset allergy can come as a surprise and be dismissed. Changes in environment, such as moving to a new area or getting a pet, can also bring new exposures. Any reaction involving breathing difficulty or swelling of the face or throat needs emergency care.

myth: You can't eat any cheese when you're pregnant.
fact: Most cheese is safe in pregnancy, including all hard cheeses such as cheddar and pasteurised soft cheeses such as cottage cheese and mozzarella. The ones to avoid uncooked are mould-ripened soft cheeses (like brie and camembert), soft blue cheeses and unpasteurised soft cheeses, because they can carry listeria.
explanation: Listeria infection is rare but can cause miscarriage or serious illness in a newborn. Cooking kills listeria, so dishes with these cheeses cooked until steaming hot are fine. Cheese is a useful source of calcium and protein in pregnancy.

sources.label: NHS — Foods to avoid in pregnancy

myth: You can't get pregnant if you have sex during your period.
fact: Pregnancy from sex during a period is less likely but possible. Sperm can survive inside the body for up to about seven days, and some people ovulate soon after their period ends.
explanation: Cycles vary, and bleeding is not always a true period. If you want to avoid pregnancy, use contraception every time.

myth: You can't get pregnant once your periods become irregular in perimenopause.
fact: Pregnancy is still possible during perimenopause. Contraception is usually advised until periods have stopped for one year if over 50, or two years if under 50.
explanation: Ovulation can still happen even when periods are irregular. Some forms of contraception can also help manage perimenopausal symptoms.

myth: You can't get pregnant the first time you have sex.
fact: Pregnancy can happen any time sperm meets an egg, including the very first time someone has sex.
explanation: Whether it is the first time makes no biological difference. Contraception and condoms protect against pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections from the start.

myth: You can't get pregnant while breastfeeding.
fact: Exclusive breastfeeding can prevent pregnancy only under strict conditions: the baby is under six months, fed only breast milk day and night, and periods have not returned. Otherwise pregnancy is possible.
explanation: This method, called lactational amenorrhoea, becomes unreliable once feeds are spaced out or other foods are added. You can ovulate before your first period returns, so many people choose other contraception.

myth: You don't need sunscreen on cloudy days.
fact: Much of the sun's ultraviolet radiation passes through clouds, so you can still burn and damage your skin on overcast days.
explanation: Because you do not feel as hot, it is easy to stay out longer and burn. Checking the UV index is a better guide than how sunny it looks.

myth: You get malaria from eating mangoes or getting wet in the rain.
fact: Malaria is caused by a parasite that is spread by the bite of infected mosquitoes. Food and rain do not cause it.
explanation: Malaria often rises in the rainy season because standing water lets mosquitoes breed, which may explain the link people notice. Sleeping under insecticide-treated nets, preventing bites and getting tested quickly for fever are what protect you. Malaria can become severe within a day, especially in young children.

myth: You get warts from touching frogs or toads.
fact: Warts and verrucas are caused by a virus (human papillomavirus, HPV) that spreads between people through close skin contact or contaminated surfaces, such as swimming pool floors. Frogs and toads do not spread warts.
explanation: The bumpy skin of toads probably gave rise to the myth. Most warts are harmless and go away on their own, though it can take months or years. Covering them and not sharing towels can help stop them spreading; pharmacists can advise on treatments.

myth: You have to get rid of your cat when you're pregnant.
fact: Cat faeces can carry toxoplasmosis, an infection that can harm an unborn baby, but you do not need to give up your pet. Avoid emptying litter trays if possible (or wear gloves and wash your hands well), and wear gloves when gardening.
explanation: Toxoplasmosis is also caught from eating raw or undercooked meat and unwashed fruit and vegetables, so food hygiene matters just as much. Most people who have had cats for a long time may already have been exposed. If you are worried you may have been infected, speak to a midwife or GP.

sources.label: NHS — Foods to avoid in pregnancy

myth: You lose a tooth for every baby.
fact: Pregnancy does not take calcium from the teeth. However, hormonal changes can make gums more prone to inflammation, and vomiting can expose teeth to acid.
explanation: Good brushing, cleaning between teeth and dental check-ups during pregnancy help prevent problems. Dental care is safe in pregnancy.

myth: You must give up coffee completely when pregnant.
fact: Health bodies advise limiting caffeine in pregnancy, usually to under 200 mg a day, rather than cutting it out entirely.
explanation: High caffeine intake has been linked to low birth weight and miscarriage. Caffeine is also in tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate, so it all adds up.

myth: You must have a bowel movement every day to be healthy.
fact: Normal bowel habits vary widely, from about three times a day to three times a week. What matters more is what is normal for you and whether there is a lasting change.
explanation: Worrying about daily bowel movements can lead to overuse of laxatives. Constipation usually means passing stools fewer than three times a week, or stools that are hard and difficult to pass. A lasting change in bowel habit, blood in the stool or unexplained weight loss should be checked by a doctor.

myth: You must never take ibuprofen and paracetamol together.
fact: For most adults it is safe to take ibuprofen and paracetamol at the same time or alternate them, as long as you do not exceed the maximum dose of each. They work in different ways.
explanation: Ibuprofen is not suitable for everyone, for example some people with asthma, stomach ulcers, kidney or heart problems, or in later pregnancy. Check the labels, avoid other products containing the same ingredients and ask a pharmacist if unsure. For children, follow the dosing for their age.

myth: You must stop HRT after five years.
fact: There is no fixed limit on how long you can take HRT. Health services advise reviewing the treatment with a doctor, usually once a year, to weigh up benefits and risks for you.
explanation: Some people take HRT for a few years and others for longer, depending on their symptoms, age and health. People who go through an early menopause are usually advised to take HRT until at least the average age of menopause, around 51. Stopping can be done gradually or all at once, and symptoms may return.

myth: You must wait 30 minutes after eating before swimming or you'll drown from cramps.
fact: There is no evidence that swimming after a meal causes drowning. A large meal might make vigorous exercise uncomfortable, but it is not dangerous.
explanation: The rule was widely repeated but never backed by data. Real drowning risks include alcohol, lack of supervision for children and weak swimming ability.

myth: You need 10,000 steps a day to get any health benefit.
fact: There is no single magic number. Health benefits start well below 10,000 steps, and adding steps from a low baseline gives the greatest gains.
explanation: The 10,000 figure is widely said to have come from a pedometer marketing campaign rather than research. Guidelines focus on at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, which can include brisk walking.

myth: You need a new flu vaccine every year.
fact: Flu viruses change frequently, and the vaccine is updated each year to match the strains expected to circulate. Protection from the vaccine also fades over months, so yearly vaccination is recommended for people at higher risk.
explanation: Some people think one flu jab should last for life like some childhood vaccines. Because flu strains shift, last year's vaccine may not match this year's virus well. Who is offered a free flu vaccine varies by country, but it commonly includes older adults, pregnant people, young children and people with long-term health conditions.

myth: You need protein shakes and supplements to build muscle.
fact: Most people can get enough protein for building muscle from ordinary food such as meat, fish, eggs, dairy, beans, lentils, tofu and nuts. Protein powders are a convenience, not a necessity, and strength training is what drives muscle growth.
explanation: People doing a lot of strength training, and older adults, may benefit from somewhat more protein than the basic requirement, spread across meals. Very high protein intakes are not proven to add extra muscle. Supplements are not regulated like medicines and some have been found to contain undeclared ingredients.

sources.label: Harvard Health Publishing — How much protein do you need every day?

myth: You need sports drinks whenever you exercise.
fact: For most everyday exercise lasting less than an hour, water is enough. Sports drinks can help during long or very intense exercise, especially in heat.
explanation: Many sports drinks contain a lot of sugar and add calories without benefit for casual exercise. They can also contribute to tooth decay.

myth: You need to keep eating gluten before being tested for coeliac disease.
fact: Tests for coeliac disease look for the body's reaction to gluten. If you have already cut gluten out, the tests can come back falsely normal, so health services advise eating gluten in more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks before testing.
explanation: Many people try a gluten-free diet first and then find it hard to get a clear diagnosis. If you suspect coeliac disease, speak to a doctor before changing your diet. If gluten makes you very unwell, a doctor can advise on the safest way to be tested.

myth: You need to take a break from the pill every few years to let your body recover.
fact: There is no health benefit to taking a break from the contraceptive pill. If it suits you and there are no medical reasons to stop, you can keep taking it, with regular check-ups, and stopping risks an unplanned pregnancy.
explanation: Health professionals review blood pressure, weight and other risk factors over time, and may suggest switching methods as you get older or if your health changes. Fertility returns quickly after stopping, so a break is not needed to 'reset' the body.

myth: You only get breast cancer if it runs in your family.
fact: Most people diagnosed with breast cancer do not have a strong family history of it. Age is the biggest risk factor.
explanation: Inherited gene changes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 account for a small proportion of cases. Being breast aware and attending screening when invited is important for everyone.

myth: You only need cancer screening if you have symptoms.
fact: Screening is for people without symptoms. Its purpose is to find cancer early, or changes that could become cancer, before they cause problems, when treatment is more likely to work.
explanation: If you do have symptoms, such as a lump, bleeding or a change in bowel habit, do not wait for a screening invitation; see a doctor. Screening programmes for bowel, breast and cervical cancer vary by country and age, so check what you are eligible for.

myth: You only need to use asthma medicine when you're having symptoms.
fact: Many people with asthma are prescribed a preventer inhaler to use every day, even when they feel well, to reduce airway inflammation and prevent attacks. Relying only on a reliever inhaler is linked to a higher risk of severe attacks.
explanation: Because symptoms come and go, it is easy to skip daily treatment when you feel fine. Treatment approaches vary, and some people are prescribed a combined inhaler used both daily and for symptoms. An asthma action plan from your doctor or nurse explains what to take and when.

myth: You should always rinse your mouth with water after brushing.
fact: Dental advice in the UK and elsewhere is to spit out toothpaste after brushing rather than rinsing, so the fluoride stays on the teeth longer.
explanation: Rinsing is not harmful, but it washes away fluoride that helps prevent decay. Using mouthwash at a different time from brushing is also suggested.

myth: You should avoid the dentist, X-rays and dental injections while pregnant.
fact: Preventive, diagnostic and restorative dental treatment, including dental X-rays and local anaesthetic, is safe at any point in pregnancy. Dental organisations and obstetricians agree that pregnant people should keep up dental care.
explanation: Pregnancy hormones can make gums more prone to inflammation and bleeding, so check-ups are especially useful. Untreated tooth infections can be harmful. Tell your dentist you are pregnant so they can plan treatment; in the UK, NHS dental care is free during pregnancy and for a year after.

myth: You should bundle up in blankets to sweat out a fever.
fact: Piling on blankets does not cure an infection and can push body temperature higher and cause dehydration. Wearing light clothing, staying in a comfortable room and drinking fluids is the usual advice.
explanation: Sweating often happens as a fever breaks, so people assume sweating caused the recovery. Over-wrapping is a particular concern for babies and young children. Seek medical help for a very young baby with a temperature, or if a fever comes with a rash that does not fade, breathing difficulty or confusion.

myth: You should cool a burn under cool running water for 20 minutes.
fact: Cooling a burn with cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes, as soon as possible after the injury, is the recommended first aid in NHS guidance. It reduces pain, swelling and the depth of the burn.
explanation: Twenty minutes can feel like a long time, so many people stop after a few seconds. Remove clothing and jewellery near the burn unless it is stuck to the skin. Keep the person warm while cooling the burn, especially small children, to avoid hypothermia. Do not use ice, iced water or creams, as extreme cold can damage the skin further.

myth: You should hold someone down during a seizure to stop them hurting themselves.
fact: Do not restrain someone having a seizure. Instead, move dangerous objects away, cushion their head, loosen anything tight around the neck, time the seizure, and once it stops place them on their side.
explanation: Holding someone down can cause injuries to them or to you, and it will not stop the seizure. Call emergency services if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, if one seizure follows another, if the person is injured, or if it is their first seizure.

myth: You should pop the blisters from a burn so it heals faster.
fact: Burn blisters should be left alone. The blister protects the damaged skin underneath, and bursting it increases the risk of infection.
explanation: Keep the area clean and covered with a non-stick dressing. If a blister bursts on its own, gently clean it and cover it. Signs of infection, such as increasing pain, redness, swelling, pus or a high temperature, need medical attention.

sources.label: American Academy of Dermatology — How to treat a first-degree, minor burn

myth: You should sponge a feverish child with cold water or put them in a cold bath to bring the temperature down.
fact: Health services advise not to sponge a child with cold water or give a cold bath to reduce a fever. It can make them shiver and feel worse, and it does not treat the cause.
explanation: A fever is the body's normal response to infection. Keep the child comfortable in light clothing, offer plenty of fluids and, if they are distressed, give a suitable dose of children's paracetamol or ibuprofen. Never use alcohol rubs. Seek urgent help for a baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or more, or for signs such as a rash that does not fade, floppiness or difficulty breathing.

myth: You should squeeze or pop a stye to make it go away faster.
fact: You should not try to burst a stye, as this can spread the infection. Most styes get better on their own within a few weeks; holding a clean warm compress against the eye for a few minutes several times a day can help.
explanation: Avoid eye make-up and contact lenses until it has healed. See a GP if a stye does not improve within a few weeks, and get urgent advice if the swelling spreads, the whole eyelid is red and swollen, or vision is affected. Rubbing a gold ring on a stye, a traditional remedy, has no proven effect.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — What is a stye?

myth: You should stop eating fish when you're pregnant because of mercury.
fact: Fish is a good source of protein and nutrients that help the baby develop, and eating fish in pregnancy is recommended. Only certain fish are limited: avoid shark, swordfish and marlin, and limit oily fish and tuna to the amounts your health service advises.
explanation: The concern about mercury applies to large predatory fish, not to fish in general. UK advice, for example, is up to two portions of oily fish a week and to avoid raw shellfish. Cooked fish such as salmon, cod and sardines are good choices.

sources.label: NHS — Foods to avoid in pregnancy
NHS — Have a healthy diet in pregnancy

myth: You should stop exercising when you're pregnant.
fact: For most people with a healthy pregnancy, staying active is safe and beneficial. Guidelines suggest around 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.
explanation: Exercise in pregnancy can help with mood, sleep and weight gain, and reduce the risk of some complications. Avoid contact sports and activities with a high risk of falling, and check with your midwife or doctor if you have a complication.

myth: You should wait to see if a severe allergic reaction gets worse before using an adrenaline pen.
fact: If anaphylaxis is suspected, the adrenaline auto-injector should be used straight away and emergency services called. If there is no improvement after about 5 minutes, a second auto-injector can be given if available.
explanation: Anaphylaxis can get worse very quickly, and adrenaline works best when given early. Using it when it turns out not to be needed is much less risky than delaying it. Everyone prescribed an auto-injector, and those close to them, should learn how to use it and carry two at all times.

myth: You should wake a child who is having a night terror.
fact: During a night terror, health services advise staying calm and waiting for it to pass, and not trying to wake the person. They may not recognise you and can become more upset; only intervene to stop them hurting themselves.
explanation: Night terrors are most common in children aged 3 to 8 and are usually outgrown. Children rarely remember them. If they happen at the same time every night, gently waking the child about 15 minutes beforehand for a couple of weeks can sometimes break the pattern.

myth: You should wash raw chicken before cooking it to get rid of germs.
fact: Washing raw chicken or other meat does not remove harmful bacteria, and splashing water can spread bacteria such as Campylobacter and Salmonella around the sink, worktops and nearby foods. Thorough cooking is what kills them.
explanation: Cook chicken until it is steaming hot throughout with no pink meat and the juices run clear. Wash hands, chopping boards and utensils after handling raw meat, and keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat foods.

myth: You shouldn't eat protein and carbohydrates together because your stomach can't digest them at the same time.
fact: The digestive system is built to handle mixed meals. Different enzymes for protein, fat and carbohydrate work at the same time, and most natural foods, such as beans, milk and grains, contain all three anyway.
explanation: 'Food combining' diets, such as the Hay diet, may help some people lose weight simply because they restrict what and how much people eat. There is no evidence that separating food groups improves digestion or health.

sources.label: NIDDK — Your digestive system & how it works

myth: You shouldn't exercise or swim during your period.
fact: It is safe to exercise and swim during a period. Physical activity may even help ease period pain for some people.
explanation: Tampons or menstrual cups can be used for swimming. Rest is fine too if you feel unwell; listen to your body.

myth: You would know if you had high blood pressure because you'd feel it.
fact: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, which is why it is called a 'silent killer'. The only way to know is to have it measured.
explanation: Many people believe headaches, nosebleeds or feeling flushed signal high blood pressure, but these are not reliable signs. Untreated high blood pressure raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease. Adults are advised to have their blood pressure checked regularly, often at least every five years over 40 in the UK, or more often if at risk.

myth: You'd definitely know if you had type 2 diabetes, because you'd feel ill.
fact: Many people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms for years, or have mild ones such as tiredness that they do not link to diabetes. It is often found through a routine blood test.
explanation: Symptoms, when they appear, include thirst, passing urine often, blurred vision, slow-healing cuts and frequent infections. High blood sugar can damage the body even without symptoms, so people at higher risk should ask about testing.

sources.label: NIDDK — Symptoms and causes of diabetes

myth: You'd know if you had osteoporosis because your bones would hurt.
fact: Osteoporosis usually causes no symptoms until a bone breaks, often after a minor fall or bump. Many people only find out they have it after a fracture.
explanation: Common fracture sites are the wrist, hip and spine; spinal fractures can cause back pain, loss of height or a stooped posture. If you have risk factors, such as early menopause, long-term steroid tablets, a previous low-impact fracture or a family history of hip fracture, ask a GP whether a bone density scan is needed.

myth: You'd notice if you had glaucoma.
fact: The most common type of glaucoma develops slowly and often causes no symptoms until vision is lost, which cannot be restored.
explanation: Regular eye tests can detect glaucoma early, when treatment can prevent further loss. Risk is higher with age, family history and certain ethnic backgrounds. Sudden eye pain with blurred vision needs emergency care.

myth: You're too old to start exercising.
fact: It is never too late to benefit from physical activity. Older adults who become active improve strength, balance, mood and independence, and lower their risk of falls.
explanation: Guidelines for older adults include balance and strength activities to prevent falls. People with health conditions can start gently and ask a health professional what is suitable.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Young children shouldn't use fluoride toothpaste until they're about 6.
fact: Health services recommend brushing a child's teeth with fluoride toothpaste as soon as the first tooth appears. Children under 3 need only a smear of toothpaste, and children aged 3 to 6 a pea-sized amount.
explanation: Fluoride strengthens enamel and is one of the most effective ways to prevent tooth decay in children. Using the right small amount and encouraging children to spit out rather than swallow keeps it safe. Supervise brushing until about age 7.

sources.label: NHS — Taking care of children's teeth

myth: Your BMI tells you exactly whether you are healthy or not.
fact: Body mass index (BMI) is a quick screening tool based on height and weight. It is useful across populations but cannot tell the difference between muscle and fat or show where fat is stored, so it does not give a full picture of an individual's health.
explanation: Very muscular people can have a high BMI without excess fat, and some people with a 'healthy' BMI carry harmful fat around their middle. BMI thresholds can also differ by ethnic background; for example, people of South Asian, Chinese, Black African or Caribbean background may have higher risk at lower BMI. Doctors combine BMI with waist size, blood pressure, blood tests and other factors.

sources.label: NHS — Calculate your body mass index (BMI) for adults

myth: Your brain switches off while you sleep.
fact: The brain stays very active during sleep, cycling through stages that are important for memory, learning and clearing waste products.
explanation: Sleep is an active process, not just rest. During REM sleep, brain activity can be similar to being awake. This is one reason sleep is so important for thinking and mood.

myth: Your metabolism crashes after 30, which is why everyone gains weight in middle age.
fact: A large study of thousands of people found that, once body size is taken into account, metabolic rate stays fairly stable from about age 20 to 60 and only slowly declines after that. Middle-age weight gain is mostly linked to eating more than the body uses, moving less and losing muscle.
explanation: Life changes in your 30s and 40s, such as desk jobs, less sport, less sleep and more stress, often explain why weight creeps up. Muscle uses more energy than fat, so keeping active and doing strength exercises helps. Blaming a 'broken metabolism' can make weight feel out of your control when everyday habits still make a difference.

sources.label: Harvard Health Publishing — The truth about metabolism

myth: Zinc lozenges cure the common cold.
fact: Zinc does not cure colds. Some studies suggest zinc lozenges or syrups started soon after symptoms begin may shorten a cold slightly, but results vary and side effects such as a bad taste and nausea are common.
explanation: Zinc plays a role in immune function, which makes it a popular cold remedy. Zinc nasal sprays have been linked to permanent loss of smell and should be avoided. Long-term high-dose zinc can cause copper deficiency.
